title: Lieutenant governor candidate’s parents say he owes them $275K in unpaid farm rent: report
text:
BLACK HAWK COUNTY, Iowa (Gray News) - The parents of a Republican lieutenant governor candidate in Iowa are reportedly claiming that he owes them hundreds of thousands of dollars.
KCCI reports that court documents filed in Black Hawk County show Derek Wulf’s parents, Duane and Jackie Wulf, say their son owes them around $275,000 in unpaid farmland rent since 2024.
The petition was reportedly filed as the parents try to protect their assets as a bank seeks to foreclose on Derek Wulf’s other unpaid debts.
Matt Craft, the attorney representing Derek Wulf’s parents, said the legal petition was filed just weeks before the election because of an Oct. 20 filing deadline.
“The judge in Derek’s foreclosure case required anyone who claimed ownership or a lien on Derek’s farm assets to speak now or forever hold their peace if they claim any ownership or interest in those seized assets,” the attorney said in a statement.
Craft added that the family has been working to privately resolve this issue for a long time.
“They are very private individuals and are embarrassed at the mess this has caused many good people in a very public way,” the attorney’s statement continued.
The Zach Lahn for governor campaign was said to not have immediately responded to requests for comment regarding his running mate’s situation.

title: Van Buren Moves On! Four More County Soccer Teams Play Saturday
text:
The County Scoreboard: Van Buren Advances, XC Regionals and Four Playoff Games Saturday
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships are underway, and we've already had a little bit of everything here in the County.
Van Buren's boys are moving on after a 3-1 victory over Schenck on Friday, while Katahdin saw its season come to an end in a close 2-1 loss to Lee Academy.
And we're just getting started.
Four more County soccer teams are scheduled for playoff games Saturday, including a pair of home matchups for Caribou's boys and Fort Kent's girls.
Meanwhile, County cross country runners are headed to Belfast for the Northern Maine Regional Championships, with state championship berths on the line.
Van Buren Moves On With Win Over Schenck
The seventh-seeded Van Buren Crusaders made the most of their home-field advantage Friday, defeating No. 10 Schenck 3-1 in the eight-person boys preliminary round.
Alex Bebout, Dom Burgess and Gavin Cormier each scored for Van Buren.
Marcus Hutchins scored the lone goal for the Wolverines.
The victory sends the Crusaders into the regional quarterfinals, where they'll face third-seeded Calais.
It's another opportunity for Van Buren to keep its season going, although the Crusaders will have a tougher test waiting in the next round.
Katahdin's Season Ends in Close Loss to Lee Academy
Sixth-seeded Katahdin came up just short Friday, falling 2-1 to No. 11 Lee Academy in another eight-person boys preliminary matchup.
Conor Schmidt scored the Cougars' lone goal, while goalkeeper Gage Phillips finished with seven saves.
Lee Academy received goals from Alberto Perez and Martin Tapiador, while Lance Haskell made eight saves.
It was a tough way for Katahdin's season to end, especially after the Cougars put together several strong performances down the stretch.
Schmidt had been one of the County's most productive scorers throughout the season, and Phillips had delivered some impressive performances in net.
The Cougars' tournament run ends in the preliminary round, while Lee Academy advances.
Saturday Brings Four More County Soccer Playoff Games
There's no shortage of soccer on Saturday's schedule, with four County teams looking to keep their seasons alive.
Eight-Person Boys: Houlton Travels to Penquis
Ninth-seeded Houlton heads to eighth-seeded Penquis for a 2 p.m. preliminary matchup.
The Shires will be looking to pick up a road victory and move into the quarterfinal round.
Class B Boys: Caribou Hosts Medomak Valley
Eighth-seeded Caribou will have home-field advantage Saturday when the Vikings welcome No. 9 Medomak Valley for a 2 p.m. preliminary game.
The Vikings finished the regular season with some strong results, including a pair of shutout victories over Hermon.
Now Caribou gets the opportunity to carry that momentum into tournament play.
Class C Girls: Fort Kent Welcomes MCI
Top-seeded Fort Kent begins its postseason Saturday afternoon, hosting eighth-seeded Maine Central Institute at 2 p.m. in a Class C North quarterfinal.
The Lady Warriors enter the tournament as the No. 1 seed, putting them in a strong position as the regional playoffs begin.
Eight-Person Girls: Katahdin Heads to Penquis
Ninth-seeded Katahdin travels to eighth-seeded Penquis for a noon preliminary matchup.
The Lady Cougars will be looking to extend their season with a road victory.
County Runners Head to Belfast for Regional Championships
Soccer isn't the only postseason action happening Saturday.
The Northern Maine Regional Cross Country Championships are being held in Belfast, with County runners competing for the opportunity to advance to next weekend's state championships.
The top seven teams and top 30 individual finishers qualify for states.
County programs are coming off an outstanding performance at last weekend's PVC Championships, where Houlton/GHCA's boys, Presque Isle's girls and Caribou's boys all captured team titles.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves also earned individual PVC championships.
Caribou's Thomas Beckum was named PVC Girls Coach of the Year, while Presque Isle's Dylan Marrero earned Boys Coach of the Year honors.
Saturday brings another opportunity for those runners and their teammates to prove themselves against the rest of Northern Maine.

title: NPR radio host Noah Adams dies at 84
text:
NPR radio host Noah Adams dies at 84
NPR radio host Noah Adams dies at 84
Noah Adams, a longtime host of NPR’s “All Things Considered” program, has died at his home in Yellow Springs, Ohio.
He was 84.
Video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
Adams had a benign brain tumor removed eight years ago, but was still experiencing complications in his later years, according to his wife, Neenah Ellis.
The native of Kentucky was always proud of his simple, Appalachian roots and relied on his blue-collar upbringing as he paved a successful career in journalism and writing.
His first radio job was at the University of Kentucky’s public radio station, WBKY (now WUKY), in Lexington.
In 1975, he started his work with NPR as a production assistant on “All Things Considered," which first hit the airwaves in 1971. By 1982, Adams was a co-host on the show.
Over the years, he covered hard-news topics and won an award from the Overseas Press Club of America in 1994 for work he did in Serbia on the roots of the country’s national extremism.
According to The New York Times, Adams was on the air from morning until after dark on Sept. 11, 2001, updating millions of listeners on the terrorist attacks that shook the nation and shocked the world.
“He is the most genuine, uncontrived voice in broadcasting,” a former colleague, Susan Stamberg, said in 1992.
His numerous written works include Saint Croix Notes: "River Mornings, Radio Nights," "Noah Adams on 'All Things Considered': A Radio Journal," "Piano Lessons: Music, Love, and True Adventures," "Far Appalachia: Following the New River North," and "The Flyers: In Search of Wilbur and Orville Wright."
Adams was known as a private and shy person away from work. He was divorced twice and then married Ellis in 1987.
He is survived by his wife and a brother.

title: Bruins rally in third, stretch unbeaten streak to eight
text:
BOSTON — David Pastrnak and James Hagens scored in a 40-second span in the third period, and the Boston Bruins extended their points streak to eight games with a 6-4 victory over the San Jose Sharks on Saturday night.
Casey Mittelstadt, Marat Khusnutdinov, Fraser Minten and Will Borgen also scored for the Bruins, who have won seven of their last eight. Jeremy Swayman made 21 saves for his seventh victory.
Michael Misa, Kiefer Sherwood, Dmitry Orlov and Will Smith scored for San Jose, and Alex Nedeljkovic made 29 saves. The Sharks had won two in a row.
The game was tied at 2-2 through two periods, with the Sharks responding each time the Bruins took a one-goal lead.
San Jose grabbed its first lead of the game when Orlov fired a one-timer on the power play at 4:03 of the third. It was the third special-teams goal of the game for the Sharks, and Orlov’s second goal of the season.
Pastrnak exited the penalty box and took a feed from J.J. Peterka before firing in a shot from the right circle for his seventh goal of the season at 8:27 of the third. The goal pushed Pastrnak into a tie for third place with Patrice Bergeron on Boston all-time goal-scoring list (427).
Just 40 seconds later, Hagens put in the rebound of an Elias Lindholm shot. Minten then scored a power-play goal with 8:00 remaining to make it 5-3.
Up next
Sharks: Host Buffalo on Tuesday night
Bruins: At Carolina on Tuesday night

title: Damien Jones leads UNE football past Husson
text:
Damien Jones scored four touchdowns to lead the University of New England to a 46-27 win over Husson in a Conference of New England football game Saturday in Bangor.
Jones rushed 13 times for 149 yards and three touchdowns (6, 60 and 27 yards), and caught two passes for 29 yards and a score (30 yards).
Jones scored twice in the first quarter to give the Nor’easters (2-5, 2-2 CNE) a 13-0 lead. They pushed it to 19-0 on a 21-yard pass from Gavin Martin to Dante Howard in the second quarter, but Husson (2-4, 2-2) got on the board with a pass from Brody Gibson to Jacob Lenz. Jones scored on a 60-yard run with 1:42 left in the first half.
Gibson completed 35 of 55 passes for 327 yards and four touchdowns.
HAMILTON 28, COLBY 14: Matthew Kearns caught 11 passes for 110 yards and two touchdowns to lead the Continentals (2-4) past the Mules (0-6) in a NESCAC game in Clinton, New York.
Hamilton quarterback Luke Kurzum completed 26 of 32 passes for 224 yards and three touchdowns.
Colby’s Jagger Matera was 19 of 30 passing for 155 yards and a touchdown, and also rushed for a touchdown.
MIDDLEBURY 31, BATES 13: Aidan Moss threw a pair of touchdown passes in the second quarter as the Panthers (3-3) took a 17-0 lead on their way to a win over the Bobcats (0-6) in Lewiston.
Yaseen Mousa added a 25-yard field goal, Beckett Long scored on a 1-yard run, and Connor McClellan had a 50-yard TD run.
Connor Hennessey of Bates threw a 43-yard touchdown pass to Jeff Vidou in the third quarter, and Jack Gilmore had an 8-yard scoring pass to Ryan Gleason in the fourth quarter.
TRINITY 10, BOWDOIN 3: Jaxon Carroll threw a 10-yard touchdown pass to Darison Hooper and Tyler Beliveau kicked a 20-yard field goal to lead the Bantams (6-0) past the Polar Bears (0-6) in Hartford, Connecticut.
Caden Perry kicked a 38-yard field goal for Bowdoin.

title: Max Andreev leads Mariners past Railers
text:
Max Andreev scored twice and the Maine Mariners won their home opener, beating the Worcester Railers 3-0 in an ECHL game on Saturday at Cross Insurance Arena in Portland.
Andreev gave Maine the lead 2:02 into the contest with an assist from Josh Bloom. He scored again from Bloom and Michael Underwood in the third.
Robert Cronin scored in the second period for the Mariners, with assists from Antonio Venuto and Ryan Francis.
Luke Cavallin made 15 saves for Maine, while Parker Gahagen stopped 21 shots for Worcester.
Maine host Worcester again at 3 p.m. Sunday at Cross Insurance Arena.

title: Six Flags says it will install seat belts on Georgia roller coaster after rider’s death
text:
(AP) - The chief executive of Six Flags says the company will install seat belts on the Georgia roller coaster from which a rider fell to his death earlier this month. The company’s rides with similar restraints will also get the safety upgrade.
The theme park operator announced the extra safeguard less than two weeks after 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta died after being ejected from his seat on the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia.
“We are reinforcing safety precautions at our parks and taking additional measures, including adding seat belts on Goliath and other coasters with a similar restraint,” John Reilly, president and CEO of Six Flags Entertainment Corporation, said in a statement Friday.
Goliath remains shut down while state and local officials investigate the Oct. 12 death.
Reilly didn’t specify which other Six Flags coasters will get seat belts. But it has temporarily closed eight additional roller coasters at five other parks in the U.S. and Canada. Those rides all share the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system.
Six Flags hasn’t said when those coasters are expected to reopen. Reilly’s statement said Six Flags has enlisted independent engineers and inspectors to review safety procedures for all rides at its theme parks.
Investigators haven’t said what went wrong on the Georgia coaster. Witnesses said they saw Kariem rise up out of his seat and fall headfirst back into the cart before being ejected. Some people who rode Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints.
All nine of the Six Flags coasters taken offline were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard. They also feature similar clamshell restraints that sit at the top of a vertical bar between each rider’s knees. The bar locks a padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.
The U.S. patent granted to Bolliger & Mabillard for the restraint system in 2001 says it’s designed to make each rider feel “that he is seated on a flying carpet or that he is at the controls of a kind of flying scooter, while still guaranteeing optimum security.”
Following the death in Georgia, non-Six Flags theme parks SeaWorld Orlando in Florida and La Ronde in Montreal, Canada, also temporarily closed one roller coaster apiece that use clamshell restraints.
SeaWorld reopened its Mako coaster Tuesday after it had been offline for a week. The Associated Press emailed the company Saturday asking if seat belts or other safety upgrades were planned for the coaster.
The AP also emailed a spokesperson for La Ronde seeking an update on its shuttered coaster.
In addition to Goliath in Georgia, eight coasters remain closed at Six Flags parks in Gurnee, Illinois; Jackson Township, New Jersey; Charlotte, North Carolina; Mason, Ohio; and Vaughan, Ontario.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia.

title: Susan Collins tailgates and Troy Jackson rallies with 10 days left until Election Day
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson spent the second Saturday before Election Day in very different settings.
Collins sipped hard seltzer while working the crowd at the University of Maine’s homecoming tailgate in Orono. Jackson started his day at a union canvass launch in Westbrook, then went on to events in Bridgton, Windham and Oxford County.
Here are four moments from the trail.
Collins: Selfies and seltzer
In Orono, Collins drew a crowd everywhere she went for more than two hours, from UMaine alumni who graduated decades ago to current students. She asked nearly all of them the same three questions: their name, what they studied at UMaine and where they’re from.
Hundreds took pictures with her. Almost none asked about her votes or the campaign. A spokesperson initially said Collins might be available for questions but returned later to say she would not have time to take them.
The question the senator heard most was whether she wanted a beer. At one point, a group of tailgaters handed her a Wild Maine blueberry hard seltzer, which she opened almost right away. After a picture with the group, she poured it into a red Solo cup and carried it with her through the crowd.
Former Gov. Paul LePage, who is running against Democrat Matt Dunlap in the 2nd Congressional District, joined Collins at one point. So did Republican Leo Kenney, who is in his second consecutive race with state Sen. Mike Tipping, D-Orono.
Jackson: ‘I’m starting to wonder if I should vote for myself’
Jackson, the former Maine Senate president from Allagash, held his Westbrook event with the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades and its president, Jimmy Williams. Jackson was a member of that union, and it was one of two that paid him as a consultant as he ran for governor between this year and last.
Republican outside groups have booked about $104 million in ads backing Collins since Jackson replaced Graham Platner as the nominee in July to $81 million from Democrats, according to AdImpact data. Jackson made a joke out of the barrage.
“I had to quit watching TV, not because I don’t like the ads or anything like that, but I’m starting to wonder if I should vote for myself,” he said.
He said the coordinated Democratic campaign had knocked on 125,000 doors as of Friday night, and that door-knocking is how his side plans to make up the difference.
Joke photos
The students were harder to read than the older people around the Collins tailgate. Many who posed with the senator said afterward that they would not vote for her.
“I took a picture with her to send to my dad as a joke. I never plan on voting for Susan Collins,” one student said after a photo with the senator and his friends.
After Collins walked away, one group of three students mockingly repeated talking points from both campaigns’ ads. One was that she votes in a bipartisan way. The other was that she cast the vote that led to the overturning of Roe v. Wade.
Jackson calls Collins a ‘puppet’ on tariffs
Reporters’ questions to Jackson focused on Friday’s news. President Donald Trump’s administration is lifting tariffs on some Canadian imports, a change meant to help Maine’s blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed industries. The Wall Street Journal reported that the move was meant to help Collins’ reelection bid.
Collins has opposed Trump’s tariffs on Canada while also lobbying for item-by-item relief, including on road salt, pulp and concrete. In a Friday statement, she said she would “continue working directly with [federal] officials to seek additional relief from tariffs.”
In Westbrook, Jackson called the exemptions “so fake” and predicted Trump would reverse them after the election. He said Trump was granting the exemptions “just so he can keep his puppet Susan Collins in Congress.”
“I can’t believe that the most powerful US senator in the world would stand there and say, ‘Well, I got this and this and this off the list,’ instead of the fact that there shouldn’t have been a list,” he said.

Halloween candy sales off to slow start amid high chocolate prices, affordability concerns
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Halloween candy sales off to slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start this year as U.S. consumers grapple with high living costs and eye-popping chocolate prices.
Related video above: Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm. Nielsen also noted an 11.7% decline in candy sales in mid-September, erasing the preseason gains that Halloween candy enjoyed the previous two years.
Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said high gas prices have worsened Americans’ concerns about affordability, and that is dampening demand for Halloween treats. As of Friday, the average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. was $4.29, up nearly 40% from the prior year.
“I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food,” Costagli said. “Some of the decisions they're making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, 'I notice it's more expensive than last year,' it's, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I've paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’”
Small bags of candy were the only sizes seeing sales growth through mid-October, Costagli noted. Large and extra-large bags were seeing the biggest declines.
U.S. candy prices have been climbing faster than the rate of inflation for several years. As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44% over a five-year period, according to government data. Prices for all food eaten at home rose 22.5% in the same period.
This week, discount grocer Aldi was advertising a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolate bars — including Milky Way, Twix and Snickers — for $19.87. That is almost the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece variety pack five years ago.
Cocoa prices are the main culprit. Global cocoa prices reached a record high of $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 because of poor weather in West Africa — which supplies 70% of the world’s chocolate — and speculative trading in the cocoa futures market, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Cocoa prices had been falling steadily since then and hit $3,241 per metric ton in March. But they began climbing again in the spring as the war in Iran disrupted Africa’s fertilizer supplies. The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to hurt production, with hot, dry conditions expected through February.
But Costagli noted that even in cases where prices are lower than last year, consumer demand is muted. The average price of nonchocolate Halloween candies, like gummies and lollipops, was $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, which was about 3% lower than last year, according to Nielsen data. But that did not lead to a bump in sales.
Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser for the market research company Circana, said one way U.S. consumers have been handling higher grocery prices is by making smaller and more frequent trips to the supermarket and buying products right before they intend to use them. That makes her wonder if shoppers are waiting until closer to Halloween to buy candy this year.
“People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general,” she said. “I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed.”
The National Confectioners Association, a trade group that represents candy makers like Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic about Halloween sales.
“We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong,” the group said Friday in a statement.

title: Some interesting insects to look for before winter
text:
With temperatures rapidly dropping, daylight hours getting shorter and impending winter conditions approaching, I wanted to use this column to point out a few animals that won’t be around much longer: some insects.
These ectothermic (relying on external sources of heat) invertebrates don’t fare too well in freezing temperatures, but there are a few pretty interesting ones to be on the lookout for before this window closes.
First up, I should mention some of the most commonly encountered, abundant and recognizable insects. The non-native Asian lady beetle is a red and black beetle; these have been around all summer, but tend to have a spike in detections in the fall as they look for warm places to spend the winter. Cold nights trigger these movements, and they are especially fond of entering human dwellings for a warmer reprieve.
The other insect you’ll find sneaking inside is the western conifer seed bug, often mistaken for a “stinkbug” because of the pungent smell it produces after being disturbed. The western conifer seed bugs are a reddish brown color and are in the family Coreidae, the “leaf-footed bugs” that have flat leaf-like sections on their hind legs. Note also that they are not a “beetle” in the order Coleoptera (like the Asian lady beetle) because they don’t have the hardened wing casings that beetles uniquely do.
Speaking of things with cool wings, most of our Lepidoptera, the scaly-winged insects, better known as butterflies and moths, are soon to be gone. During these last warm days, you may see butterflies like clouded sulphur (mostly yellow) and American ladies (mostly orange with spots) flying around. We do have some November records of monarchs in Maine, but flowers will be hard to come by for any pollinators needing sustenance at that point.
Another lepidopteran to look for has one of my favorite names in the animal kingdom: Bruce spanworm. This native moth has an interesting approach to successful reproduction — it waits until there aren’t many threats around. As it gets cold in November, and very few predators of moths are around (bats have migrated or begun hibernating), the adult males will take advantage of a warm night to have large flights in search of females. The females, which are actually flightless, wait at the tips of a host tree limb. They attract males with a seductive pheromone. Unfortunately, there is also a non-native species of moth that does the same thing, the winter moth. These are very similar species, both in the genus Operophtera, and cannot be visually distinguished. You’d need to dissect them to actually tell them apart.
Not an insect, but an arachnid worth mentioning is the dreaded eastern black-legged tick. These blood suckers are paradoxically one animal you don’t want to see … unless it’s on you, and then you do before it digs into your skin. Adults are especially active in fall with their biggest spike in activity in October, so despite many invertebrates being inactive, you should keep doing tick checks after spending time outdoors.
The last plug I have to make, which is also a good way to avoid getting ticks, is to leave your leaves on the ground. Those leaves will provide important nutrients for the soil and shelter for many beloved animals, from wood frogs to woolly bear caterpillars (aka Isabella tiger moths). So drop the rake and kick your feet up, or grab your binoculars and spend that time outside looking for late butterflies and migrating birds. The snow will be here soon (northern Maine has already seen flurries), so enjoy the fall days and help your backyard wildlife at the same time.
Have you got a nature or wildlife question of your own? It doesn’t have to be about birds! Email questions to [email protected] and visit www.maineaudubon.org to learn more about birding, native plants, and programs and events focusing on Maine wildlife and habitat. Maine Audubon Staff Naturalist Doug Hitchcox and other naturalists lead free bird walks on Thursday mornings starting at 7 am, at Maine Audubon’s Gilsland Farm Audubon Sanctuary in Falmouth.

title: High schools Saturday: Falmouth boys soccer upsets Portland
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Conor Kirkham scored the eventual winning goal 46 seconds into the second half, lifting 11th-seeded Falmouth Navigators past sixth-seeded Portland, 3-1, in a Class A South preliminary-round game on Saturday in Portland.
Falmouth (5-8-2) advances to face No. 3 Gorham in the quarterfinals on Tuesday.
The Navigators took a 1-0 lead early in the first half when Penn Giard headed in a pass from Kian Long. Kirkham made it 2-0 when he gathered a ball in the box and booted it inside the far post.
Portland (8-5-2) pulled within one when Feliciano Logapo scored on a free kick, but Falmouth got an own goal to seal it.
Wyatt Bennett made fives saves for Falmouth, while Mateo Pulaski stopped two shots for Portland.
GIRLS SOCCER
SKOWHEGAN 4, LAWRENCE 0: Vivian Hart’s hat trick propelled the sixth-seeded River Hawks (13-1-1) past the No. 11 Bulldogs (3-9-3) in a Class B North preliminary-round game in Skowhegan.
Lydia Herrick also scored and added an assist. Mae Dubois, Addie Bubier and Charlotte Libby each recorded an assist. Chloe Cyr stopped two shots for the shutout.
Riley Soucy made 23 saves for Lawrence.
Skowhegan will face third-seeded Presque Isle (9-3-2) in the quarterfinals.
THORNTON ACADEMY 3, GORHAM 1: The ninth-ranked Trojans (7-6-2) scored twice in the first half and beat the No. 8 Rams (7-6-2) in a Class A South preliminary-round game in Gorham.
Thornton advances to face No. 1 Scarborough in the quarterfinals on Tuesday.
Goals by Julia Collins and Olivia Martin gave the Trojans a 2-0 lead. Neve Hanley pulled Gorham with one in the second half, but Malia Collins added an insurance goal for Thornton.
FOOTBALL
CAPE ELIZABETH 42, HOULTON 6: Rosco Hampton passed for three touchdowns and ran for another as the Capers (6-2) ended their regular season with a win over the Shiretowners (1-7) in an eight-man Large School game in Cape Elizabeth.
Hampton connected with River Duffy (60 yards), Logan Knightly (18 yards) and Sam Hews (26 yards). Hampton’s 22-yard touchdown run late in the second quarter gave the Capers a 30-6 halftime lead.
Will Gray (2 yards) and Henry Boucher (4 yards) each adding a rushing TD.
Connor Lilley scored on a 2-yard run for Houlton.
YORK 21, HAMPDEN ACADEMY 7: Wyatt Hebert threw two long touchdown passes as the Wildcats (3-5) won for the third time in their last four games, beating the Broncos (0-8) in Hampden.
York grabbed a 14-0 lead in the first quarter. Hebert connected with Jack Hilbourne for a 46-yard scoring play, and Colin McCann added a 17-yard TD run.
Hampden cut into its deficit in the second quarter on a 7-yard run by Dresden Sherwood, then was driving for a potential tying touchdown early in the third before York’s defense held. Moments later, Asher Kuhn beat double-coverage to grab a pass from Hebert for a 61-yard touchdown.

title: 'Create, create, create': Artist turns vision loss into inspiration
text:
Artist 'Benny Blindspots' turns vision loss into inspiration
Benny "Blindspots" Schwartz, a Pennsylvania-based artist, has turned his vision loss into a source of inspiration, creating art that is now displayed in galleries and corporate spaces across North America.
Schwartz was diagnosed in 2014 with neuromyelitis optica, a rare autoimmune disorder that affects the optic nerve.
"It did leave me with lasting blind spots in the center of each visual field of my eye," Schwartz said. "And it kind of comes out as, like I would say, it's white lights that are missing parts of the picture."
After his diagnosis, Schwartz spent five years struggling to come to terms with his condition.
"I had always been thinking God owed me vision, you know, but that's not true," he said. "And perhaps only through this illness and this kind of struggle and this blindness, am I going to reach my potential."
A friend and fellow artist encouraged Schwartz to embrace his creativity.
"Create, create, create," Schwartz recalled his friend saying. "He offered to put me in a pop-up art show if I started to try to paint the blurriness that I was seeing."
Schwartz began painting, finding a sense of control and purpose through his art.
"I found myself making lines and shapes and then finding the images, bringing them out," he said. "All of a sudden, I was back in control of my visual field for a little bit, you know, for just those moments of doing the art."
His studio is now filled with pieces from his early brushstrokes to his current works, many of which are displayed in galleries and corporate spaces, including State Street and JP Morgan Chase. These opportunities were made possible through ArtLifting, a company that markets and advocates for artists with disabilities.
"It's hard to be an artist. It's even harder to be an artist who maybe has a disability that limits the way that they can participate or show up in the art world or in the corporate art market," said Michael Korcek, marketing director with ArtLifting. "So ArtLifting exists to knock down those doors, knock down those barriers for these artists."
ArtLifting represents 235 artists across North America, including Schwartz.
"He really kind of answers the question, what does an artist make with vision loss, not despite it," Korcek said. "He started exploring art as an avenue for healing, connection, and really found his voice."
Schwartz expressed gratitude for the platform ArtLifting provides.
"They've lifted each of those artists up and given them a platform to, you know, not only express themselves, inspire others, and make an income, which is free. You know, that's a home run," he said.
His art is also featured in TAG in Boston.
To reach out to Benny Blindspots to inquire about his art, visit his website.

title: More tribal leaders step into Maine’s fraught Senate race
text:
Amid a bruising and expensive knock-down-drag-out U.S. Senate race in Maine, Wabanaki leaders are stepping into the fray. It hasn’t been entirely smooth.
Chief William Nicholas Sr., of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Motahkomikuk (Indian Township), told the Portland Press Herald on Friday that he’s endorsing the five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
He joins Chief Amkuwiposohehs “Pos” Bassett of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik (Pleasant Point), who announced his support for Collins last week in what seems to be a first for the senator. Democrat Troy Jackson, Collins’ opponent, picked up his first tribal endorsement in the Senate race from the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians chief and tribal council on Monday.
Jackson was endorsed by the Mi’kmaq Nation when he ran in the Democratic primary for governor this spring.
Maliseet Chief Clarissa Sabattis noted Jackson’s long-standing commitment to tribal sovereignty in a statement announcing her endorsement.
“From championing clean drinking water initiatives to his role in creating the commission to reexamine the 1980 Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, Troy has consistently proven that he listens to indigenous voices and stands with the Wabanaki people,” she said.
Nicholas praised Collins’ directing of federal dollars to his community and her responsiveness.
“Every time we’ve had an issue in our community and she’s been called upon, she’s personally stepped up,” Nicholas said.
He rattled off a list of projects — 335 heat pumps, 70 hybrid hot water heaters, 230 doors and exterior and storm doors and at least 10 single-family homes — that Collins has helped fund. He was touched by the senator’s visit to the reservation this summer.
“It’s hard to turn away from an ally and a friend who has done so much for this community,” Nicholas said.
As both sides fire volleys of nasty accusations at one another, Nicholas felt compelled to cut through the noise.
“People are going to base their information on what they’re seeing,” he said. “But you know, every time somebody turns on a heat pump, somebody helped us with that.”
Collins said in a statement Friday afternoon that she was honored by the endorsement and looks forward to continuing to work with the tribe.
Although Collins has not championed tribal sovereignty in the way some Wabanaki leaders would hope, Nicholas is backing Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree to address the issue at the state level.
Nicholas was careful to state that he personally is endorsing Collins as tribal chief — but that he does not speak for the entire community, which remains divided.
His counterpart in Sipayik, Bassett, drew criticism when he alone penned an endorsement letter on behalf of the tribe.
After the Collins campaign celebrated what they billed as the endorsement of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Pleasant Point, several tribal members questioned the chief’s authority to make a unilateral endorsement without consulting the tribal council.
“Absent direction by the tribal community or its governing body, the chief does not have the authority to speak for the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik,” tribal member Gail Dana, who narrowly lost the election for chief against Bassett last month, wrote in an opinion column in the Bangor Daily News.
Council member Adam Newell said he was blindsided by the announcement.
At a minimum, Newell said, Bassett should have consulted the council in advance. He voiced his objections to the chief directly and on Facebook, where he sought to distance himself from the divisive race.
“It’s a new thing for tribes to start doing it,” he said, warning “it’s a slippery slope for me.”
The campaign referred questions to Bassett, who did not respond to a request for comment.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Schafir can be reached at rschafir@pressherald.com.

title: WWE legend Ric Flair recovering after being hospitalized for fall, reports say
text:
(Gray News) - WWE legend Ric Flair was hospitalized after falling outside of a Florida restaurant, according to multiple reports.
The 77-year-old retired American professional wrestler, whose real name is Richard Morgan Fliehr, said in an Instagram post Saturday that he spent the night in a Tampa hospital.
“Thank You All For The Messages And Prayers! I Will Get Back To You Each Individually As I Get Stronger,” Flair wrote in a post Saturday. “Thank You To All The Tampa General Hospital Staff And Doctors That Put Up With Me Until 4:30am. I Appreciate You All And Thank You For Everything You Did For Me!”
Flair had fallen outside a Wagamama restaurant in Tampa on Friday, cutting his head and eye, TMZ reported.
The wrestling icon said he’s on the mend.
“I Am Focused On My Healing And Recovery Right Now,” he said, adding, “I Will Be Okay!”
He shared a photo of himself smiling with a patch covering one of his eyes.
Just hours before his fall, Flair had told his fans he had to cancel an appearance at the Washington State Horror Con in Seattle due to a blood clot in his leg.

title: Covering the Co$t: The Necessity and Luxury of Buying a Car
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With affordability a main issue ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, politicians and economists alike are weighing the factors leading to the high cost of living. One often-overlooked piece is the cost of transportation.
Cars, once considered a luxury, are now described as a necessity. Most Americans need a vehicle of some kind to get from point A to point B, at a typical cost of thousands of dollars.
The price of buying a new vehicle continues to rise. Dr. David Bieri, an economist at Virginia Tech, said the average cost is now around $50,000.
“In terms of median income, that’s close to about eight months’ worth of pay,” Bieri said.
Bieri said new car sales remain healthy, but the cost and method of purchasing a vehicle point to a complicated market, with increasing insurance premiums, inflation, and lingering tariffs adding to the mix. He also said “pay as you go” payment plans are becoming more popular: a sometimes dangerous method that could lead some buyers to shop outside their purchasing power.
Bieri said one of the biggest issues is a lack of affordable vehicle options built domestically.
“We don’t really have any domestic low end entry points,” Bieri said.
Total vehicle costs including payments, gas, and maintenance take up anywhere from 10% to 20% or more of Americans’ monthly income, making it one of the most important purchases someone will make.
Bieri said spending, though, is only one half of the affordability puzzle.
“It’s also the problem of wages not growing fast enough for certain segments,” Bieri said, pointing out that a general increase in wages could make a massive dent in the overall affordability crisis.
The last time the federal minimum wage was raised in the U.S. was 2009.

title: At Maine Maritime, the football program’s rebuild continues
text:
CASTINE — Maine Maritime Academy has already given Matt Gagin so much.
“I’ve always really wanted to sail. I’ve crossed the Atlantic five or six times now. I’ve been all over the world,” said Gagin, a junior from Upton, Massachusetts. “I’ve gotten to see things I never would’ve seen without this school.”
There’s one thing Gagin would love to give back to MMA before he graduates: a win in a football game. The Mariners came so close to that goal Saturday at Ritchie Field, falling 17-14 to New England College. It was MMA’s closest game since the school announced the program was coming out of mothballs in 2023.
Close isn’t a win, though, and now the Mariners’ losing streak stands at 43 games.
MMA’s last win came on Oct. 14, 2017, just over nine years ago, when the Mariners prevailed 34-16 against Coast Guard. On its face, the victory drought is misleading. The Mariners did not play from 2020 through 2022, then played one game in 2023 and three in 2024 before resuming a full varsity schedule last season.
Maine Maritime paused the football program in 2020, citing the budget concerns that came with the COVID-19 pandemic. A few years later, alumni spearheaded a fundraising effort that brought in more than $560,000, and football was reinstated.
The Mariners are past the point of moral victories. New England College is like them, a new program just starting out. The Mariners saw the contest Saturday as a winnable game, and left the field with the frustration of a team that let one slip away. Heads down. Shoulders slumped.
An interception inside the Pilgrims 5-yard line squashed one scoring opportunity. A blocked field goal at the end of the first half evaporated another.
The Mariners know they’re improving, and sooner or later that improvement won’t be measured in a good play, or a good drive. It will be quantified with a win.
“They see (the improvement), and know,” said MMA coach Nick Sheehan. “You can see from our reaction, it’s a tough one.”
Sheehan’s sales pitch to recruits is simple. Come build something at one of the finest engineering schools around. Come to a school where graduates routinely step into six-figure jobs right after earning their diploma, and help rebuild a once-proud and thriving football program. Play right away.
That all sounded great to Gagin. Newcastle native Lucas Houghton thought it sounded good, too. He went to Lincoln Academy, a school without a football team, but he remembered the joy he had playing peewee football, and thought rebuilding something sounded fun.
“It was the best sport, because as long as you gave your best effort, you could feel like you accomplished something,” said Houghton, a junior defensive back who led the Mariners with 12 tackles Saturday. “I’ve played all kinds of sports. Soccer, baseball, basketball, whatever. There’s nothing that compares to football.”
Bill Mottola knows what MMA football can be, because he knows what it was.
MMA’s athletic director, Mottola grew up around the team. His father, also Bill Mottola, was MMA’s head coach from 1968 to 1978 and was AD for 25 years after that. Bill the younger grew up on the sidelines of Mariners games, going to team dinners, working as a ball boy, and seeing the way his father built relationships with his players.
It led Mottola into the football coaching, and he spent time at Division I schools Kent State, Miami (Ohio) and Army. The athletic director at MMA since 2024, Mottola views the football program’s pursuit of a victory as a personal quest.
“It will be sooner rather than later. We’re making progress,” Mottola said. “I’ve seen football players. I know what they’re supposed to look like, and I know what the game is supposed to look like.”
What he sees on the field now is a team making strides, Mottola said. Anonymous trolls on social media who see the lopsided scores of many games and mock the team, who look at the losing streak without context, don’t see below the surface. They don’t see what’s being built, he said.
The players see that a bond has formed, and it’s tight.
“No team in the country has been through what we’ve been through the last three years. I just want to keep fighting for these guys,” said Gagin, a linebacker who made 10 tackles on Saturday.
One play at time, one game at a time, Sheehan said. You create the bigger picture by focusing on the little ones.
“In 10 years, when I look back and the program is winning games and being successful, hopefully I’ll be proud of everything we accomplished,” Houghton said.
The Mariners’ next chance for a win comes next Saturday, at home against Endicott.

title: Jury convicts man of rape, murder 14 years after college student’s death
text:
DURHAM, N.C. (AP) - A man accused of killing a North Carolina college student 14 years ago was convicted Friday of first-degree murder, rape and other charges after prosecutors told jurors that forensic evidence was “screaming his name.”
Faith Hedgepeth was a 19-year-old sophomore at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill when she was beaten to death in her off-campus apartment in September 2012. Miguel Salguero Olivares was arrested nine years later after being pulled over for driving while intoxicated and providing a DNA sample that prosecutors say matched evidence from the crime scene.
Salguero Olivares, 33, did not testify during the trial, and his attorneys rested their case without calling any witnesses. Jurors deliberated for six hours over two days before convicting him of murder, rape, sexual offense and burglary. He was then sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole on the murder charge plus 45-65 years on the other charges.
Hedgepeth’s mother, Connie Hedgepeth, told the judge that she forgave her daughter’s killer long ago.
“It was just three weeks after her death. It didn’t matter who done it, I knew that I had to forgive, and I do forgive, but my heart aches for his family,” she said. “It was just such a senseless and cruel act, but we have to go on, and we just have to trust God and go on with our lives.”
Roland Hedgepeth, Faith’s father, said losing his daughter was like having his heart ripped out. He called her a beacon of hope who was born at a low point in his life and admitted it had been easier over the past 5,158 days to say he forgave someone he didn’t know.
“Today it got very real,” he said. “Nevertheless, I say it without reservation, I forgive Miguel for what he did.”
Calling those statements “powerful and kind,” defense attorney James Rainsford said he also could speak about his client and his client’s family but decided not to. “For me to try to blend the two things, I don’t think that’s what everybody needs at this point.”
Defense argued the client was falsely accused
In closing arguments Thursday, defense attorneys accused investigators of having “tunnel vision” in assuming that their client was a monster and not a “19-year-old boy” who had consensual sex with the victim days before her death. Prosecutors, meanwhile, urged jurors to rely on DNA evidence instead of distractions from the defense team.
“We know who did it. The forensic evidence is screaming his name,” said prosecutor Angela Garcia-Lamarca, who described the “uncurable agony” Hedgepeth’s family has endured.
“When the defendant brought that bottle down on her head and she started to bleed, that was the start of a bleeding that still hasn’t stopped,” she said. “He sentenced her to death. He sentenced everybody else who loved her to life. There was no one there to protect her. There was no one there to stop him — until now. Y’all are here. You’re here now, and you can stop him.”
Prosecution suggests victim spurned defendant’s advances
Nearly two dozen witnesses testified for the prosecution, including crime scene technicians, state and local law enforcement, a DNA expert and Hedgepeth’s friends.
Hedgepeth’s roommate, Karena Rosario, testified that she was drunk and sick when Hedgepeth drove them home from a club around 2 a.m. that Sept. 7. She said she later called a friend to pick her up, leaving Hedgepeth in the apartment alone. She returned hours later to find her roommate’s body.
Though no witnesses corroborated the theory, prosecutors suggested Salguero Olivares may have attended a barbecue hosted by Hedgepeth’s neighbor that night, unsuccessfully hit on the young women in the parking lot and then returned, embarrassed and angry, after Rosario left.
Forensic evidence was a focus
Experts testified that the defendant’s fingerprints and palm print were found on a wine bottle at the scene and that his DNA was found in Hedgepeth’s body, on a note written on a fast-food bag found at the scene and on a rum bottle covered in blood that investigators identified as the weapon in the killing.
Defense attorneys questioned Rosario’s account of that night, the processing of the crime scene and the reliability of some DNA evidence. They pointed out that police failed to search some areas of the apartment and later lost some possible blood evidence and emphasized that DNA from sexual intercourse can remain for days afterward.
“Maybe he was living the same life as other 19- and 20-year-old children that we’ve heard about in this case,” defense attorney Jason Murphy said. “Maybe he had too much to drink, maybe he forgot about an encounter.”
But special prosecutor Lisa Coltrane dismissed that as “noise.”
“No matter what kind of mistakes were made or things that were missed, it doesn’t erase the palm print; it doesn’t somehow lift the DNA out of Faith,” she said. “They didn’t talk to every single person in Chapel Hill, and it doesn’t matter. They still got the guy because he left his DNA like confetti all over that room.”

title: Pets of the Week: Plunger and Spalding
Mom arrested after 12-year-old daughter found weighing 47 pounds, authorities say
text:
ORANGEBURG COUNTY, S.C. (WCSC/News) - A mother in South Carolina was arrested after her 12-year-old daughter was allegedly found severely underweight, according to authorities.
Chiquitta Dawkins, 43, was charged with unlawful conduct toward a child, deputies say.
Orangeburg County Sheriff Leroy Ravenell said deputies were called to a location in Bowman, where they found the child suffering from severe malnutrition, according to the arrest warrant.
The investigation found that the girl limped because of her condition, had frail bones and weighed 47 pounds.
Deputies also determined that there were no education records for the child after kindergarten, according to an incident report.
“There are no reasonable people on this planet who could possibly think this is fine,” Ravenell said. “Leaving a child to become this sick, this malnourished is the utmost in despicable.”

title: Prosecutor says he will seek death penalty for mom charged with murder in twins’ deaths
text:
BOISE, Idaho (AP) — An Idaho prosecutor is seeking the death penalty against a woman charged with murder in the 2025 deaths of her twin toddlers.
Andrea Shaw, 23, has pleaded not guilty and has said the 18-month-old twins became sick and died after receiving flu shots and routine childhood vaccinations. But Payette County Prosecutor Mike Duke wrote in court documents that an autopsy revealed symptoms consistent with smothering and wrote that suffocation “is the only conceivable explanation” for their deaths.
Deputy prosecuting attorney Ryon Sirucek notified the court of his intent to seek the death penalty last week.
In the court document, Sirucek said the state would try to show that four aggravating factors make capital punishment appropriate in the case: That more than one murder was committed at the time; that the killings were especially heinous, atrocious or cruel; that the defendant showed “utter disregard” for human life; and that she would likely pose a continuing threat to society.
“That’s outrageous,” said Shaw’s attorney, Joseph Filicetti. “They’re not going to be able to prove the underlying case beyond a reasonable doubt, so there’s not a chance the death penalty is going to come into play.”
Filicetti said the defense team will be filing a motion to dismiss the case. The county coroner found the cause of death to be undetermined but consistent with hyperthermia or overheating, Filicetti said, but the coroner was not on the witness list for the grand jury. It is not clear whether jurors were informed of his findings. The pathologists who examined the twins also said their causes of death were undetermined, Filicetti said.
The prosecutor’s office wrote in court documents that the temperature in the twins’ room would often reach 100 degrees, but that the children had survived high temperatures before and that their time of death didn’t correlate to the peak temperature of the day.
“They don’t have any motive, they don’t have any backstory, they don’t have any confession ... She didn’t do any of that, and they can’t prove she did any of it,” Filicetti said.
The twins were found dead in their shared bed May 1, 2025, according to court records. They had been vaccinated eight days earlier, and the day after their vaccinations Shaw took them to the emergency room, reporting that they were lethargic and felt feverish. The doctor felt the symptoms were a reaction from the vaccinations, and the twins were given Tylenol and a popsicle and sent home, according to the court records.
A few days after the twins’ deaths, Shaw went on an internet show produced by Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine group founded by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He has not been affiliated with the group since December 2024, when he formally resigned as chairman to join President Donald Trump’s administration.
Medical experts point out that the childhood vaccines at issue — hepatitis A, influenza and DTaP — are safe and effective for kids and recommended by various medical groups.
Shaw is also a plaintiff in a federal lawsuit brought by Children’s Health Defense and others against the American Academy of Pediatrics, accusing the organization of racketeering and lying about the safety of vaccinations. The American Academy of Pediatrics has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, calling it the “latest missive in a campaign targeting” the academy and its “use of science-backed evidence in vaccine policy.”
A grand jury indicted Shaw on the murder charges in July, and she is being held without bond. A trial has been set for January.
___
This story was first published on Oct. 21, 2026. It was updated on Oct. 22, 2026, to clarify that the grand jury did not hear testimony from the coroner, but it is not clear whether jurors were informed of his findings.”
___
Associated Press writer Josh Kelety contributed.

title: Maine Celtics select Josh Roberts in NBA G League Draft
text:
The Maine Celtics selected Josh Roberts sixth overall in the NBA G League Draft on Saturday, one of three picks they made to round out their roster for the upcoming season.
Maine also selected Kaleb Lowery with the 23rd pick and Desmond Cambridge with the 37th pick.
Roberts, a 6-foot-9 power forward, was named the MAAC Defensive Player of the Year while at Manhattan College in 2023. He has played for various teams overseas the last three seasons.
Lowery played one season for the University of Nevada, averaging 4.6 points and 3.1 rebounds. Cambridge played 35 G League games last season between Santa Cruz and San Diego, averaging 6.0 points and 3.1 rebounds.
Maine’s roster will also include two-way players Devin Carter, Dillon Mitchell and Amari Williams, as well as returning players Hayden Gray and Hank Morgan.
The Celtics open their season against the Westchester Knicks on Nov. 7 in Portland.

title: Campaign financing is outrageous, out of control
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I am appalled by the amount of money that is spent on political campaigns, and I’m outraged by the number of requests for donations that appear in my message box every day. With billionaires and trillionaires pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into campaigns for their favorite candidates throughout the country, we can hardly hope to compete with our little contributions. Yet, every day, the texts get more desperate.
Campaign financing has become really lopsided, with a few extravagantly rich individuals poised to commandeer our democracy for their own ends.
Once the midterms are over, I hope we can focus on meaningful change to campaign finance regulations — among the myriad of other problems this country is facing. Wouldn’t it be wonderful if a good chunk of the money that has been spent on these elections could have been put to useful purposes like healthcare and affordable housing, childcare and education.
Perhaps if these individuals were paying their fair share of taxes, those dreams could be realized.
That’s a topic for another day.
Christine Hopf-Lovette
Wiscasset

text:
Kamden Sixkiller passed for 450 yards and three touchdowns, leading Campbell to a 35-6 win over Maine in a Coastal Athletic Association football game Saturday afternoon in Orono.

title: Singing Maine’s praises, one county at a time
text:
Elizabeth Lardie Thompson couldn’t quite believe what she was hearing.
She was playing pub trivia in Sydney, Australia, more than 20 years ago. The quiz master began the bonus round by saying, “There’s this silly song Americans sing if they grow up in Maine and it’s got all the counties in it.” Could anyone in the pub sing it?
“We sang that song at least once a week in fourth grade, and then it just carried into something we did incessantly, even into to high school,” said Thompson, 43, a theater performer and writer who lives in Bath. “So when they asked if anyone could sing it, I was like, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me.'”
The “Maine County Song” has been taught in Maine schools for decades, at least since the 1950s. It began as an easy way for kids to learn some strange-sounding Maine county names, like Androscoggin, Piscataquis or Sagadahoc. Today it’s a grassroots Maine tradition, a source of pride for adults who can still sing it at a moment’s notice.
The fact that a quiz master in Australia had heard about it — from another Aussie who had spent a college semester in Maine — is testament to how unique and long-lasting the 30-second song is.
In Maine, people talk about the divide between rural and urban areas, locals and tourists, the 1st District and the 2nd District. But for several generations, the “Maine County Song” is a unifier to the tune of “Yankee Doodle.”
“I just think it’s a point of pride, that we all know the 16 counties because of that song,” said Denise Michaud, 61, administrative assistant for South Portland Public Works. “It’s like ‘Oh, you don’t know the counties in your state? I know the counties in my state, because I can sing them.'”
A SINGING SUCCESS
As an educational tool, the song’s success is undeniable. It’s so well-known that it’s become part of the state’s popular culture.
The Downeasters Chorus, a Maine-based barbershop harmony group, added it to their repertoire this year and sang it at the Yarmouth Clam Festival in July. Marpheen Chann, of Portland, who is running for Cumberland County commissioner in November, posted a video of himself singing the song on social media after reading a ton about Maine county government in preparation for his campaign. He said he first sang it at Acton Elementary School.
The Law Offices of Joe Bornstein produced a series of TV ads a couple of years ago to celebrate the firm’s 50th anniversary, featuring “American Idol” finalist Julia Haven (formerly Julia Gagnon) of Cumberland, singing the song. The firm wanted to create a “unifying message” for its anniversary and thought the “Maine County Song” was the perfect way to do that, said Nate Bergeron, the marketing director.
Emily Little, a nurse who grew up on Mount Desert Island but now lives in Virginia, has taught the song to her three kids. She laments that they’ll never know the joys of singing about all of the counties in their state —Virginia has 95 counties, way too many to remember or fit into a song.
On a summer visit to Maine last year, her kids, husband and parents joined her in making a video of the whole family singing the song, one voice at a time.
When Little went to Vassar College in Poughkeepsie, New York, she organized Maine-themed parties with other students from the Pine Tree State and singing the county song was always part of the program.
“No one else had a state party. It was like no other state had its own identity. And singing the county song was part of that,” said Little, 41.
Three classes of fourth graders at the Congin School in Westbrook were learning the song this month as part of a Maine studies unit. Kids could be heard at recess or in bus lines singing it.
In class on a recent Tuesday morning, they sang it repeatedly without any missteps — though some students admitted having trouble pronouncing some of the counties at first, including Androscoggin and Sagadahoc.
Most had heard of Cumberland County, which includes Westbrook, and nearby York County. They were also learning about the structure of U.S. government, and how it’s broken down by state, county and towns so that all people, in every place, can have a voice.
Part of the lesson is that “one person cannot do it all, so having local help makes it easier for everyone,” said Wendy Nugent, a fourth grade teacher.
WORD OF MOUTH
The song’s origins seem to be organic. Some people remember learning it in their public school classrooms as early as the 1950s, and it’s easy to find many who learned it from the 1970s on. Several teachers interviewed for this story said it had been taught in their schools since at least the ’80s or ’90s.
The song is not a mandated part of any curriculum and there’s no single official version, so a few of the words and the order of the counties are sometimes different. Some people call it “The 16 Counties Song.”
But hundreds of teachers have used it during the fourth grade year as part of the required Maine studies unit.
Michaud said she was “shocked” when her son, Ben Michaud, came home from school and sang a version of the “Maine County Song” that was different than the one she learned at Dora Small School in South Portland in the 1970s.
Ben Michaud, now 30, had learned a version that ended with “Oxford and Penobscot” instead of “Aroostook and Penobscot.” While being interviewed for this story, Michaud sang her version of the song, to prove she still could.
The Maine Secretary of State Kids’ Page lists lyrics to two versions of the song, along with audio clips. But a spokesperson for the office says no one there knows when the information was added to the website, or when the song was first taught.
The first version on the website is: “The 16 counties in our state are/Cumberland and Franklin/Piscataquis and Somerset/Aroostook, Androscoggin/Sagadahoc and Kennebec/Lincoln, Knox and Hancock/Waldo, Washington and York/Oxford and Penobscot.”
The second version reads: “There are 16 counties in our state/There’s Cumberland and Franklin/Piscataquis and Kennebec/Oxford, Androscoggin/Waldo, Washington and York/Lincoln, Knox and Hancock/Sagadahoc and Somerset/Aroostook and Penobscot.”
Both are sung to the tune of “Yankee Doodle” and both sound pretty much the same to those of us who didn’t learn the song in school. But dozens of people responding to a Facebook query were adamant that the version they learned was the correct one.
SCARES BEARS, PAYS FOR COLLEGE
Emma and Nora Conrad have found myriad uses for the “Maine County Song” since learning it in Winthrop as grade schoolers. The sisters sang it to pass the time on long car trips, sometimes shouting it out the window at passing traffic. They sang it at a Christmas parade in their father’s Pennsylvania hometown. They sing spontaneously when walking, kayaking or hiking.
Once, while hiking in Colorado, they sang it to scare any nearby bears. It was a song they knew well enough to sing at the top of their lungs, a sort of default safety song.
Emma Conrad, who works for the Natural Resources Council of Maine, said the song is a comfortable way to break the ice when she meets other people who grew up here.
“Maine is a big small town and, with just 16 counties, you’re never far removed from people all around the state,” said Conrad, 28, of Portland.
The song has helped put Maine students through college. Massachusetts-based dairy company H.P. Hood promoted its Milk Money Scholarship program in Maine in the late 1990s by offering a $4,000 scholarship to one student in each of the 16 counties.
To apply for the scholarship, students had to show up in person and successfully sing the county song. Grades and recommendations, interviews and other non-musical criteria were considered, too.
Lauren Rioux, 45, grew up in East Machias in Washington County and applied for the scholarship in 1999. She sang the county song at the University of Maine at Machias and later found out she had gotten the $,4,000 award, which she used while studying music at the University of Southern Maine.
Rioux, who lives in Scarborough, is a fiddler who teaches at her home studio and at Waynflete School in Portland. Sometimes when people ask her to sing the “Maine County Song,” she jokes that she once got paid a lot of money to play it. But she’s happy to play it for free, and to teach it to others.
During the pandemic, when she couldn’t teach in-person, Rioux made videos. She made one singing the “Maine County Song.” Her baby daughter, Caroline, is seen sleeping in a carrier as she sings. Rioux said she can’t remember exactly why she decided to record the song. But she’s glad she did.
“It’s part of our state’s lore, it’s fun and it’s happy.”

title: President Trump says he ordered lawsuit that could delay Alaska Senate election results
text:
President Trump says he ordered lawsuit that could delay Alaska Senate election results
President Trump said he ordered a lawsuit in Alaska that could delay the state’s Senate race results, while his administration faces criticism over efforts to address voter integrity in California and other states.
President Trump says he ordered lawsuit that could delay Alaska Senate election results
President Trump said he ordered a lawsuit in Alaska that could delay the state’s Senate race results, while his administration faces criticism over efforts to address voter integrity in California and other states.
The Trump administration has initiated legal actions in Alaska and California, citing concerns over election integrity, as millions of Americans have already cast their votes ahead of the midterm elections.
President Donald Trump said he personally ordered a lawsuit in Alaska that could delay certification of the state's Senate race.
"I'm the one that said do it," Trump said when asked about the Alaska lawsuit.
The lawsuit focuses on the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the Alaska ballot, one a Republican senator seeking reelection and the other a candidate whose name appears without a party designation.
The Department of Justice alleges the second Sullivan is deliberately trying to draw votes away from the Republican incumbent to help Democrat Mary Peltola.
The DOJ argues that voters could confuse the two, potentially altering the election's outcome, and is seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying the results if the Republican incumbent loses and votes cast for the other Sullivan could have changed the outcome. The department wants certification delayed while officials investigate whether voters intended to support the incumbent.
"Alaska's Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot," a Justice Department spokesperson told Hearst Television. "Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters."
Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski criticized the lawsuit, saying the DOJ should never have filed it.
Alaska's Division of Elections initially sought to disqualify the second Sullivan, but state courts overturned that decision. Alaska's Supreme Court ruled that he could remain on the ballot, and the DOJ is now asking a federal court to intervene.
In California, the DOJ is demanding that election officials in at least 18 counties verify whether certain voters are U.S. citizens and set aside ballots if citizenship cannot be confirmed. Officials have been given 48 hours to provide identifying information about those voters.
The administration says the move is intended to prevent noncitizens from voting. However, California officials have questioned the accuracy of the federal government's information and warned that eligible voters could be affected.
A hearing in the California case is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 27, but the administration is also asking an appeals court to intervene sooner.
In a separate case, a federal judge ordered limits on certain Homeland Security investigations in nine states. Agents have been going door to door, asking residents if they are U.S. citizens and whether they have voted. The judge expressed concerns that such actions could intimidate eligible voters. The order was initially put on hold until Oct. 23 to allow the administration to appeal.
Meanwhile, Trump has announced he is exempting certain Canadian products from his 50% tariffs, including packaging and equipment used by farmers in Maine.
The decision follows pressure from Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who is facing a tough reelection race. The changes will take effect Oct. 30, just four days before the midterms. However, the administration is also increasing tariffs on other Canadian goods, indicating that the trade dispute with Canada is ongoing.

title: Husband receives prison sentence, culminating family’s years-long fight after wife’s AIDS death
text:
CONYERS, Ga. (ANF/Gray News) - A Conyers man accused of spreading HIV to multiple women — one of whom later died — will avoid trial on murder charges after pleading guilty to three counts of reckless conduct.
Cleveland Broadie was sentenced Oct. 7, 2026, to 15 years in prison, with possible release after eight years. If released, he must stay out of Rockdale County; have no contact with victims’ families; share medical records with probation; and stay on HIV medication.
One of Cleveland Broadie’s victims was his wife Denise Broadie, who died April 2, 2022, from pneumonia and respiratory failure “due to Human Immunodeficiency Virus-Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome,” according to her death certificate. They’d been been married since 2014.
Denise Broadie didn’t learn she had HIV - which progressed to AIDS - until shortly before her death. Doctors said it went undiagnosed and untreated for years. Denise had been in and out of the hospital fighting cancer so her family never thought her struggles could be coming from an additional illness. They didn’t discover until it was too late.
Denise Broadie’s daughters, Karen Young and Tammy Hammonds, alleged their mother had not been active sexually with anyone else. (NOTE: Cleveland Broadie is not related to Denise Broadie’s daughters.)
“Our main goal was to hold him accountable and we’ve done that,” Tammy Hammonds said after the plea deal.
“We’re satisfied that we have some justice,” Young said.
Atlanta News First Investigates first reported on the case in 2023, and Hammonds and Young believe the media attention led to a police investigation.
“Had it not been for [Atlanta News First Investigates], we would not be in this position,” Young said. “We fought tooth and nail trying to get attention and get police to investigate.”
The Rockdale County Sheriff’s Office eventually arrested Cleveland Broadie for reckless conduct-HIV infected person. The warrant said he knew his HIV status since 2006 but did not tell his wife, Denise Broadie.
The case grew at two other women came forward saying Cleveland Broadie did not disclose his status prior to unprotected sex.
Cleveland Broadie was eventually indicted on five charges: malice murder, felony murder, and three counts of reckless conduct.
In a May 2025 hearing, Rockdale County prosecutors argued Cleveland Broadie intentionally hid his diagnosis; was not regularly taking medication; and had unprotected sex with his wife as well as other women.
His defense attorney argued he had disclosed his status to his wife in writing before they married, a claim Denise Broadie’s family disputed.
The plea deal brought Hammonds and Young peace.
“It’s better for our mental health [and] our wellbeing to accept an outcome, because no amount of time was going to be sufficient enough for our mother’s loss of life,” Hammonds said.
“We’ve been through a lot and we’re ready to move on in life and mourn our mother, which we haven’t had a chance to do and enjoy life like she would’ve wanted us to.” Young said. “I think she’s proud we saw it through and got justice for her and the other victims.”

title: Cooper Flagg diagnosed with mild shoulder sprain
text:
DALLAS — Mavericks star Cooper Flagg will miss Saturday night’s home game against the San Antonio Spurs after an MRI revealed a mild sprain of his left shoulder suffered just before halftime of Dallas’ win at Indiana a night earlier.
Last season’s Rookie of the Year will be reevaluated next week.
Flagg, of Newport, was driving to the basket after making a steal near midcourt Friday night in the final minute of the first half. As he went up for a dunk, he was fouled from behind by Aaron Nesmith, a play that was ruled a Flagrant 1 foul. Flagg landed behind the baseline on his left shoulder and didn’t reenter the game.
Flagg was leading all scorers with 14 points in 17 minutes, along with five rebounds, six assists, three steals and a block. Dallas led 77-43 at halftime and went on to beat the Pacers 121-105.
Flagg scored 32 points in the Mavericks’ opener on Wednesday night, a 128-110 loss at Houston. Last season, he averaged 21 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists.
Saturday’s game will be the home debut of Mavericks coach Dusty May, who led Michigan to the NCAA championship last season.

title: Here’s why shoppers may be buying less candy for Halloween this year
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start this year as U.S. consumers grapple with high living costs and eye-popping chocolate prices.
Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm. Nielsen also noted an 11.7% decline in candy sales in mid-September, erasing the preseason gains that Halloween candy enjoyed the previous two years.
Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said high gas prices have worsened Americans’ concerns about affordability, and that’s dampening demand for Halloween treats. As of Friday, the average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. was $4.29, up nearly 40% from the prior year.
“I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food,” Costagli said. “Some of the decisions they’re making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, ‘I notice it’s more expensive than last year,’ it’s, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I’ve paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’”
Small bags of candy were the only sizes seeing sales growth through mid-October, Costagli noted. Large and extra-large bags were seeing the biggest declines.
U.S. candy prices have been climbing faster than the rate of inflation for several years. As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44% over a five-year period, according to government data. Prices for all food eaten at home rose 22.5% in the same period.
This week, discount grocer Aldi was advertising a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolate bars – including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers – for $19.87. That’s almost the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece variety pack five years ago.
Cocoa prices are the main culprit. Global cocoa prices reached a record high of $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 because of poor weather in West Africa – which supplies 70% of the world’s chocolate -- and speculative trading in the cocoa futures market, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Cocoa prices had been falling steadily since then, and hit $3,241 per metric ton in March. But they began climbing again in the spring as the Iran war disrupted Africa’s fertilizer supplies. The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to hurt production, with hot, dry conditions expected through February.
But Costagli noted that even in cases where prices are lower than last year, consumer demand is muted. The average price of non-chocolate Halloween candies, like gummies and lollipops, was $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, which was about 3% lower than last year, according to Nielsen data. But that didn’t lead to a bump in sales.
Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser for the market research company Circana, said one way U.S. consumers have been handling higher grocery prices is by making smaller and more frequent trips to the supermarket and buying products right before they intend to use them. That makes her wonder if shoppers are waiting until closer to Halloween to buy candy this year.
“People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general,” she said. “I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed.”
The National Confectioners Association, a trade group that represents candy makers like Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic about Halloween sales.
“We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong,” the group said Friday in a statement.
