title: Paul LePage isn’t a full-time Maine resident. That should disqualify him from representing us in Congress.
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Sandra Caron of Orono is a retired professor and recipient of the 2019 Distinguished Maine Professor Award, and a 2023 Maine Women’s Hall of Fame inductee.
My friends who live outside Maine always marvel at my literal close proximity to my elected representatives. It’s normal to see our federal representatives out and about, even if they are spending half their time annually in Washington, D.C.
Maine may be large geographically, but it’s small in terms of where we gather to worship, celebrate and shop. Years ago a friend ran into Olympia Snowe when she was still a senator. Olympia was pushing a cart at the local Hannaford. My friend was a little starstruck and blurted out that she was surprised to see her there. Olympia smiled and replied, “Hey, I have to eat like everyone else!”
In the past year alone, I’ve encountered most of our state’s most prominent politicians socially. I did the geriatric boogie to Willie Nelson at a Bangor waterfront concert with Gov. Janet Mills and Sen. Angus King, who were having a grand old time in the next section. Last October, I ran into Troy Jackson and Matt Dunlap at the University of Maine homecoming tailgates, happily chatting with anyone who approached them. Less than two weeks ago, I sat 20 feet from Sen. Susan Collins at the Alfond Arena, part of a sellout crowd cheering on the UMaine hockey team.
While my friends may be amused that Mainers spot their reps “in the wild” so often, what they really envy is the incredible constituent service that has been the Maine norm for decades. Our federal elected officials return home and visit their field offices often. They demand personalized and prompt constituent response. This ethos is also ingrained in state elected officials, regardless of party. Many state legislators freely publish their private cellphone numbers and email addresses for their constituents. We know we can call or write any representative with a gripe or compliment, and we’ll generally get a personal response.
I believe this tradition will be broken if Maine’s 2nd Congressional District elects Paul LePage. It’s generous to describe him as a part-time Maine resident. LePage has spent most of his time in Florida since leaving the governor’s office in 2018, and has faced tax controversies since then over homes he and his wife have owned as Florida residents.
He had a short stint back in Maine in 2022 when he ran for governor. After that failed campaign, he returned to the 3,800-square foot home in Florida he and his wife have owned since 2018. Does anyone really believe he lives now in that sad little apartment in Augusta above a barber shop that he leased from a prominent Republican last spring, just before announcing his current run?
LePage admits he is a “snowbird,” planning to spend the winter months in Florida, not Maine. He says it’s too cold and “he doesn’t play hockey anymore.” I don’t begrudge anyone the choice of spending winters somewhere warm. But that’s a choice for a retiree, not someone who wants to represent me come 2027.
The next winter promises to be brutal for Mainers. Between soaring heating oil costs and the collapsing healthcare system, there will be many Mainers desperate for help from their representatives. Instead, when he isn’t in Washington, D.C., LePage will apparently be spending his winter in Florida sunning himself by his heated pool, literally phoning it in for his constituents.
Matt Dunlap is a year-round Maine resident. If he is elected, when not in Washington, D.C., he will be shoveling snow and cursing his latest fuel oil bill just like the rest of us. He will likely know neighbors struggling to pay medical bills. He will feel our pain. And yes, he will also share our joy, live and in person, when we cheer on our beloved UMaine Black Bears.
LePage may know the hardships of living in Maine from his formative years. But times have changed, and to know Maine now you have to live here now, especially when you are signing up for a job that will keep you in D.C. for much of the year. LePage has apparently decided he’s either too old to live here full time, or he’s too entitled to think it’s a necessity.
I believe his lack of full-time residency in Maine disqualifies him from serving as our representative.

title: Will we succeed in saving the right whale?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Cindy Lowry is a Maine-based environmental advocate with more than two decades of experience protecting marine wildlife, including work on high-profile whale rescue efforts and national conservation campaigns.
To celebrate the United States’ first 250 years, a time capsule was buried in Philadelphia on July 4, to be opened in another 250 years. Maine contributed seven items, a vertebra from a North Atlantic right whale among them.
The bone was from a whale who was found dead near Boothbay in 2016. Researchers named her EgNo 3654. It was believed fishing gear was the cause of her death; she was found with fishing gear wrapped around her head, mouth, flippers and tail.
In addition to her vertebra being included in the capsule, her jaw and flipper bones will be on display when the Maine State Museum reopens on Oct. 24. Museum Director Bernard
Fishman proposed including her vertebra in the capsule. 
Fishman told the Portland Press Herald he wanted the capsule to ask the future a question: “Did we — did you — save the right whales?”
Only about 380 right whales are left, and only 70 of those are reproductive females, according to NOAA. Fishing gear and ship strikes are the leading causes of death.
Entanglement is rarely quick. Whales can drag gear for months, unable to feed or swim freely, before dying of infection, exhaustion or starvation. It’s up to us if we want to fight for a future where North Atlantic right whales continue to migrate off the Gulf of Maine every year, or if they’ll be gone by the time the capsule is opened.
In this time and place, we collectively have the moral obligation to protect our fellow sentient beings. Fortunately, options such as ropeless gear and other technologies exist that the fishing industry could use to ensure right whales have a future. Ropeless, or on-demand, gear keeps traps on the seafloor without a vertical line to the surface until fishermen send a signal to bring them up. Solutions like these should be worked out with lobstermen, not postponed for seven more years.
A bill pending in the Senate could have irreversible impacts on North Atlantic right whales. H.R. 9436, the Northeast Lobstermen Protection Act, co-sponsored by Reps. Jared Golden and Mike Lawler, would extend the pause on new federal right whale protections from the end of 2028 to 2035.
Since 2022, that pause has blocked new rules to reduce entanglements, such as added
gear requirements and fishery closures. No new protections could be added until 2035. The Senate is expected to vote on it in November. A pause on new protections risks more right whales dying in the way that EgNo 3654 did back in 2016.
If you want to be among the people who can make a difference both now and into the future, please call or write to the offices of Sen. Susan Collins and Sen. Angus King before the Senate votes in November, and urge them to oppose Golden’s bill.
EgNo 3654’s bones will be on display at the Maine State Museum in Augusta this fall and my hope is that her story inspires action. We are truly lucky to share our waters with North Atlantic right whales in 2026. Someday, someone will open the capsule and reflect on the vertebra and Fishman’s question. We still have time to decide how they react. Was this a species that we saved?
Let’s hope so.

title: Cooper Flagg out with shoulder injury following hard foul Friday against Pacers
text:
INDIANAPOLIS — A jarring flagrant foul knocked Cooper Flagg awkwardly to the floor and eventually out of the game Friday night.
Now it’s unclear whether the Dallas star will miss any more time.
Last season’s NBA Rookie of the Year did not play in the second half of Dallas’ 121-105 victory Friday night over the Indiana Pacers after landing hard on his left shoulder after Aaron Nesmith tried to block his shot from behind to prevent a breakaway dunk.
Instead, Flagg landed hard on his shoulder.
“Cooper has left shoulder soreness, he’ll be evaluated in the next couple of days,” Mavericks coach Dusty May said before addressing whether Flagg needed an MRI. “I really don’t know. I saw him in the locker room, he’s in good spirits. We’ll know in the next couple days what’s next.”
Flagg did not speak to reporters following the game.
He was off to a fast start in his second pro season. Two days after scoring 32 points to become the highest scoring teenager in a season opener in league history, Flagg was on pace for his first triple double of the season. He finished with 14 points, five rebounds and six assists in 17 minutes.
But it was how he left that had everyone talking and scuffling as Mavericks players came to the defense of their hurting teammate.
Forward Naji Marshall confronted Nesmith under the basket, drawing players from both teams into a brief fray. After a replay review, the refs assessed double technical fouls to Nesmith and Marshall. Flagg then made 1 of 2 free throws and continued to rub his shoulder as he walked toward the locker room.
Two Mavericks players also appeared to leave the bench though May said he thought both went to check on Flagg, perhaps avoiding any disciplinary action from the league.
“Look, Nesmith is a great guy, a heck of a player. I’ve known him since he was in high school,” said May, who reached two NCAA Final Fours and won last year’s national championship just a few blocks away from Gainbridge Fieldhouse. “Obviously, an unfortunate play. Hopefully, Coop’s fine.”
Another brief scuffle broke out between the teams near midcourt in the second half though it led to technicals or flagrant fouls. Pacers coach Rick Carlisle noted that Indiana has now played two games that have resulted in multiple scuffles.

title: Lyme disease cases in Maine tracking ahead of last year
text:
Lyme disease cases in Maine so far this year are tracking slightly ahead of 2025, when the state set a record for the tickborne disease.
Megan Porter, health educator with the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention, said she can’t project whether 2026 cases will break the record, but the deer ticks that cause Lyme disease are currently active.
“Ticks are active anytime the temperature is above freezing,” Porter said. “The ticks are everywhere, so Mainers should take steps to prevent tickborne diseases.”
As of Oct. 20, the Maine CDC reported 3,976 Lyme disease cases so far this year. Through October 2025, the state had reported 3,763 cases of Lyme en route to logging a record of 4,257 cases last year.
Griffin Dill, who manages the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s Tick Lab, said he expects there will be high levels of deer tick activity through mid-November.
Dill said deer ticks are now in their adult stage, and are currently searching for hosts, to prepare for laying eggs and surviving the winter. Despite the arid conditions — ticks prefer rainy and humid weather — the arachnids are still active, Dill said.
“They’re pretty well adapted to survive these adverse conditions,” Dill said. “It is by no means a booming year for tick activity, but we are not seeing a significant decrease in activity even though we’ve had dry weather.”
The lab receives thousands of tick submissions every year for identification and research.
The Maine CDC also reported that, through Oct. 20, there had been 1,223 anaplasmosis cases and 425 cases of babesiosis. The diseases, like Lyme, are transmitted to humans by deer ticks. Lyme and anaplasmosis are bacterial infections, while babesiosis is an infection caused by microscopic parasites.
In 2025, the state recorded a total of 352 cases of babesiosis and 1,604 cases of anaplasmosis, according to the Maine CDC.
Symptoms of the three diseases are similar, including fever, chills, fatigue, headaches and body aches, according to the U.S. CDC. Lyme can sometimes cause a bulls-eye rash. Lyme and anaplasmosis can be treated with a course of antibiotics, while babesiosis patients receive anti-parasitic medicine.
Porter said deer ticks are expanding their geographic range. They used to be mostly in coastal, southern Maine, but are now seen farther inland and Down East.
“We are seeing the ticks push into Down East, and increasing cases of tickborne disease in Western Maine,” Porter said.
Ticks are expanding their range due to climate change, scientists have said.
Porter said people can prevent tick bites by doing frequent checks after doing outdoor activities in tick habitat, tucking socks into pants and using repellent. After outdoor activities, Porter said, put clothes worn during the activity into the dryer on high, which will kill ticks.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Joe Lawlor can be reached at jlawlor@pressherald.com.

title: Woman sentenced after faking pregnancies, including with ‘The Bachelor’ contestant
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) — A woman convicted of tricking men into thinking she was pregnant, including “The Bachelor” contestant Clayton Echard, will spend 30 days behind bars after a plea agreement.
After a plea agreement, prosecutors laid out how they said Laura Owens manipulated the men as she was sentenced.
Echard targeted, prosecutors say
Prosecutors said Laura Owens faked pregnancies to force men into relationships and filed a lawsuit that included several allegations, including abortion coercion and domestic violence. Prosecutors also said Laura Owens stole a woman’s ultrasound and passed it off as her own.
Prosecutors said Laura Owens contacted Echard, a former contestant on “The Bachelor” and Scottsdale realtor, on May 17, 2023, about a real estate deal. The two had oral sex on May 20, prosecutors said, but no intercourse, and Laura Owens claimed she was pregnant on June 1 after obtaining HCG injections from a spa, which she claimed helped improve her skin. She filed for paternity in August 2023, prosecutors said.
“The method that she chose was HCG,” a prosecutor said, describing how she created false positive pregnancy tests.
Stolen ultrasound
Prosecutors said Laura Owens stole a twin ultrasound from Stormy Mitchell, who said she lost one to vanishing twin syndrome.
“It is the only photo I will ever have of my twins together,” Mitchell said in a statement read in court.
Prosecutors also said Laura Owens edited photos to look pregnant.
“Parts of the body are obscured and taken away so you can make yourself look pregnant,” a prosecutor said.
Victims speak
Echard told the judge, “I’ve been fighting for the last three and a half years.”
In a statement read in court, victim Greg Gillespie said Laura Owens caused him to spend years defending his reputation, livelihood and name. He is seeking nearly $300,000 in restitution, according to the statement.
Parents ask for mercy
Laura Owens’ mother, Jan Owens, said Laura lives in a casita on their property and is a vital caregiver. She said Ronn Owens, Laura Owens’ father, has several medical issues and relies on his daughter for daily care.
Jan Owens said over the past 10 years, it has been gut-wrenching to watch her daughter as the target of unspeakable emotional and physical abuse and cyber harassment.
“She has been pregnant. She has had verified medical proof of pregnancy. She has been abused. She has been suffocated and strangled by men she has been with,” Jan Owens said.
She asked for probation only for Laura Owens.
Ronn Owens, 81, a longtime Bay Area radio broadcaster, told the court, “I love my daughter more than I can put into words.”
He asked the court not to take Laura Owens away for whatever time he has left.
Laura Owens emotional over threats
Laura Owens became emotional talking about threats she said she and her family received. She said supporters of victims sent death threats, posted her family’s address online and told her to take her own life.
“We didn’t know what was gonna happen if this person was going to actually come to my family’s house and shoot my mom, and I felt so guilty about it,” Laura Owens said.
She also told the court, “I want the rest of my life, and not just my words today, to show how completely, terribly sorry I am for everybody I’ve harmed.”
The judge said in deciding the sentence he weighed “whether or not she’s this sophisticated con person or a very sad individual making some poor choices.”
“Obviously, I think it’s the latter,” the judge said.
The judge imposed 30 days of flat time plus 12 months of deferred jail starting Oct. 22, 2027. Laura Owens faces up to 12.5 years in prison if she violates probation.

title: Sunshine for the weekend
text:
Sunshine for the weekend
Sunshine for the weekend
Saturday is off to a cool start, with many areas reaching temperatures below freezing this morning. High pressure is overhead, meaning that we have dry and clear skies today. The extra sunshine will help Saturday temperatures warm into the upper 50s.
Winds will shift and come out of the southwest on Sunday, which will kick off a few days of warmer-than-normal temperatures. Warm air will move in from the south, creating temperatures in the low to mid-60s on Sunday.
Temperatures will be even warmer on Monday, reaching the mid to high 60s. Scattered showers are possible for mountain and even inland areas on Monday as a cold front passes over Maine.
Cold air flowing in behind the front will flip the temperature trend and make for cooler-than-normal conditions on Tuesday and Wednesday. Outside of the slight rain chances on Monday, most areas will stay dry through most of the week.

title: Man who fatally hit deputy after his son was killed by police is convicted of murder
text:
CINCINNATI (WXIX/Gray News) - A jury has found an Ohio man guilty of killing a Hamilton County deputy last year.
Rodney Hinton Jr. was found guilty of murder, reckless homicide and felonious assault for deliberately hitting and killing Deputy Larry Henderson on May 2, 2025.
He will be sentenced on Nov. 16. Prosecutors said they want Hinton to serve 15 years to life in prison.
“His family will never truly be able to fill that void, but we hope that today’s verdict brings them some sense of justice and peace,” prosecutors said.
Hamilton County Sheriff Charmaine McGuffey said the verdict gives her office some sense of closure after reliving Henderson’s death throughout the trial.
“We do believe that is an appropriate finding,” McGuffey said. “Now we can come together and hug each other and tell each other, we’re here. We have some finality.”
Two sides of the case
The jury was tasked with determining if Hinton purposefully tried to kill Henderson as he directed traffic near Burnet Woods.
The crash occurred hours after Hinton watched body camera video of his son, Ryan Hinton, 19, who was fatally shot by a Cincinnati police officer.
Hamilton County Prosecutor Connie Pillich said Rodney Hinton’s son was running from police, dropped a gun and later picked it back up. That shooting was later deemed justified.
Defense attorney Clyde Bennett argued Rodney Hinton was not aiming for the deputy.
Bennett claimed his client was suffering from acute psychotic symptoms and severe mental illness, meaning he did not understand the wrongfulness of his actions at the time.
Prosecutors said the evidence left no doubt that Hinton intentionally drove his car into Henderson.
They argued Hinton saw Henderson’s uniform, reacted to losing his son, and decided to take the life of one of their own.
Appeal to come
Bennett talked with reporters after the verdict was announced Friday.
He said he was “disappointed” in the jury’s verdict, adding he thinks the video of the crash is what sealed the murder conviction.
Bennett plans to file an appeal within 30 days of Hinton’s sentencing.
State AG responds
Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson issued a statement on the verdict:
“The senseless murder of Deputy Larry Henderson Jr. shattered a family and left a community mourning the loss of a dedicated public servant. We are thankful to the jury for its verdict, which accurately reflects the evidence in this case.
Deputy Henderson spent 33 years honorably serving his community in law enforcement. He died fulfilling his duty. His death is a painful reminder of the risks that law enforcement officers face every day while working to keep us safe. They deserve our gratitude.’

title: UMaine, Husson men’s basketball facing off in exhibition game Sunday
text:
The University of Maine men’s basketball team will entertain neighbor Husson University from Bangor for an exhibition game on Sunday on the Skip Chappelle Court in the Memorial Gym in Orono.
Tip off is at 4:30 p.m. and there is no admission fee. Doors will open at 3:30 p.m.
The teams played an exhibition game a year ago at the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor, with UMaine triumphing 89-47.
Both teams are inundated with newcomers as they prepare for their season openers.
UMaine will begin its season at Providence College at 7 p.m. Monday, Nov. 2, and Husson will host Clark University at 2 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 8.
UMaine is coming off an 8-24 season, 6-10 in America East. The Black Bears were ousted in the America East quarterfinals by third seed the New Jersey Institute of Technology, 60-58.
UMaine has been picked to finish eighth in the nine-team America East conference this season.
Husson was 16-10 a year ago, 15-3 in the North Atlantic Conference. The Eagles were upset by the University of Maine at Presque Isle, 78-74, in overtime in the NAC semifinals.
“It’s a great opportunity for our fans to play in front of fans with the lights on and see if we can really test ourselves in terms of where we’re at and what we’ve been working on up until this point,” said UMaine head coach Chris Markwood. “We’ve got a long ways to go. We’ve been going since July and we want to test ourselves against somebody else.”
UMaine’s top five scorers off last year’s team are gone, but the Black Bears do return sophomore forward and All-America East Rookie Team selection Ace Flagg from Newport and junior guard Caleb Crawford, who was second on the team assists and third in steals.
The Black Bears will regain the services of 6-foot-10 forward Killian Gribben and redshirt sophomore point guard Darius Lopes, who both underwent season-ending foot surgery.
Gribben appeared in one game after leading the team in blocked shots two years ago with 34. He also averaged 5.3 points and 3 rebounds in 2024-25.
Lopes was pencilled in to be the starting point guard a year ago after being a redshirt his first year according to Markwood.
Flagg averaged 6.7 points and 4.1 rebounds but had 14 points and 8 rebounds, both team-highs, in the playoff loss to NJIT.
“I’m definitely excited about the potential of our roster,” said Markwood, who is in his fifth season at the helm and led the 2024-25 team to a 20-14 record, which matched the most single-season wins in 25 years, and a berth in the America East title game for the first time in 21 years.
“It has been an awesome group to coach. They work really hard and they love being in the gym,” Markwood added.
Markwood said senior guard and Holy Cross transfer DeAndre Williams and Drexel transfer Villiam Garcia Adsten, a senior guard-forward, are among the newcomers who could be immediately impactful.
“DeAndre is a proven player at our level. Villiam is a really unique player who is a 6-foot-9 wing and can play all over the floor. He has played in a lot of big games,” Markwood said.
Williams averaged 6.8 points, 2.9 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 94 games at Holy Cross. Adsten averaged 3.5 points and 3.8 rebounds at Drexel a year ago.
Two other transfers, Ohio University’s Ayden Evans and Oliver Faubert from St. Mary’s, will provide an inside presence at 6-foot-10 and 6-9, respectively. Faubert is currently nursing an injury.
Two freshmen who could earn significant minutes are guard Hudson Franz and forward Wesley Waddles, according to Markwood.
Returning forward Yanis Bamba showed promise a year ago and could figure more prominently.
Husson has lost its top two scorers but third-leading scorer Andre McCauley (14.7 points) and number five point-producer Christian Smith (11.6) are back. Smith’s 3.2 assists per game led the team and McCauley averaged 2.9.
McCauley also averaged 3.8 rebounds and Smith grabbed 2.4. Both are guards.

title: White House holds little-known American art collection
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The White House, known as the home of the president of the United States, also houses an art collection that author Leslie Greene Bowman says rivals museums anywhere in the world.
Bowman, an American art historian, served under four presidents on the Committee for the Preservation of the White House. She has written a new book, “Art for the White House,” detailing the art collection inside the executive mansion.
“Most Washingtonians, most Americans, don’t really know very much about it. And yet here it’s just right on par with any of the great museums in this city and their American art collections,” Bowman said.
Bowman said the collection started with one image.
“The finest in the collection is the great, iconic, full-length portrait of George Washington as our first president. And it moved into the White House before any other furniture did,” Bowman said.
The White House art collection remained largely unchanged until First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy grew the gallery, using landscapes and portraits to represent the people, history and culture of the nation. Since then, every presidential administration has added to the collection.
Bowman said although beautiful, the collection serves a broader purpose.
“It’s a wonderful ambassador for our civilization and our culture through the lens of great art,” Bowman said.
People can view the White House art collection by booking an in-person tour, taking a virtual walk-through on the White House Historical Association’s website, visiting The People’s House, or reading “Art for the White House.”

title: Fire devastates Eagle's Nest retreat built for Hitler in Germany; A suspect is detained
text:
A fire devastates the Eagle's Nest retreat built for Hitler in Germany. A suspect is detained
A fire swept through the mountaintop retreat built for Adolf Hitler and known as the Eagle's Nest as emergency services struggled to tackle the blaze in snow and wind, and a man was arrested on suspicion of arson, authorities said Saturday.
Related video above: World War II medal returned to veteran’s family after being lost for years
Emergency services in the Berchtesgaden district, in the Bavarian Alps in Germany's southeastern corner, were alerted to the fire by an alarm at about 9:15 p.m. Friday. Firefighters and police rushed to the scene — located at the end of a narrow road that winds up the mountain, in part through a series of tunnels — and could see the flames as they approached.
They stopped and arrested a man on a motorcycle driving the other way down the road.
Prosecutors said the 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but does not currently live there, was questioned. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building's history. Police said there were no current indications that anyone else was involved.
Rain that turned into the year's first snow, accompanied by strong wind, complicated the already difficult task of tackling the blaze, and firefighters had to pull out overnight after several hours, officials said. No one was injured in the fire, and firefighters hoped to finish their work Saturday, though they were not able to enter the building because of a danger of falling material.
The building, known in German as the Kehlsteinhaus, is located on a cliff 1,834 meters (6,017 feet) above sea level. It is reachable by an elevator built inside the rock from the end of the mountain road, which is closed to public traffic but used during the day by buses for visitors.
It has been operated as a cafe and restaurant since 1952 and contains an exhibition on its history. The Nazi dictator himself rarely used the Kehlsteinhaus — unlike the Berghof residence, also in the Berchtesgaden area, the ruins of which were blown up in 1952.
The Obersalzberg Documentation Center, further down the mountain, is home to the area's main historical exhibition and was unaffected by the fire.
Officials indicated that the Eagle's Nest would be restored, though they were vague so soon after the blaze about how exactly that would be done.
“We're not going to leave a ruin there,” Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, told reporters in Berchtesgaden. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.
“I think we will be able to find a sensible solution,” Herrmann added. Bavaria's state government owns the building.
The minister stressed that “it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance.”

title: Falmouth’s Georgia Moon pulls away in A South cross country regional
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
CUMBERLAND —Georgia Moon’s game plan Saturday was to stay with the pack until she felt ready to kick, and then just go for it.
Moon timed her move perfectly as was able to hold off Portland’s Nora Schmidt by just over a second to win the Class A girls race in the Southern Maine regionals at Twin Brook Recreation Area.
Moon, a senior at Falmouth, finished in 18 minutes, 11.51 seconds, while Schmidt’s time was 18:12.63.
“(My strategy) just ended up being challenging,” Moon said. “But it works out in the end. Down the stretch, I just kept thinking ‘I know I have (strength) in my legs.’ I’ve done the workouts, I’ve done the physical work. I know it’s there. I just had to trust that I know it’s there.”
Allie Schmitt of Cheverus (19:00.38) finished third. The results were a swap from last year’s regional final, when Schmidt held off Moon, with Schmitt rounding out the top three.
Moon also won the girls race at the Festival of Champions in Belfast last month.
Portland once again swept the Class A South boys and girls titles. In the girls race, the Bulldogs scored 63 points, followed by Thornton Academy (70) and Falmouth (71). Portland (47 points) cruised to the boys title, beating out Thornton (64) and Bonny Eagle (117). The Bulldogs had four boys in the top 10, led by Ambrose Clarke (17:12.41), who was sixth.
Scarborough senior Atticus Merriam, the winner at the Festival of Champions, had a strong finishing kick to hold off Falmouth’s Mateo Diaz (16:32.94) and win the Class A boys crown with a time of 16:21.36.
“I was trying to be a little conservative today, try to save myself for states a little bit,” Merriam said. “I ended up fighting pretty hard. Mateo and Ryan both gave me pretty good races. But I felt strong enough that I could make a move, and it worked out … I’m feeling good (for states). I’ve gotten some quality training in. My coaches have helped me out a lot. I’m just doing my workouts and feeling great.”
Ryan Bolduc (16:48.49) of Thornton was third.
Lincoln Academy’s Karen Higgins had the most dominant race of the day, winning the Class B title in 19:14.29. She was more than a minute faster than Freeport teammates Ella Oshteski (20:17.99) and Stella Kryzak (20:18.04).
“This race has been one I’ve wanted to win for a while,” Higgins said. “It was good to do it, and it was fun. (The trail) wasn’t muddy. The only issue I had (with the course) was the pebbles weren’t pebbles. They were pretty big rocks. That was a little difficult to navigate, but I just stayed on the trail.”
Freeport (50 points) repeated as B South girls champion, followed by Yarmouth (63) and Cape Elizabeth (67).
Yarmouth junior Bowen Mitchell (16:38.98) held off teammate Jackie Chalmers (16:47.06) for the individual boys title.
“There’s no better feeling than a win,” Mitchell said.
The duo led a dominant day for the Clippers, who placed four runners in the top five. Eli Chalmers (16:52.01) finished third.
“From day one of summer training, Jackie and I have been saying we’re going to go 1-2 at states,” Mitchell said. “Our team was so great (today), and I definitely think it’s a possibility.”
Yarmouth scored 23 points, finishing well in front of Freeport (78). The Falcons were led by fourth-place finisher Mungu Tussing (16:54.70). Cape Elizabeth (92) was third.
Dirigo senior William Morris, who won the Mountain Valley Conference championship last weekend, continued a strong postseason by winning the Class C boys race with a time of 16:19.81. James Vaillancourt (16:42.79) of North Yarmouth Academy was the runner-up and Winthrop freshman Sawyer Wess (16:43.66) was third.
Winthrop (44 points) repeated as team champion, with Maranacook (106) the runner-up. Carrabec (124) was third.
Reagan Mattson of Maranacook (19:52.98) won the Class C girls race and celebrated the victory with a cartwheel as she crossed the finish line. McKenzie Boyle (20:36.89) of Dirigo finished second and Kylie Van Tassel (20:46.30) of Winthrop placed third.
Maine Coast Waldorf (60 points) won the C girls crown, followed by Boothbay/Wiscasset (91) and Maranacook (101).
Temperatures were ideal for running, in the high 50s with blue skies and little cloud coverage.

title: Fraternity suspended until 2030 after hazing investigation
text:
TUSCALOOSA, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - A University of Alabama fraternity has been suspended for nearly four years.
According to a report on the university’s End Hazing website, Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc.’s Eta Chi chapter will not be recognized by the university through May 2030.
The report cites an investigation that found seven people hazed new members,
The report continued, stating that members were subjected to verbal and physical abuse, which included forcing or coercing the members into participating in acts of personal servitude, physical discomfort, illegal activities and degrading activities.
The report claimed these activities led to some members being hurt while alleging new members were denied privileges and provided alcohol and drugs.
The incident was said to have occurred off campus in September 2025 and was reported through an anti-hazing hotline nearly a month later.
The report noted an investigation was resolved in May. No arrests were made.
The University of Alabama and Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc.’s national headquarters did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the situation.

title: Van Buren Moves On! Four More County Soccer Teams Play Saturday
text:
The County Scoreboard: Van Buren Advances, XC Regionals and Four Playoff Games Saturday
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships are underway, and we've already had a little bit of everything here in the County.
Van Buren's boys are moving on after a 3-1 victory over Schenck on Friday, while Katahdin saw its season come to an end in a close 2-1 loss to Lee Academy.
And we're just getting started.
Four more County soccer teams are scheduled for playoff games Saturday, including a pair of home matchups for Caribou's boys and Fort Kent's girls.
Meanwhile, County cross country runners are headed to Belfast for the Northern Maine Regional Championships, with state championship berths on the line.
Van Buren Moves On With Win Over Schenck
The seventh-seeded Van Buren Crusaders made the most of their home-field advantage Friday, defeating No. 10 Schenck 3-1 in the eight-person boys preliminary round.
Alex Bebout, Dom Burgess and Gavin Cormier each scored for Van Buren.
Marcus Hutchins scored the lone goal for the Wolverines.
The victory sends the Crusaders into the regional quarterfinals, where they'll face third-seeded Calais.
It's another opportunity for Van Buren to keep its season going, although the Crusaders will have a tougher test waiting in the next round.
Katahdin's Season Ends in Close Loss to Lee Academy
Sixth-seeded Katahdin came up just short Friday, falling 2-1 to No. 11 Lee Academy in another eight-person boys preliminary matchup.
Conor Schmidt scored the Cougars' lone goal, while goalkeeper Gage Phillips finished with seven saves.
Lee Academy received goals from Alberto Perez and Martin Tapiador, while Lance Haskell made eight saves.
It was a tough way for Katahdin's season to end, especially after the Cougars put together several strong performances down the stretch.
Schmidt had been one of the County's most productive scorers throughout the season, and Phillips had delivered some impressive performances in net.
The Cougars' tournament run ends in the preliminary round, while Lee Academy advances.
Saturday Brings Four More County Soccer Playoff Games
There's no shortage of soccer on Saturday's schedule, with four County teams looking to keep their seasons alive.
Eight-Person Boys: Houlton Travels to Penquis
Ninth-seeded Houlton heads to eighth-seeded Penquis for a 2 p.m. preliminary matchup.
The Shires will be looking to pick up a road victory and move into the quarterfinal round.
Class B Boys: Caribou Hosts Medomak Valley
Eighth-seeded Caribou will have home-field advantage Saturday when the Vikings welcome No. 9 Medomak Valley for a 2 p.m. preliminary game.
The Vikings finished the regular season with some strong results, including a pair of shutout victories over Hermon.
Now Caribou gets the opportunity to carry that momentum into tournament play.
Class C Girls: Fort Kent Welcomes MCI
Top-seeded Fort Kent begins its postseason Saturday afternoon, hosting eighth-seeded Maine Central Institute at 2 p.m. in a Class C North quarterfinal.
The Lady Warriors enter the tournament as the No. 1 seed, putting them in a strong position as the regional playoffs begin.
Eight-Person Girls: Katahdin Heads to Penquis
Ninth-seeded Katahdin travels to eighth-seeded Penquis for a noon preliminary matchup.
The Lady Cougars will be looking to extend their season with a road victory.
County Runners Head to Belfast for Regional Championships
Soccer isn't the only postseason action happening Saturday.
The Northern Maine Regional Cross Country Championships are being held in Belfast, with County runners competing for the opportunity to advance to next weekend's state championships.
The top seven teams and top 30 individual finishers qualify for states.
County programs are coming off an outstanding performance at last weekend's PVC Championships, where Houlton/GHCA's boys, Presque Isle's girls and Caribou's boys all captured team titles.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves also earned individual PVC championships.
Caribou's Thomas Beckum was named PVC Girls Coach of the Year, while Presque Isle's Dylan Marrero earned Boys Coach of the Year honors.
Saturday brings another opportunity for those runners and their teammates to prove themselves against the rest of Northern Maine.

title: Judge allows lawsuit against Maine salmon firm to proceed
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A judge has ruled that the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) can move forward with its lawsuit in Maine against Cooke Aquaculture, one of the world’s largest salmon producers, for allegedly violating the Clean Water Act.
The Canadian company has 13 active sites in Maine, including in Cobscook Bay and Machias Bay, where the company grows millions of salmon.
The company strongly denies the allegations and had filed a motion to have CLF’s suit dismissed. However, on September 30 U.S. District Court Judge Karen Frink Wolf ruled that all but one of the six claims in CLF’s lawsuit could proceed and a portion of that one claim can also be considered by the court.
Concerning the allegation that Cooke is violating the state’s effluent limitations through unlawful discharges, the judge found that two sections of the National Pollution Elimination Discharge System (NPDES) permit issued by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) are unenforceable, since they do not explain what Cooke must do to comply with the permit’s provisions. The judge declined to dismiss the portion of that claim that alleges that Cooke discharges pollutants containing materials that are hazardous to aquatic life.
“This ruling brings us one step closer to protecting the health of Maine’s waters and the ecosystems, industries and communities that rely on them,” says CLF senior attorney Maggie Nivison in a release. “These enormous salmon cages are like sewage pipes to the marine environment. Accountability matters, and we need to enforce our laws to safeguard Maine’s bays and communities.”
Most of Cooke’s salmon cage sites are located in coastal communities where lobstermen and fishermen depend on clean and unpolluted water for their livelihoods. Fish feces, uneaten food and uncollected pieces of dead fish fall through the bottom of Cooke’s cages onto the seafloor to form a thick layer of sediment, according to CLF, which alleges that pollution kills food sources for lobster and bottom‑feeding fish, like flounder, cod and haddock.
CLF sued Cooke in 2025 for violations of the Clean Water Act. The environmental advocacy organization alleges that salmon confined to net pens suffer from disease and parasites such as sea lice at an unnaturally high rate.
“These diseases and parasites can spread from the cages to passing wild fish,” the organization states in a release. “In addition, Cooke’s cages periodically develop holes from exposure to weather and predators like seals, which allow caged salmon to escape. When cage raised salmon breed with wild salmon, the genetic fitness of the wild salmon population is diminished.”
CLF states that Cooke’s NPDES permit does not allow the discharge of escaped fish, sea lice, disease or trash, which CLF alleges continues to occur at the salmon pen sites. The organization alleges that Cooke’s net pen sites are discharging effluent in violation of the permit’s sulfide limitation. As for fish escapes, the notice points to the 50,000 salmon that escaped from the Cross Island sites in Machias Bay in May 2023, following a seal attack.
Cooke Aquaculture, though, has previously stated in a release that the allegations “are false, misleading and lack any substantiating evidence.” The company says it is in full compliance with the laws set forth by the Maine DEP, the Maine Department of Marine Resources and its operating permits.
“Cooke’s Maine Atlantic salmon farms are routinely inspected by state regulators and subject to regular monitoring reports. These laws are designed to protect Maine waters as well as Maine’s heritage fisheries,” states the release, which was issued by Steven Hedlund, director of public affairs for Cooke Aquaculture USA.
The release points out that the company’s salmon farms are also routinely audited and certified by third-party sustainability organizations. Cooke was one of the early adopters of the Global Seafood Alliance’s Best Aquaculture Practices third-party certification program.
As part of this independent, voluntary program, all of Cooke’s Maine salmon aquaculture farms, hatcheries, processing plants and feed mills are audited against standards for environmental responsibility, social accountability, animal health and welfare and food safety.
Additionally, Atlantic salmon farmed in Maine is rated as a “good alternative” by the Monterey Bay Aquarium’s Seafood Watch program.
In the release, Hedlund notes that finfish aquaculture has coexisted with fisheries, such as lobstering, in Maine waters for more than 40 years.
“Lobster landings are not negatively affected by Atlantic salmon farms,” the release states. “In fact, lobster gear is set alongside and within aquaculture lease boundaries.”
However, from 2014 through 2024, the Maine DEP did issue 26 warnings and notices to Cooke and reached one consent agreement that imposed a fine for violations of its Maine Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (MEPDES) permit for net‑pen aquaculture. Many of those violations involved failure to meet the DEP’s reporting requirements or exceeding the maximum number of fish per pen. The consent agreement issued in September 2019 imposed a monetary penalty of $156,213.
The Conservation Law Foundation believes that, to comply with the law, Cooke will need to hire more employees and experts to increase its monitoring and inspections, properly maintain and clean its equipment and mitigate the impact on the environment.

title: What’s on the November ballot in the Kennebunks?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
With no local races on the ballot in the Kennebunks, residents will step into the voting booth on Nov. 3 to approve referendum questions set forth by the towns’ select boards.
The referendums include two Kennebunkport questions on funding for Christmas Prelude, potential tightening of Kennebunk’s rules surrounding recalls of elected officials, and a proposed expansion of the Kennebunk Light and Power District’s debt limit.
Voters in both town will also elect a state senator and state representative.
Here’s what you need to know.
KENNEBUNK
Kennebunk residents will vote to on eight questions, which include amendments to the town charter and planning and zoning ordinances.
Article A would open the door for the Select Board to authorize funding for a public service. Currently, undesignated funds from the municipal operating budget may only be used if an emergency is declared. If the amendment is approved, the Select Board would be able to designate funds — from either the town’s surplus budget or unanticipated revenues — for a public need, as the board deems necessary.
Article B, if approved, would require any article proposals from the budget board to be presented to the Select Board before heading to the ballot.
Article C is an amendment that would give the town manager an extra 30 days to submit their budget proposal to the budget board and Select Board.
Article D would amend the circumstances for recall of an elected official, imposing stricter requirements.
One proposed requirement would raise the number of valid signatures required to petition a recall from 25 registered voters to 50. The amendment would also change the guidance on what reasons qualify for attempting a recall.
Referendum article E would increase the debt limit for the Kennebunk Light and Power District from $6 million to $30 million. The last time the utility’s debt limit was raised was 2006, according to the district.
Approval of this article wouldn’t automatically authorize any funding but would instead give the utility the ability to request to borrow up to that limit. According to the KLPD, a five-year plan identified critical investments required to adequately maintain the electric system, so increased borrowing is anticipated.
Article F would terminate a lease agreement the town has held on land beside Main Street to allow for a public walkway on privately owned property. Now, the town has since acquired adjacent property and established a public walkway between the Waterhouse Center and the public parking lot. Town Engineer Chris Osterrieder said that acquisition makes the lease agreement moot, and Article F is simply to finalize its termination.
Article G’s approval would allow the town to give the Neighborhood Housing Trust a portion of town-owned property to turn into affordable housing. The nonprofit organization is dedicated to providing affordable housing in Kennebunk, Kennebunkport and Arundel.
Trust Executive Director Larissa Crockett said in September, in an interview about another project, that the goal of the referendum was to establish a few affordable single-family homes off Factory Pasture Lane.
The final article, Article H, would amend the town’s zoning ordinance to allow residents in the Shoreland Zone to apply for preemptive alterations to their property to protect from future issues like weather events that could be worsened by climate change. Osterrieder said that change wouldn’t allow immediate changes but would open the door for property owners to apply.
KENNEBUNKPORT
Residents of Kennebunkport will decide on four referendum questions, two of which are based around town funding for Christmas Prelude.
The first two questions, however, are amendments to the town’s land use ordinance. Question 1 would, if approved, make conditional uses in each zone subject to review by the planning board or code enforcement officer. Currently, these conditional uses are subject to review by the Zoning Board of Appeals.
A list of the conditional uses in question can be found on the town’s website.
Question 2 would divide home occupations under the zoning ordinance into two types: Type A and Type B. Type A covers normal residences, while Type B is a designation for home businesses that could generate vehicular traffic from patrons. Type A homes would fall under the jurisdiction of the code enforcement officer, while Type B residences would require planning board approval.
The last two questions relate to Prelude. Funding for the event has been at the epicenter of local discussions over the past year, ever since the discovery of an ordinance that indicated the town could not cover any municipal cost incurred by the event, even though it had been for years.
In June, the town held a nonbinding vote to gauge how residents felt about municipal funds going to the event and how much, if any, should be spent. A majority of voters supported at least some funding — 41% backed full funding, while another 22% preferred partial funding — so the Select Board agreed that the solution that had the highest chance of passing in November was covering half of the municipal cost.
Question 3 on the ballot is to amend the mass gathering ordinance to allow the town to fund a portion of the event, including the annual Dock Square tree lighting, Cape Porpoise tree lighting and one of the parades.
Question 4 is to approve $17,500 of town funds for this year’s Prelude.
STATE RACES
Voters in both towns will elect a new state senator for District 34, which also includes Berwick, North Berwick and Wells. Residents will decide between Democrat Dan Sayre, currently serving as state representative for District 135, and Republican Jonathan Fallon.
Residents will also elect state representatives.
Those in House District 134 — encompassing Kennebunkport and the coastal portions of Kennebunk and Biddeford — will decide between three-term incumbent Democratic Rep. Traci Gere and Kennebunkport Select Board member Allen Daggett, an independent.
The voters of House District 135, covering the inland parts of Kennebunk, will decide between Kennebunk Select Board member Lisa Joy Pratt, a Democrat, and independent Scott Craig, a retired supply chain executive who unsuccessfully sought this seat in 2024.

title: National Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial opens Saturday
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A new monument on the National Mall honors those who served in the first Gulf War.
The National Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial officially opened after more than four years of construction.
The memorial honors those who served while educating visitors about the conflict and the 34-country coalition that participated in the war defending Kuwait.
U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum spoke at the opening.
“We left our homes and our families and traveled thousands of miles and fought in strange places because it became our duty,” Burgum said. “We reflect on that powerful and effective coalition. And today, as a country and a world, we pray for a similar rallying together for freedom.”
The monument was constructed using materials reflecting the environment and battle conditions in the Gulf.
It is located just north of the Lincoln Memorial.

title: Jury convicts man of rape, murder 14 years after college student’s death
text:
DURHAM, N.C. (AP) - A man accused of killing a North Carolina college student 14 years ago was convicted Friday of first-degree murder, rape and other charges after prosecutors told jurors that forensic evidence was “screaming his name.”
Faith Hedgepeth was a 19-year-old sophomore at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill when she was beaten to death in her off-campus apartment in September 2012. Miguel Salguero Olivares was arrested nine years later after being pulled over for driving while intoxicated and providing a DNA sample that prosecutors say matched evidence from the crime scene.
Salguero Olivares, 33, did not testify during the trial, and his attorneys rested their case without calling any witnesses. Jurors deliberated for six hours over two days before convicting him of murder, rape, sexual offense and burglary. He was then sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole on the murder charge plus 45-65 years on the other charges.
Hedgepeth’s mother, Connie Hedgepeth, told the judge that she forgave her daughter’s killer long ago.
“It was just three weeks after her death. It didn’t matter who done it, I knew that I had to forgive, and I do forgive, but my heart aches for his family,” she said. “It was just such a senseless and cruel act, but we have to go on, and we just have to trust God and go on with our lives.”
Roland Hedgepeth, Faith’s father, said losing his daughter was like having his heart ripped out. He called her a beacon of hope who was born at a low point in his life and admitted it had been easier over the past 5,158 days to say he forgave someone he didn’t know.
“Today it got very real,” he said. “Nevertheless, I say it without reservation, I forgive Miguel for what he did.”
Calling those statements “powerful and kind,” defense attorney James Rainsford said he also could speak about his client and his client’s family but decided not to. “For me to try to blend the two things, I don’t think that’s what everybody needs at this point.”
Defense argued the client was falsely accused
In closing arguments Thursday, defense attorneys accused investigators of having “tunnel vision” in assuming that their client was a monster and not a “19-year-old boy” who had consensual sex with the victim days before her death. Prosecutors, meanwhile, urged jurors to rely on DNA evidence instead of distractions from the defense team.
“We know who did it. The forensic evidence is screaming his name,” said prosecutor Angela Garcia-Lamarca, who described the “uncurable agony” Hedgepeth’s family has endured.
“When the defendant brought that bottle down on her head and she started to bleed, that was the start of a bleeding that still hasn’t stopped,” she said. “He sentenced her to death. He sentenced everybody else who loved her to life. There was no one there to protect her. There was no one there to stop him — until now. Y’all are here. You’re here now, and you can stop him.”
Prosecution suggests victim spurned defendant’s advances
Nearly two dozen witnesses testified for the prosecution, including crime scene technicians, state and local law enforcement, a DNA expert and Hedgepeth’s friends.
Hedgepeth’s roommate, Karena Rosario, testified that she was drunk and sick when Hedgepeth drove them home from a club around 2 a.m. that Sept. 7. She said she later called a friend to pick her up, leaving Hedgepeth in the apartment alone. She returned hours later to find her roommate’s body.
Though no witnesses corroborated the theory, prosecutors suggested Salguero Olivares may have attended a barbecue hosted by Hedgepeth’s neighbor that night, unsuccessfully hit on the young women in the parking lot and then returned, embarrassed and angry, after Rosario left.
Forensic evidence was a focus
Experts testified that the defendant’s fingerprints and palm print were found on a wine bottle at the scene and that his DNA was found in Hedgepeth’s body, on a note written on a fast-food bag found at the scene and on a rum bottle covered in blood that investigators identified as the weapon in the killing.
Defense attorneys questioned Rosario’s account of that night, the processing of the crime scene and the reliability of some DNA evidence. They pointed out that police failed to search some areas of the apartment and later lost some possible blood evidence and emphasized that DNA from sexual intercourse can remain for days afterward.
“Maybe he was living the same life as other 19- and 20-year-old children that we’ve heard about in this case,” defense attorney Jason Murphy said. “Maybe he had too much to drink, maybe he forgot about an encounter.”
But special prosecutor Lisa Coltrane dismissed that as “noise.”
“No matter what kind of mistakes were made or things that were missed, it doesn’t erase the palm print; it doesn’t somehow lift the DNA out of Faith,” she said. “They didn’t talk to every single person in Chapel Hill, and it doesn’t matter. They still got the guy because he left his DNA like confetti all over that room.”

title: Russian disinformation group targets James Talarico with baseless claim in AI-generated video
text:
Russian disinformation group targets James Talarico with baseless claim in AI-generated video
A social media video purporting to show a former student accusing Texas Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico of sexual misconduct is the latest example of how Russian groups are generating false information to influence U.S. elections, researchers say.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
As of Oct. 22, X had suspended the account that originally posted the baseless claim, but other accounts have since shared it. NewsGuard, a company that tracks online misinformation, reported that X said the account was created in September with Romania as the signup country.
Talarico spokesperson JT Ennis issued an emailed statement to PolitiFact about the video.
“The most powerful people in the world know they can’t beat James Talarico with the truth, so they’re slandering him with AI deepfakes, foreign bots, and conspiracy theories to protect their broken, corrupt political system,” Ennis said.
What we know about the video’s origin
Darren Linvill, a Clemson University professor and head of its Media Forensic Hub, said the video is the work of Storm-1516, a Russian propaganda campaign he said made a similar baseless attack on Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz in 2024 when Walz ran for vice president. In 2024, the group used a paid actor from West Africa to attack Walz, Linvill said.
Linvill said this video was generated to look like a real man who has an account on another platform. The video shows a man claiming to have been a former student of Talarico at Rhodes Middle School in San Antonio, Texas, where Talarico taught Language Arts before his political career as a state representative.
Graphika, a social media analytics company, said in a blog post that the X account that originally shared the video “very likely” impersonated a Facebook user by the same name. That person lives in Texas and was a former student of Talarico. The man has praised Talarico on his Facebook page on several occasions, as recently as February, Graphika noted.
Fact-checkers at Lead Stories spoke with that man and he said the video is not of him, and denied accusing Talarico of misconduct. PolitiFact reached out to him via Facebook, but he didn’t immediately respond. PolitiFact’s review of the man’s Facebook page found no video of him accusing Talarico.
NewsGuard reported that the videos had many signs of AI generation, such as unnatural eye movements and stagnant facial expressions, and that an AI detection tool showed a 98% likelihood of being a deepfake. A deepfake is a machine generated image or video that changes faces, bodies or voices, making people appear to do and say things that they never did or said.
Graphika said social media accounts known to amplify Storm-1516 content and several accounts from U.S. conservatives shared the video. It said a prominent Storm-1516 amplifier, SGAnon, originally shared the video, then deleted it, writing on X that an analysis showed it was “artificially generated.”
The Russian disinformation playbook
Linvill said Storm-1516 typically uses the same influencers to spread false narratives into political conversations.
“If you examine the recent content of the influencers who first shared this narrative you can easily identify other Storm-1516 lies,” Linvill said. “We believe they are paid to do this. In the same way marketing companies pay influencers to share products, the Russians pay influencers to share lies.”
The New York Times recently reported that Russia and other foreign governments have stepped up efforts to influence U.S. elections, mostly targeting Democrats.
Linvill co-wrote a recent report about Storm-1516 and its work targeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and found such campaigns often are not aimed at changing people’s behavior or opinions, but seek to shape public discourse.
He said the study’s findings apply to this baseless Talarico narrative.
“By entrenching people in this view of Talarico, the Russians likely hope to exacerbate extreme partisanship and also encourage people to get off the couch and vote for Ken Paxton,” Linvill said. “People who already like Talarico are going to dismiss this claim as the obvious fake it is, but they aren’t the audience.”
We rate the claim that this video shows Talarico’s former student accusing him of misconduct False.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Retired custodian gets new elementary school named in her honor
text:
AUBREY, Texas (WFAA) — A new elementary school in Texas will be named after Marilyn Hampton, a retired custodian who worked for the district for 39 years.
The Aubrey Independent School District surprised Hampton with the announcement during a red carpet presentation at Wednesday’s board meeting.
Surprise announcement
Hampton was asked to roll out a red carpet, a task similar to those she performed during her career as a custodian. It took her several seconds to realize what the carpet was for.
“Oh my goodness,” Hampton said. “Oh, God. You all are the best.”
The school, previously known only as Elementary School Number Five, will be named Marilyn Hampton Elementary.
“I still can’t believe it. I haven’t stopped crying,” Hampton said.
A 39-year career
Hampton spent 39 years as an Aubrey Independent School District custodian.
Superintendent Shannon Saylor said Hampton did more than custodial work during that time, including buying and delivering school supplies and helping students study for tests.
“She is truly Aubrey ISD,” Saylor said.
Saylor said Hampton left behind “her teaching legacy” about being kind, working hard and persevering.
Hampton is one of eight siblings and the only one to graduate high school. She said she used to think of herself as a failure for not going to college.
“I just thought, ‘You know, Marilyn? God put you where you are supposed to be.’ And I’m very happy with the way things turned out,” Hampton said.
Second career
Hampton now spends time in a rocking chair at the Aubrey Independent School District Early Bird Learning Center, feeding a young girl named Claire.
“She’s a sweetheart. She’s got pretty eyes,” Hampton said of Claire.
The district gave Hampton a Marilyn Hampton Elementary shirt to mark the announcement ahead of the school’s opening.
“Can you believe it? I can’t. I cannot. All I can say is God is good,” Hampton said.
Marilyn Hampton Elementary opens next August.

title: Survivors of Lewiston mass shooting mark anniversary, honor victims with cornhole tournament
text:
LEWISTON — Jason Barnett tossed a beanbag in the air. It hit the cornhole board opposite him with a thud. He threw another that flew into the hole, earning the familiar nod of his teammate, John Petrocelli.
Barnett and Petrocelli were cornhole partners Saturday, like they were nearly three years ago at Schemengees Bar & Grille in Lewiston when they survived the mass shooting that killed 18 people and injured 13. They played this weekend at Just-in-Time Recreation, the bowling alley the shooter attacked on Oct. 25, 2023, before he headed to Schmengees.
Just-in-Time closed after the tragedy but reopened six months later, while Schmengees permanently shuttered. This was the third year TB Events held a cornhole tournament around the anniversary of the attack to raise funds for Maine Resiliency Center — an organization dedicated to helping people navigate the impacts of the shooting — and to unite survivors, families of victims and others who were affected.
“It gets us all back together, it keeps that alive, and it heals us at the same time,” Barnett said.
In April, Just-In-Time owners Justin and Samantha Juray began ripping out six bowling lanes to create a carpeted space for cornhole. The change combines the two activities many of the survivors of the shooting love, but found too painful to participate in, in the months and years after the attack. Survivors of the shooting wore shirts that said “Survivor” on the back and “Lewiston Strong” on the front.
“To see people get over that fear and walk through those doors for the first time again is pretty awesome,” said Justin Juray, who survived the attack while running the bowling alley.
Danielle Jasper said she and a group of other survivors who endured watching other cornhole players die in the shooting regularly get together to play weekly, not just on the anniversary.
“People that I didn’t know before that night are like family now,” Jasper said.
Tyler Babb, owner of TB Events, said turnout at the event exceeded his expectations — he had laid out eight games, but added two more to accommodate the nearly 170 people who signed up across the afternoon and evening tournaments. Entry was $20 per team, which the Maine Resiliency Fund uses to help connect people affected by the shooting with counseling and other resources.
It was not only survivors and the immediate family members of victims who came to play — some drove multiple hours because they enjoy cornhole and wanted to support the fund.
Kathy Bartley, of Houlton, organizes a weekly cornhole league at home and tries to travel to other Maine towns to play, too — she has a friend who was injured in the shooting at Just-in-Time. And Trina Cayford, a professional cornhole player from Bangor who competes nationally with her husband, Phil Cayford, said she came just to connect with people and support the cause.
“Everyone grieves in their own kind of way,” Babb said. “For a lot of people, they’re die-hard cornhole players and community members. And I think that means more to them than anything else ever would.”
The Maine Resiliency Center will hold a candlelight vigil at Simard-Payne Memorial Park,46 Beech St., from 6-8 p.m. It will begin at the entrance of the park, with attendees walking together to the Longley Bridge for the vigil.

title: Some interesting insects to look for before winter
text:
With temperatures rapidly dropping, daylight hours getting shorter and impending winter conditions approaching, I wanted to use this column to point out a few animals that won’t be around much longer: some insects.
These ectothermic (relying on external sources of heat) invertebrates don’t fare too well in freezing temperatures, but there are a few pretty interesting ones to be on the lookout for before this window closes.
First up, I should mention some of the most commonly encountered, abundant and recognizable insects. The non-native Asian lady beetle is a red and black beetle; these have been around all summer, but tend to have a spike in detections in the fall as they look for warm places to spend the winter. Cold nights trigger these movements, and they are especially fond of entering human dwellings for a warmer reprieve.
The other insect you’ll find sneaking inside is the western conifer seed bug, often mistaken for a “stinkbug” because of the pungent smell it produces after being disturbed. The western conifer seed bugs are a reddish brown color and are in the family Coreidae, the “leaf-footed bugs” that have flat leaf-like sections on their hind legs. Note also that they are not a “beetle” in the order Coleoptera (like the Asian lady beetle) because they don’t have the hardened wing casings that beetles uniquely do.
Speaking of things with cool wings, most of our Lepidoptera, the scaly-winged insects, better known as butterflies and moths, are soon to be gone. During these last warm days, you may see butterflies like clouded sulphur (mostly yellow) and American ladies (mostly orange with spots) flying around. We do have some November records of monarchs in Maine, but flowers will be hard to come by for any pollinators needing sustenance at that point.
Another lepidopteran to look for has one of my favorite names in the animal kingdom: Bruce spanworm. This native moth has an interesting approach to successful reproduction — it waits until there aren’t many threats around. As it gets cold in November, and very few predators of moths are around (bats have migrated or begun hibernating), the adult males will take advantage of a warm night to have large flights in search of females. The females, which are actually flightless, wait at the tips of a host tree limb. They attract males with a seductive pheromone. Unfortunately, there is also a non-native species of moth that does the same thing, the winter moth. These are very similar species, both in the genus Operophtera, and cannot be visually distinguished. You’d need to dissect them to actually tell them apart.
Not an insect, but an arachnid worth mentioning is the dreaded eastern black-legged tick. These blood suckers are paradoxically one animal you don’t want to see … unless it’s on you, and then you do before it digs into your skin. Adults are especially active in fall with their biggest spike in activity in October, so despite many invertebrates being inactive, you should keep doing tick checks after spending time outdoors.
The last plug I have to make, which is also a good way to avoid getting ticks, is to leave your leaves on the ground. Those leaves will provide important nutrients for the soil and shelter for many beloved animals, from wood frogs to woolly bear caterpillars (aka Isabella tiger moths). So drop the rake and kick your feet up, or grab your binoculars and spend that time outside looking for late butterflies and migrating birds. The snow will be here soon (northern Maine has already seen flurries), so enjoy the fall days and help your backyard wildlife at the same time.
Have you got a nature or wildlife question of your own? It doesn’t have to be about birds! Email questions to [email protected] and visit www.maineaudubon.org to learn more about birding, native plants, and programs and events focusing on Maine wildlife and habitat. Maine Audubon Staff Naturalist Doug Hitchcox and other naturalists lead free bird walks on Thursday mornings starting at 7 am, at Maine Audubon’s Gilsland Farm Audubon Sanctuary in Falmouth.

title: Ex-soldier sentenced to 59 years in prison for killing wife, stuffing body in storm drain
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - An Alaskan man was sentenced this week, three years after authorities say he murdered his wife and attempted to conceal it.
On Friday, former U.S. Army Spec. Zarrius Hildabrand, 24, was given a 59-year prison sentence for fatally shooting his wife, 21-year-old Alaska National Guard Spec. Saria Hildabrand, on Aug. 6, 2023.
Both were actively serving at the time of the murder.
Hildabrand was convicted on second-degree murder and tampering with physical evidence charges in June, although he was also acquitted of a first-degree murder charge.
The prosecution said during the nearly two-week trial that after a night out celebrating his 21st birthday, Hildabrand shot his wife after she discovered him cheating.
The defense pushed back against the state’s argument and claimed that Saria Hildabrand died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Following Saria Hildabrand’s death, authorities said Zarrius Hildabrand reported her missing and moved her body to a storm drain near the couple’s apartment.
The former soldier then assisted in search efforts until her body was later discovered.

title: Police say 110,000 people march in Paris as protest ends with tear gas and water cannon
text:
PARIS (AP) — Clashes erupted in Paris as a mass march drew to a close Saturday, with more than 400,000 people rallying across France over school funding and soaring living costs in a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron. Police made nearly 1,000 arrests, the government said.
The Paris march began peacefully, a week after widespread rioting and looting during protests across the country. But near the demonstration’s endpoint in eastern Paris, masked protesters hurled objects and fireworks at police, who answered with clouds of tear gas, deafening sound grenades and jets of water cannons.
Officers with megaphones urged protesters to disperse. Some demonstrators panicked as tear-gas canisters landed in their midst, scattering with screams. Veteran protesters shouted after them: “Don’t run!”
The Interior Ministry put nationwide turnout at 410,000 — fewer than the 550,000 it said protested last weekend — while the CGT union that helped organize some of Saturday’s protests estimated nearly 800,000. The ministry’s estimate included 110,000 in Paris, where authorities confined the march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the center. The CGT put the number of protesters in Paris at 250,000.
Unrest is challenging Macron’s final months in power
More than a month of unrest that started with protests in high schools for more funding and teachers is testing Macron’s authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May.
The stakes are high: The far-right National Rally party has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for its candidate Marine Le Pen. On the far left, presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has backed demonstrators and criticized policing that has left some teenage protesters with life-changing injuries.
As dusk fell Saturday, violence erupted at the end of some of the 289 protests counted by the Interior Ministry nationwide. Street fires burned in the cities of Marseille and Lyon. Police used tear gas in Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Strasbourg and Bordeaux and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Nice, far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown and 11 people were arrested, regional authorities said.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police made nearly 1,000 arrests but added that the number is expected to increase significantly as more are counted.
Nuñez said beefed-up policing, with 70,000 officers backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and other support, helped prevent a repeat of widespread looting and damage to shops the previous weekend.
A small protest became a national movement
What began last month as a protest over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris spread nationwide, drawing students demanding more funding for education and workers seeking help with soaring costs for fuel and other necessities.
In Paris, Bénédicte Pittion, a 46-year-old teacher, marched with her 16-year-old daughter, Garance, a high school student — in their first protest together.
“The young people who have been demonstrating have not been heard, and as a parent and as a teacher, I stand with them,” Pittion said.
Garance said she’d been “really scared” after seeing the previous weekend’s violence, but felt that staying away would hand the government a victory.
Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.
Some protests were banned
Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, complained that authorities in Paris wanted to stifle protesters by making them march on the capital’s outskirts, keeping them away from the center where the Louvre and other major museums closed exceptionally.
“But it won’t stop the movement. It won’t stop students from demanding better conditions in schools,” she said.
Other protesters expressed anger about record poverty and wealth inequality under Macron. Camille Chesnier, 27, said she hasn’t found work despite having an engineering degree and a master’s degree.
“There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren’t privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it’s very tough,” she said.."
In Marseille, police put attendance at 17,000, while the CGT union estimated 100,000. In the southwestern city of Toulouse, 26,500 people joined the protests, according to authorities. Authorities had banned rallies in cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier.
Trade unions criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
Thousands also marched Saturday in Orléans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Le Pen’s National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.
Shops board up and museums close
Gendarmes stood guard Saturday beneath the Arc de Triomphe and shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician’s shop.
“I got the call last night,” he said. “The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life.”
Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
Students and workers are angry
Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system.
Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros ($224) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.
Energy prices in France were 21.3% higher in September than a year earlier, helping drive overall inflation to 3.1%, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE.
Paris protester Louis Ledoux--Xatard voiced frustration over inequality.
“Looking at countries like the United States, we don’t want to end up like them, where part of the population has everything and the others have nothing,” he said.
“I never imagined that I’d be taking to the streets so much before my thirties.”
___
Associated Press writers Samuel Petrequin and Sylvie Corbet in Paris contributed.
