title: Sexual harassment rules for Congress are under review after flurry of ethics cases
text:
Sexual harassment rules for Congress are under review after a flurry of ethics cases
When Rep. Kat Cammack began work on a task force this spring to combat sexual misconduct on Capitol Hill, the Florida Republican soon heard from former staffers who wanted to share their stories.
Related video above: California Rep. Eric Swalwell resigns amid sexual misconduct allegations
They “came out of the woodwork,” she said, and had stayed silent because it was well established that coming forward would be the end of a career they had worked so hard to achieve.
“Those were some of the hardest conversations to have," Cammack said. "And the stories were gut-wrenching."
This year's spike in House Ethics Committee investigations related to sexual misconduct prompted congressional leaders to set up a working group led by Cammack and Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, D-N.M. What they have found is disturbing, Cammack said.
Victims are unclear about where they can go for help. They do not trust there will be repercussions for the perpetrator. And the current requirements for reporting harassment can work against them, such as a 180-day “shot clock” for filing a claim after an alleged violation.
“It's a disaster," Cammack said. “The entire system on Capitol Hill is really designed to create a chilling effect for victims."
The task force is expected to release recommended changes after the Nov. 3 elections with a goal of taking action before the end of the year.
A deluge of ethics cases led to this moment
In a Congress that has generally struggled this year to do more than keep the federal government running, the House Ethics Committee has been caught in the middle of some of the biggest stories coming out of Washington.
Three lawmakers resigned this year rather than face the prospect of an expulsion vote. Two of those cases involved alleged sexual misconduct. Another member was censured for his interactions with two female aides on his staff. Other investigations are ongoing.
Those stories emerged at a time when Congress was confronted by public outrage over the government's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case. In the previous months, members of the Democratic Women's Caucus had multiple meetings with survivors who were pushing for the release of Epstein-related files at the Department of Justice.
In April, the Ethics Committee began an investigation into whether then-Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., engaged in sexual misconduct toward an employee working under his supervision. Swalwell would soon resign as colleagues called for his expulsion.
Similarly, Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned as the committee investigated whether he had engaged in sexual misconduct toward an employee in his office. Gonzales had acknowledged an affair with a staff member who later died by suicide.
Most recently, the committee recommended the censure of Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., following an investigation that concluded he engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct toward two young female staffers in his office. The House went along with the recommendation by a vote of 413-2.
Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., is also the subject of a committee investigation into whether he may have engaged in sexual misconduct with a House staffer. Gomez said he would cooperate with the investigation but also stressed that his actions were consensual in nature and did not violate the law or House Ethics rules. He also apologized to his family and constituents.
The committee is also investigating whether Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., engaged in sexual misconduct or dating violence, among other allegations. Mills has denied the allegations and recently lost a Republican primary.
Lawmakers felt called to action
Cammack said that as stories began to surface about some of the cases before the committee, she and colleagues began talking about what they could do to “clean up the House.” She approached Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., about getting on board.
Johnson’s response, she said, was: “Well, good timing because I was going to come to you and ask you to take this effort up.”
Leger Fernandez was also talking with Democratic leadership about reforms when Cammack reached out to her about working together.
“What was neat is on both sides of the aisle, the Democratic Women's Caucus and the Republican Women's Caucus were both saying there needs to be structural changes. We need to work together,” Leger Fernandez said.
The working group started with listening sessions that included lawmakers and staff. They also reached out to people in the military, corporate America and victims advocacy groups for advice on best practices. Cammack and Leger Fernandez held a packed-room meeting with staff in July.
Several ideas for reform are on the table
Congress has tried to address the issue of sexual harassment before.
It passed legislation in 2018 that, among other things, required lawmakers to reimburse the Treasury Department for awards and settlements related to sexual harassment cases. It also required that staff have access to a dedicated advocate who can guide them through the process of filing a claim with the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights.
Some recommendations from the task force will involve changing House rules. Lawmakers are already banned from having sexual relationships with members of their own staff or their committees' staff. But the task force wants to expand the ban to include all congressional staff.
“If you are looking to advance your love life on Capitol Hill, you're there for the wrong reason, in my opinion,” said Cammack, who served as a congressional aide for several years before winning election to the House.
The working group is also seeking to streamline the reporting system for staff to report harassment. Many simply do not know where to go with a complaint.
“I call it a 911 for sexual harassment line that you can make one call and find out what all the alternative options might be for somebody,” Leger Fernandez said.
Another change could be to give alleged victims more time to file a complaint. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which enforces antidiscrimination laws, also enforces a 180-day window for filing a complaint, but that can be extended to 300 days in cases covered by a state or local anti-discrimination law.
Increasing the time for filing a complaint would be an update to the Congressional Accountability Act, which requires Congress to follow many of the same employment laws that apply to the private sector. Updating current law would also require Senate buy-in, complicating prospects.
The working group is also looking to increase accountability for lawmakers and senior members of their staff who engage in harassment.
“The fact that we're still trying to insist that it is not OK to sexually abuse or harass women in 2026 is outrageous and, if you're a woman, is so incredibly frustrating and sad," Leger Fernandez said.

title: A few degrees warmer tonight, then the great weather continues
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - It will be a few degrees warmer than last night then the stunning stretch of fall weather we have been in will continue through almost all of next week. High pressure will continue to control the pattern over the state and the pattern of comfortable days and cooler nights will continue for the foreseeable future. Lows will be chilly overnight, with most nights into the 20s but highs will get close to 60 at least through the weekend and early next week. A weak cold front will pass through the state Monday brining down temps but likely won’t bring any rain with it.
Tonight: Usual chilliness and clear
Temps will be seasonably chilly with lows dropping close to or into the 20s for most inland with 30s along the coast. Winds will be light.
Sunday: A few degrees warmer, still clear skies.
Another flawless late October day. We may reach up into the 60s for some with everyone else still in the 50s. Winds will again be quite light.
Sunday night: A few clouds and a couple degrees warmer
Fewer areas may see the 20s on Sunday night with more areas likely staying in the 30s. A few clouds may also drift by, though nothing of major note.
Monday and beyond: The beat goes on with clear days and chilly nights
There is little if any precip on the horizon here in Maine which does not help our drought conditions but my goodness is this a stellar stretch of sun filled fall weather. If you have the chance to be outside this week take advantage because weeks like this aren’t exactly typical once we get into the true winter season on its way.
Saturday: Sunny with highs in the 50s. Winds light.
Saturday night: Clear with lows in the 20s and 30s. Winds light.
Sunday: Sunny with highs in the 50s and 60s. Winds light.
Sunday night: Mainly clear with lows in the 20s and 30s. Winds light.
Monday: Mainly sunny after a few early clouds with highs in the 50s. Winds light.

title: George Stevens runner pulls off big upset at North cross country regionals
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
BELFAST — Shock, pain and disbelief. There was an outpouring of multiple emotions as George Stevens Academy’s Ripley King-Ofsiany crossed the finish line Saturday at Troy Howard Middle School.
The junior had never in her life won a cross country race. What better time then Saturday, as King-Ofsiany crossed the finish line in 20 minutes, 43.77 seconds to win the Class C girls race at the Northern Maine championships.
“I’m so happy,” said King-Ofsiany, who was still crying tears of joy 10 minutes after her win. “It’s just something I’ve really been working for. I can’t believe the first race I’ve won was Northerns. I’m just so proud of myself.”
Caribou’s Emma Graves (Class B, 18:44.40) and Hampden Academy’s Addison Elliott (19:21.39) won the other girls races at Troy Howard. Pierce Gorneault of Caribou (Class B, 16:01.03), Brady Cox of Orono (Class C, 16:48.44) and Sam Bergmark of Bangor (Class A, 15:51.07) won the boys races.
The Caribou boys (61 points) and Mount Desert Island girls (40 points) were Class B team champions, and the Houlton/Greater Houlton Christian Academy boys (26) and GSA girls (46) won in Class C. The Hampden Academy boys (63) and girls (27) swept Class A.
Gorneault, a sophomore, easily defended his Class B regional title. His time was the best in a B North boys race since Medomak Valley’s Connor Daigle (15:53.52) in 2021. Daigle’s younger brother, Colby, was runner-up to Gorneault in 16:53.72.
A third-place finish from Tewolde Stewart (16:59.73) and a fourth from Peyton Gorneault (17:12.04) helped power the Caribou boys to victory over John Bapst (83 points) and Presque Isle (83, lost tiebreaker). Paxton Darrell (17:15.20) of Presque Isle rounded out the top five.
“I wish I could have shaved off one second (to finish sub-16), but I feel good about it,” Pierce Gorneault said. “I’m really happy with how my teammates performed, and I hope to see them grow in the future even more.”
Caribou’s success continued in the girls race, with Graves beating out MDI’s Kulani Granholm (18:54.88). The Vikings (84 points) placed third behind MDI, which claimed its seventh consecutive B North championship by beating out Presque Isle (64 points).
“I had hoped (I could beat Granholm) because I had beaten her or gotten close to her at some of the other meets,” Graves said. “The weather was great, and the course was in good condition. … Our team did really good; one of my teammates (Isabella Albert) got a PR.”
Cox was followed in the Class C boys race by a quartet of Houlton/GHCA runners: Malachi Witmer (16:52.80), Brayden Drake (16:59.00), Wyatt Quint (17:01.89) and Logan Witmer (17:13.72). That helped the Shiretowners beat GSA (48 points) and Orono (71) for the team title.
Then came King-Ofsiany’s win in the C girls race. King-Ofsiany finished fourth to Orono’s Ellie Arsenault and Ruby Beane and teammate Paige Carter a week earlier at the Penobscot Valley Conference championships. This time, she finished ahead of Beane (20:52.01) and Carter (21:17.19), while Arsenault dropped out because of an injury.
“I think (finishing fourth at PVCs) kind of lit a fire in me to really push harder today,” King-Ofsiany said. “I knew I could do it; I just told myself, ‘This is my race,’ and I just followed through on me. … (That belief), I think, is what made me win.”
And she helped GSA claim the team title, too. Olesya Shafarina (21:20.27) finished third for Orono, giving the Eagles and Red Riots two runners each in the top four. With the two teams pretty much even the rest of the way, GSA edged Orono by two points to dethrone the Red Riots as champs.
Bergmark defended his Northern Maine title in Class A, ahead of the Mt. Blue duo of Lucas Demarco (16:09.98) and Wyatt Oliver (16:33.25). Noah Seigh (16:55.77) of Camden Hills took fourth, while Jack Scott (17:03.38) finished fifth for champion Hampden.
Elliott’s win for the Hampden girls was her second straight North title. Elsie Mann of Camden Hills took second in 19:38.71. Isabelle Clark (19:56.99) placed fourth for the Broncos, who defended their Northern Maine crown.

title: Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday, saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally.
Trump and first lady Melania Trump arrived at their West Palm Beach polling location at the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections office together after the president spent the morning at his nearby golf course. Trump has been criticized in the past for voting by mail despite his long history of railing against that method of submitting ballots.
Asked if he voted the party line, Trump, who was wearing an “I Voted” sticker, said, “Very much so.”
Speaking to reporters at the poll site, Trump again defended an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. The ad has faced intense blowback for featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton, who lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.
Trump also defended his decision to instruct his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
As for the war in Iran, he said, “I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they’ll make a deal, but I’m not sure. Either way, we win.”
Melania Trump, who this week brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid could be delivered and civilians evacuated, was asked whether she might travel to Ukraine.
“We will see,” she told reporters.
In Florida, Trump has endorsed Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who is running against David Jolly, a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat, to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.
He has also campaigned for Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, who is running to fill the last two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s former Senate term against progressive state lawmaker Angie Nixon.
___
Colvin reported from New York.

title: Brewers’ Misiorowski breaks World Series pitching record: ‘So much adrenaline’
text:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Jacob Misiorowski stepped on the mound for a World Series debut like no other.
“I had so much adrenaline built up,” he said.
He threw a pitch the likes of which had never been seen in the Fall Classic.
The Miz broke the World Series velocity record with his very first delivery, a 103.5 mph fastball to the Tampa Bay Rays’ Yandy Díaz that was taken high out of the strike zone for a ball. He allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter, helping the Milwaukee Brewers to a 3-2 victory in Friday night’s opener.
“I don’t even know how to tell you how I felt,” the 24-year-old right-hander said a half-hour after the end of a crazy ninth inning, prolonged by a game-extending video review. “I still don’t know how I felt. I feel like I’m still trying to take everything in and understand what happened.”
Misiorowski gave up four hits and one walk, striking out a season-low three.
Aroldis Chapman of the Chicago Cubs had the previous mark for fastest Series pitch at 103.2 mph in the ninth inning of Game 2 in 2016, an offering that resulted in a groundout to second by Cleveland’s Coco Crisp. The previous high by a Series starting pitcher since tracking began in 2008 was 101.1 mph by the New York Mets’ Noah Syndergaard to Kansas City’s Ben Zobrist that was taken for a ball in the first inning of Game 3 in 2015.
Miz reached 100 mph with 38 pitches, topping the previous Series high of 24 by Chapman in Game 5 of 2016. The most by a starting pitcher in the Series had been six by Tampa Bay’s Tyler Glasnow in the 2020 opener against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Tampa Bay scored in the fourth when Jonathan Aranda walked, took third on Junior Caminero’s double over center fielder Garrett Mitchell and came around on Liam Hicks’ grounder to first baseman Jake Bauers.
Nearing the end of his first full major league season, Misiorowski has reached 100 mph with 134 of 260 postseason pitches. But his spin rate was down, a sign of a season in which he has pitched 188 innings — up from 141 1/3 innings last year. And he got just seven swings and misses, five on his fastball.
Tampa Bay batters fouled off 20 of his 78 pitches and tipped another.
During the regular season, Misiorowski reached 100 mph with 1,115 pitches, including a high of 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27.
“What we’re used to seeing in the regular season was Miz just mow through people and have two strikeouts an inning. That’s unrealistic,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. “This is the best team in the American League.”
Miz’s first pitch was so fast the scoreboard at American Family Field couldn’t keep up, flashing 103.4 mph — one-tenth of a mile less than it registered on MLB’s Statcast system.
“He’s such a special pitcher,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I felt like for him to be out of the game at five innings, there’s a small win in that.”
Misiorowski threw fastballs on 10 of his first 12 pitches, then mixed in more offspeed stuff. In all he tossed 48 fastballs, 17 cutters, seven sliders and six curveballs.
Miz finished with 30 pitches at 101 mph or higher, 11 of 102 mph or more and three at 103-plus mph.
Warming up in the bullpen, he couldn’t take in the introductions before Milwaukee’s first World Series game in 44 years. He thought about how far he had come, how he was at Double-A Biloxi two years ago.
“It was crazy,” he said. “It’s everything I dreamed of.”
___

title: Commentary on Portland must remain grounded in truth
text:
Mark Dion is the mayor of Portland.
As public discourse ramps up during election season, it is vital that debate remains grounded in the full context of an issue rather than mischaracterizations. Recent public statements by political candidates regarding the city of Portland’s budget, public safety operations and emergency shelter procedures require clarification.
Portland residents deserve accurate information about how their tax dollars and other revenue sources are allocated and how municipal services operate.
While claims that public safety services consume the largest share of local city tax dollars are factually accurate, it does not give the full context of how the city allocates its budget. Our Health and Human Services and Fire Department budgets each have higher total spending allocations, and Health and Human Services in particular has a higher total state and local tax dollar allocation.
While public safety — which includes police, fire and 911 dispatch services — is a core municipal responsibility, these functions represent only one component of a comprehensive city budget heavily invested in social safety nets, public health and community support.
The additional assertion that the Portland Police Department does not possess a behavioral health program is completely false. In fact, Portland’s co-response model is recognized as a national benchmark and has been in existence since 2010. The Police Department’s Behavioral Health Unit is led by a licensed clinician and includes a substance use liaison and alternative response liaisons.
The city recently expanded this team to six alternative response positions to directly resolve mental health and substance use calls, diverting individuals away from arrest and connecting them to treatment, detox, case management and crisis stabilization. Because of these efforts, the United States Department of Justice designated Portland’s Behavioral Health Unit as one of only 14 law enforcement mental health learning sites in the entire nation, and is one of the original seven mental health learning sites.
Suggesting that no behavioral health programming exists undermines the proven, compassionate work our professional clinicians and officers perform daily.
Finally, recent statements regarding the district attorney referring individuals involved in the criminal justice system directly to the city’s Homeless Services Center misrepresent how municipal emergency shelters operate. Access to the Homeless Services Center follows standard intake procedures managed through the city’s Prevention and Diversion Program at 39 Forest Ave. to ensure safety, equitable access and structured housing plans.
Emergency shelter beds cannot be treated as court-mandated diversion slots or substitute residential psychiatric or substance use treatment beds. Addressing justice-involved individuals experiencing severe mental illness and substance use requires state-level judicial platforms, court-directed treatment plans (such as progressive treatment plans) and dedicated residential treatment facilities — not the informal referral or dropping off of defendants at a municipal emergency shelter.
Addressing the intersection of unhoused populations, mental health crises and public safety requires honest coordination among city, county and state partners. Mischaracterizing city finances, ignoring established public safety programs and confusing shelter protocols do not advance real solutions.
Portland city staff and first responders work tirelessly to serve our community with compassion and accountability, and they deserve a public conversation rooted in truth.

title: Cracking a smile regularly may be good not just for your mood but for your health
text:
Cracking a smile regularly may be good not just for your mood but for your health
Research backs up the fact that smiling goes a long way
Cracking a smile regularly may be good not just for your mood but for your health
Research backs up the fact that smiling goes a long way
Reminding yourself to smile often can not only make more friendships, but it can also make you feel better.
And rather than wait for a reason to smile, just making the physical change of literally turning that frown upside down could impact emotions, according to experts.
Research backs up the fact that smiling goes a long way.
Related video above: Does a Russian lab worker’s death carry pandemic risk? Not based on what we know now, experts say
Some older research has focused on this "facial feedback hypothesis," according to Jeanne Tsai, a longtime psychology professor at Stanford University who runs the Culture and Emotion Lab. In one classic study in the late 1980s, researchers would have subjects put a pencil between their lips and adopt a smile or a frown while viewing a positive movie clip like a cartoon. Some subjects who smiled would feel the sensation of the smile more and be more amused.
"When we've done that demonstration in classes, it works," Tsai said. "When you're doing it in a room by yourself, you're not doing it in a social interaction; maybe it's making you remember, or it's an effect of remembering some good thing that happened, and that would put you in a better mood."
At the Orange County Academy of Sciences and Arts in Southern California, the power of a smile is taken very seriously. An entire section on the charter school group's website is dedicated to its philosophy that a smile can make a difference.
"Smiling creates a supportive classroom culture that makes students relaxed, active, and motivated," according to the website. "It increases emotional well-being, lowers stress, and gives students confidence."
How smiling can benefit health
Dr. Judy Ho, a Los Angeles clinical and forensic neuropsychologist who also teaches at Pepperdine University, discusses smiling as a coping strategy with some patients suffering from depression or anxiety.
"I'm not suggesting that that's the only way they can fix things," Ho said. "It's just like another thing that you can add to your toolbox."
Smiling can affect one's level of cortisol, a hormone the body releases partly to help regulate stress and mood, according to Ho. Smiling can affect brain chemicals that are associated with positive feelings, including endorphins, dopamine and serotonin.
"People who smile during stressful tasks generally demonstrated lower heart rates during recovery than those maintaining neutral expressions," Ho said. "Smiling also reduced aspects of the body's physiological stress response."
The hope is that if you smile enough, you will start feeling it emotionally.
"In some ways it's like a mediating effect," she added.
The value of a smile varies from culture to culture
How smiling and even the openness of a smile are perceived are not universal. Tsai, the Stanford professor, has conducted research on how emotion in American culture puts value on trying to always feel positive and minimizing negativity and sadness. In East Asian cultures, emotion is more about balance.
"It's like the positive and the negative emotions are braided together, and so you don't want to feel too positive or too negative," Tsai said. "You want more of a balance between the two."
Her past studies also examined how European Americans and East Asians — including Taiwanese, South Koreans, Japanese and Hong Kong Chinese — look at a "neutral or a calm" smile versus a full-on grin. Subjects rated the differing facial expressions on warmth and trustworthiness. While some Americans saw the excited smiles as friendlier, some East Asians characterized those facial expressions as "emotionally unstable" or "unreliable."
"What kind of smile matters — whether it's a calm, closed-mouth smile more like the Dalai Lama or a big, toothy excited smile like Julia Roberts," Tsai said. "We've done some series of studies in Taiwan and other East Asian contexts. They don't like the big, toothy, excited smile unless it's really situationally appropriate."
In Thailand — known as "The Land of Smiles" — smiling is embedded in the culture. There are nearly 30 Thai words for "smile." Many teach-abroad programs where people can teach English as a foreign language in Thailand cite that smiling often with children and colleagues is key to showing respect, good manners and calmness.
At the OCASA charter schools, smiling is part of an effort to make children feel seen.
"I've always believed in wanting school to be a happy place for kids," said RaNae Posey, principal of OCASA Capistrano Elementary School. "To actually help them form habits of looking at the bright side of things."
Mandating smiles may lead to more frowns
Women in recent years have smacked down the idea that they have to smile in the workplace while men do not. Smiling can feel like a catch-22 for some women and sometimes for people of color who may be stereotyped as unapproachable or cold if they don't smile enough.
Last year, retailer Target was ridiculed across social media for instituting a smiling policy. Workers had to smile and make eye contact if a customer was within 10 feet (3 meters) and personally greet them if they were within 4 feet (1.2 meters).
People do not like feeling like they have no "emotional autonomy," according to Nicholas Coles, an assistant professor who runs the Social Science Collaboratory at the University of Florida in Gainesville.
"In those scenarios, what we find is that it's more that you're smiling your way to misery," Coles said. "It's only when it feels authentic and voluntary that I think it'll have any real effect."
With the holidays approaching, more people may have to muster smiles with family if sensitive topics like politics and religion come up. Those could be good times to see if smiling helps.
"If we were able to just smile and be like 'Look, this is somebody that historically cares about you and loves you,' maybe that would change the way that we respond to them even in a moment of tough conversation," Ho said.

title: State plans Central Maine Healthcare hearing as concerns over Prime grow
text:
The state will hold a public hearing to determine whether Prime Healthcare Foundation is meeting staffing and care standards in operating Central Maine Healthcare, which includes Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston and several other facilities.
State Rep. Julie McCabe, D-Lewiston, requested the hearing in a letter Monday to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. Over the past year, the state health department required Prime Healthcare Foundation, a nonprofit based in California, to make several commitments to maintain essential health services, safe patient volumes and trauma center status at Central Maine Healthcare before it could acquire the health system.
Compliance with those agreements is being called into question.
“The people of Lewiston deserve a hospital system that is safely managed and adequately staffed, that upholds the agreements entered into with the state of Maine, and that follows the laws of the state,” McCabe wrote. “Based on the many conversations I have had with healthcare providers and patients, it is my belief that Prime Healthcare is not currently abiding by their (agreement).”
A public hearing is “an appropriate step,” said Lindsay Hammes, Maine DHHS spokesperson, in an email Thursday. She said it will be scheduled in the next several weeks.
Central Maine Healthcare includes hospitals in Bridgton and Rumford and a number of physician practices. McCabe said changes at the health system, including workforce attrition, sterilization equipment issues and the premature termination of a contract with an emergency department physician group, which staffed 35 providers across the three hospitals, pose a “clear and present danger” to patients.
State officials have acknowledged the Lewiston hospital did not meet a requirement earlier this month intended to verify progress toward reestablishing trauma center status, a designation that lapsed before Prime took over — leaving just two destinations in Maine for around-the-clock emergency surgery.
Early termination
Central Maine Healthcare notified BlueWater Health last month that it was terminating early its three-year contract to staff three emergency departments in the Lewiston, Bridgton and Rumford hospitals, effective Jan. 12.
The departments were short 17 physicians and relying heavily on locum tenens, or temporary providers, when the Brunswick-based physician group signed the three-year contract in early 2025, said Dr. Jay Mullen, CEO of BlueWater Health. The group has since filled those vacancies and recruited 18 more physicians, nurses and physician assistants to Central Maine Healthcare.
Mullen said it’s difficult to retain board-certified emergency physicians because they can get jobs anywhere in the country, “so rural areas are always struggling.” Most of their recruits to Maine came from out of state.
With the termination, Mullen said 80% of the 35 providers will leave Central Maine Healthcare when their contract ends in January. Two-thirds will take roles elsewhere with BlueWater Health, which he said staffs emergency departments across New England and which recently signed a contract with St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center in Lewiston. Others are moving out of state.
One emergency department physician leaving the health system for another role with BlueWater Health, who asked to remain unnamed, said instability is driving her away.
“There is some fatigue of the chaos that seems to kind of be currently encircling Central Maine,” she said, “a lot of loss of the medical staff and nursing changes. I think a lot of members of my group would agree with me that people feel that they need to step away from Central Maine.”
A Central Maine Healthcare spokesperson said the health system is in ongoing discussions with BlueWater Health and Vituity, a California-based emergency physician group. “Regardless of the outcome of these negotiations,” the spokesperson said, “most physicians that have provided ED services at Central Maine Healthcare will have the opportunity to continue to do so with the firm that is selected.”
McCabe, the Lewiston lawmaker, said it was negligent for Central Maine Healthcare to terminate the BlueWater Health contract with only a few months’ notice and no arrangement to “fill the void.”
Hospitals are required by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to report the rate of emergency department visitors who leave without being seen by a physician. More than a year into the BlueWater contract, Central Maine Healthcare’s rate dropped from 7.2% to 3.5%. In the past three months, it’s climbed back up to 5.7%, according to data shared by McCabe and verified by Mullen.
The national benchmark is 2%.
“When you have increased wait times, people leave without being seen, and that doesn’t mean that they’re not sick. It just means that they gave up,” McCabe said. “And when you have those kinds of repeated interactions at the ED, you’re going to lose faith in your healthcare system.”
Trauma center in limbo
Maine’s health department regulates how ownership acquisitions, mergers and other major healthcare changes can happen in Maine, and by who.
To acquire Central Maine Healthcare, Prime Healthcare Foundation needed the state’s approval. One challenge: CMMC let its level three trauma center designation lapse in December 2025, a month after the state made it a mandatory condition of the acquisition.
The loss of a trauma center in Lewiston has impacted patients — sometimes with life-threatening conditions — who had to travel farther to reach the other trauma centers in Portland and Bangor. It’s also uprooted dozens of EMS agencies and increased trauma patient volumes at the other hospitals.
The state approved Prime Healthcare Foundation’s acquisition of the Maine health system earlier this year, but with the condition that CMMC must regain full trauma status by 2028. The hospital was also required to obtain a trauma manager — the person who leads the center and communicates with other hospitals ― by Oct. 2.
Hammes said on Oct. 6 that CMMC had made an offer to a candidate for the trauma manager position but that “hiring has not yet been completed.” The department, she said, “will be closely monitoring the outcome of the offer to assess compliance with the condition.”
On Thursday, she said the state had not received an update about the status of the offer and could not verify compliance.
A CMMC spokesperson has not responded to questions about the trauma manager requirement.
“We should be one of three trauma hospitals in the state, and from every indication, Prime doesn’t seem like they want that responsibility,” McCabe said. “I think our community is going to be, frankly, in danger if they are not able to adequately staff the emergency department, which provides life or death care.”
“We have many ER physicians who are very knowledgeable and interested in the care of trauma patients,” the BlueWater physician said. “I hope that there isn’t decreased momentum to gaining the level three trauma designation due to the departure of ER physicians who were ready and willing to be participatory in that process.”
Oct. 25 will mark the anniversary of the Lewiston mass shootings, which left 18 dead and more than a dozen wounded on a Wednesday night three years ago.
“On that night and in the days that followed, our teams demonstrated the critical role our hospitals and emergency services play in this community,” a CMMC spokesperson said. “We remain deeply proud of the extraordinary care they provided and mindful of our responsibility to be here for our communities every day.”
That night, it was trauma manager Tammy Lachance who made the call to secure blood from nearby hospitals, which “contributed in great measure to the survival of our operative patients,” said Dr. Richard King, a former CMMC trauma surgeon who responded to the emergency department within minutes of the shooting along with 30 other surgeons.
Lachance died after a battle with cancer last year. King hopes she is honored at CMMC this week.
It pains him to see the degradation of the trauma program they built, he said.
“Tammy was more than that one night,” King said. “She was the heart and soul of that trauma program for many years.”
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Hannah Kaufman can be reached at hkaufman@centralmaine.com.

title: Gov. Mills orders flags lowered Sunday in honor of anniversary of Lewiston shooting
text:
Gov. Mills orders flags lowered Sunday in honor of anniversary of Lewiston shooting
Sunday marks 3 years since the mass shootings that took the lives of 18 people
Gov. Mills orders flags lowered Sunday in honor of anniversary of Lewiston shooting
Sunday marks 3 years since the mass shootings that took the lives of 18 people
Gov. Janet Mills has ordered flags to be lowered to half-staff statewide Sunday in honor of the three-year anniversary of the Lewiston mass shootings.
All United States and State of Maine flags will be lowered from sunrise until sunset.
"On Sunday we remember and honor the eighteen people who were taken from us on Maine’s darkest day. We keep in our hearts the loved ones they left behind, and we offer our deepest gratitude for the heroes and first responders who saved countless lives," Gov. Mills said in a statement Saturday.
On Oct. 25, 2023, 18 people were killed, and many others were injured in mass shootings at Just-In-Time Recreation and Schemengees Bar and Grille in Lewiston.
"As we pause to remember those we lost, may we find strength in remembering the outpouring of love and support that Maine people showed for one another — from everyday acts of kindness to the sea of blue hearts in store windows that conveyed our love for our Lewiston neighbors," Gov. Mills said. "Three years later, we will never forget the hard moments, and we will always remember the humanity and compassion that Maine people found in one another."

title: Covering the Co$t: The Necessity and Luxury of Buying a Car
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With affordability a main issue ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, politicians and economists alike are weighing the factors leading to the high cost of living. One often-overlooked piece is the cost of transportation.
Cars, once considered a luxury, are now described as a necessity. Most Americans need a vehicle of some kind to get from point A to point B, at a typical cost of thousands of dollars.
The price of buying a new vehicle continues to rise. Dr. David Bieri, an economist at Virginia Tech, said the average cost is now around $50,000.
“In terms of median income, that’s close to about eight months’ worth of pay,” Bieri said.
Bieri said new car sales remain healthy, but the cost and method of purchasing a vehicle point to a complicated market, with increasing insurance premiums, inflation, and lingering tariffs adding to the mix. He also said “pay as you go” payment plans are becoming more popular: a sometimes dangerous method that could lead some buyers to shop outside their purchasing power.
Bieri said one of the biggest issues is a lack of affordable vehicle options built domestically.
“We don’t really have any domestic low end entry points,” Bieri said.
Total vehicle costs including payments, gas, and maintenance take up anywhere from 10% to 20% or more of Americans’ monthly income, making it one of the most important purchases someone will make.
Bieri said spending, though, is only one half of the affordability puzzle.
“It’s also the problem of wages not growing fast enough for certain segments,” Bieri said, pointing out that a general increase in wages could make a massive dent in the overall affordability crisis.
The last time the federal minimum wage was raised in the U.S. was 2009.

title: Trump says he called Google to rename the Atlantic Ocean. Here’s how they responded
text:
(Gray News) - President Donald Trump said he called Google CEO Sundar Pichai and asked to rename the Atlantic Ocean.
Trump, who made the remarks at a South Carolina rally for U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, said he told Pichai that Google was “really great with the lake,” referencing when Google Maps relabeled the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
“I only like two oceans: The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. I’m not going to put either Trump or America on any other ocean but these two,” he said. “I said: ‘Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean.’”
Trump said Pichai told him, “No, no, no. This time I’m not doing it. Oceans are different, sir. They cover a lot of countries. Please don’t ask us to do that.”
Trump told the crowd, “I’ll probably pass.”
“I think let’s keep it the Atlantic Ocean,” he said.
Trump also talked about how he signed executive orders to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America and the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
He told the crowd that he has been looking for a river to rename, possibly the Hudson River or Mississippi River.

title: Nuclear power could more than triple by 2060, UN agency says
text:
Nuclear power could more than triple by 2060, UN agency says
The head of the U.N. nuclear agency said Friday that he expects the use of nuclear power could more than triple by 2060.
Rafael Grossi said in the International Atomic Energy Agency's annual report to the U.N. General Assembly that this will be driven by electrification, data centers powered by artificial intelligence and "technology companies' appetite for reliable, carbon-free power."
Nuclear energy is seen by a growing number of countries as key to improving their energy security, he said, stressing that it is on par with solar energy and "safer than every other option."
"In 2025, more than 400 operating reactors in more than 30 countries produced 10% of global electricity and a quarter of its low-carbon electricity," the IAEA director-general said. "More than 60 new reactors are under construction and the projections for future nuclear capacity have shifted dramatically upward."
In addition to the growing use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, Grossi spoke about the nuclear programs in Iran and North Korea, the "unprecedented threats to nuclear safety" from the war in Ukraine, and worrying reports that other countries he didn't name are talking about acquiring nuclear weapons.
On Iran, whose nuclear sites were struck by the U.S. last year before the U.S. and Israel launched a war on Feb. 28, Grossi told U.N. member nations that the necessary technical work for a diplomatic agreement has been done.
"I call on the parties to redouble their efforts towards agreeing a diplomatic solution that includes the IAEA's indispensable verification role, without which no agreement can be sustainable," he said. "IAEA inspectors must be able to return to Iran expeditiously. That requires a return to the negotiating table."
In North Korea, where leader Kim Jong Un has a growing nuclear program without any IAEA oversight, Grossi warned that it "stands as a stark reminder of the consequences when red lines are crossed" in violation of U.N. Security Council resolutions banning nuclear weapons production.
In Ukraine, he singled out the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, Europe's largest, saying it remains "in a precarious position" with frequent power losses, limited back-up diesel supplies "and military activity threatening the plant and the people who work there."
On a positive note, Grossi said the IAEA has made "significant progress" in clarifying and resolving outstanding questions regarding Syria's nuclear activities after nearly two decades of uncertainty. That's as a result of engaging with the government of interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa, he said.
He reported in September that the Bashar Assad-era government — which was ousted in December 2024 by opposition forces led by al-Sharaa — was constructing a nuclear reactor that was configured to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons.

title: What do we owe our dogs when we put them in someone else’s care?
text:
Meredith Perdue and Michael Cain live in South Portland.
When we hand our dogs over to a dog walker, groomer, trainer or pet sitter, we are entrusting someone with a member of our family. We ask ourselves whether that person is kind, experienced and trustworthy. But how often do we ask the harder questions about exactly how they operate?
In June, our 6-year-old dog, Thatcher, was lost while in the care of a professional pack-style dog walker. After nearly 24 hours of searching, we found his body on I-95.
Since then, we have thought often about the questions we wish we had asked before handing over his leash. We hope other Maine dog owners will ask these questions in order to prevent a similar tragedy. Likewise, we would urge professional pet-care providers to use these questions and develop a plan for when the unexpected happens.
We were aware of some of the trails our dog would be visiting, but we did not know that he would be taken to a specific location surrounded by busy roads and so close to I-95. Had we known, we would not have agreed to it. We believe owners should know which trails and locations their dogs will visit, particularly when dogs are allowed off leash.
The day our dog went missing, the walker had eight dogs in their care at a land trust where posted signs indicated that only two off-leash dogs were permitted at a time. Dog owners should know not only how many dogs a walker is handling, but whether the size of that group is appropriate for the location and permitted by the property.
When our dog disappeared, we were told that his absence was not noticed until a head count was conducted. That leaves questions about supervision we wish we had thought to ask beforehand: When dogs are off leash, where is the person responsible for them? Are they positioned to see the dogs? What happens when a dog falls behind or runs ahead?
We were not notified that our dog was missing for multiple hours after he disappeared. We cannot know what might have happened if we had been called immediately. A missing dog is an emergency and hours matter. A lost dog has a much better chance of being found when the people who know him best are searching immediately and calling their name.
These are not unreasonable questions. They are basic questions about safety.
We tend to evaluate pet-care providers by how much our dogs like them, how happy they appear in photographs and whether other people recommend them. Those things matter. But they are not enough. A beautiful photograph of a pack of dogs running through the woods tells us very little about how those dogs are supervised, what happens when one disappears, or whether the environment itself is appropriate for off-leash dogs.
As dog owners, we have a responsibility. We need to ask questions before we hand over the leash. What are your credentials? Where will my dog go? How many dogs will be there? How are they supervised? What happens if one gets lost? How quickly will you call me? What happens if there is an injury or an accident?
Thatcher was a beloved member of our family. Like so many Maine dogs, he trusted the people around him completely.
We cannot change what happened to Thatcher. But perhaps we can use what happened to encourage other dog owners to ask more questions, and to encourage the people who care for our dogs to welcome those questions and have a plan.

title: Campaign financing is outrageous, out of control
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I am appalled by the amount of money that is spent on political campaigns, and I’m outraged by the number of requests for donations that appear in my message box every day. With billionaires and trillionaires pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into campaigns for their favorite candidates throughout the country, we can hardly hope to compete with our little contributions. Yet, every day, the texts get more desperate.
Campaign financing has become really lopsided, with a few extravagantly rich individuals poised to commandeer our democracy for their own ends.
Once the midterms are over, I hope we can focus on meaningful change to campaign finance regulations — among the myriad of other problems this country is facing. Wouldn’t it be wonderful if a good chunk of the money that has been spent on these elections could have been put to useful purposes like healthcare and affordable housing, childcare and education.
Perhaps if these individuals were paying their fair share of taxes, those dreams could be realized.
That’s a topic for another day.
Christine Hopf-Lovette
Wiscasset

title: Ukraine says Starlink speed limits lifted after slowdown that hobbled its drones
text:
Ukraine says Starlink speed limits lifted after a slowdown that hobbled its drones
Ukraine’s military has regained full use of Starlink satellite links for its drones and other fast-moving equipment, the defense minister said Saturday, ending speed restrictions that Ukrainian officials said had disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.
Related video above: Trump waives new sanctions on Russia under law named for late Sen. Graham
The restoration comes as U.S. envoys launched a new push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by First Lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region.
The Defense Ministry’s monitoring systems in Ukraine reported stable connections on objects traveling faster than 400 kph (250 mph), Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told reporters.
The limitations placed on Starshield — SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication — last week alarmed the country’s military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.
The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump’s reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.
Khmara credited “direct dialogue” and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most “for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.”
Zelenskyy on Friday said Ukraine was still experiencing Starlink and Starshield speed limits.
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Elon Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow’s attacks.
Trump has maintained that he did not make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement.
Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said Saturday.
Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks.
Ukraine’s General Staff said Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city.
Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday’s attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.
___
Morton reported from London.

title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Winthrop
text:
Election Day is almost here, and early voting ends Oct. 29. Whether voting early or heading to the polls, voters should know what to expect before casting their ballot.
Winthrop voters will weigh in on school board and town council races, in addition to a referendum on revising the town charter. On the state level, voters will also choose candidates for the Maine State Legislature, governor and U.S. House of Representatives and Senate.
Many of the candidates participated in the Press Herald Voter Guide, where readers can learn more about each race.
Voting is set to take place from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3, at the Winthrop Town Hall, 17 Highland Ave., Winthrop. Early voting is available through Oct. 29 at the Winthrop Town Hall.
Here’s what to expect on the local Winthrop ballot.
TOWN COUNCIL
Roy Weymouth, Aaron White
Two candidates, Roy Weymouth and Aaron White, are running for reelection for the two available seats on the Winthrop Town Council.
White, who currently serves as vice chair for the council, was first elected to the seat in 2023. White said he strives to continue strengthening Winthrop’s financial position and ensuring the town government remains affordable and effective. Winthrop should focus on continuing to invest in roads and infrastructure, creating a government responsive to residents and businesses and revitalizing the downtown.
Weymouth, who was first elected in 2023, did not respond to the Voter Guide survey.
SCHOOL BOARD
Partial term: Ella Braaten, Tracy Hovance, Julie McFarland
Three candidates are running for a partial-term for the remainder of what would have been board Member Erica Dennett’s seat.
Dennett resigned from her term in March, and the school board appointed Erin Steorts to fill the vacancy until the next annual meeting, which for Winthrop is its next municipal election. Steorts is instead running for a full-term seat. The partial-term seat will expire December 2027.
Ella Braaten, an attorney and local parent, said she wants to focus on improving academic achievement, supporting student success and being strategic and thoughtful with the school budget.
Julie McFarland is a high school math teacher and a current member of Winthrop’s Wellness Committee and Parent Teacher Organization. Her top three priorities are transparency and collaboration with families and the Winthrop community; advocating for every child and providing students with the best education by upholding Winthrop’s core values, code of ethics and laws.
Tracy Hovance did not respond to the Voter Guide survey.
Full term (two seats): Bethany Drouin, Whitney Kahn, Erin Steorts, Timothy Alan Wess
Four candidates are vying for two full-term seats on the school board currently held by Timothy Alan Wess and Bethany Drouin, both are running for reelection.
Wess, a special education teacher who has served two terms on the board, said his top three priorities are making sure students have what they need to be successful, maintaining school infrastructure and preventing female transgender students from playing on girls sports teams.
Steorts, who was first appointed to a partial term on the school board in April, said she is focused on supporting student achievement and well-being; strengthening communication and trust between families, staff, administration and the school board and ensuring responsible use of district resources.
Whitney Kahn, a cybersecurity professional, said her top priorities are having a sustainable budget, ensuring transparency with board deliberations and decisions and retaining teachers through manageable class sizes, competitive pay and seriously considering staff concerns and needs.
Bethany Drouin, a community engagement director and leader of the local Parent Teacher Organization, said her top priorities are retaining and hiring teachers, responsible and fair funding and creating equitable experiences for all students.
REFERENDUM
Question 1: Winthrop charter revision
Winthrop voters will decide whether to approve revisions to the town municipal charter proposed by the Town of Winthrop Charter Commission who conducted a comprehensive review of the charter for the first time since 2007.
Proposed revisions include updating and streamlining the charter to comply with state law, a recall provision to regulate the removal process for elected officials, a conflicts-of-interest provision for town council members, establishing clearer timelines for town and school budgets and giving the town council the authority to call bond elections.
A yes vote would approve the new town charter with the proposed revisions, while a no vote would not allow the revisions to go into effect.
KENNEBEC COUNTY COMMISSIONER
District 2: Noel Madore, Joseph Pietroski Jr.
Joseph Pietroski Jr., a Republican from Winthrop, has served as the District 2 Commissioner for Kennebec County since 2022. Democrat Noel Madore, who did not respond to the Voter Guide survey, is running to unseat Pietroski; he’s from Readfield.
Pietroski said he is focused on improving coordination and communication between county and state governments to help control costs, protect taxpayers and ensure the county receives the services residents need.
OTHER RACES
In Maine Senate District 14, voters will choose between incumbent Craig Hickman, a Democrat, and Republican Steven McGee.
Voters in House District 57 will decide between Democrat incumbent Tavis Hasenfus and Republican David Potvin.
Read more about all of the candidates on the Press Herald Voter Guide.

title: Lieutenant governor candidate’s parents say he owes them $275K in unpaid farm rent: report
text:
BLACK HAWK COUNTY, Iowa (Gray News) - The parents of a Republican lieutenant governor candidate in Iowa are reportedly claiming that he owes them hundreds of thousands of dollars.
KCCI reports that court documents filed in Black Hawk County show Derek Wulf’s parents, Duane and Jackie Wulf, say their son owes them around $275,000 in unpaid farmland rent since 2024.
The petition was reportedly filed as the parents try to protect their assets as a bank seeks to foreclose on Derek Wulf’s other unpaid debts.
Matt Craft, the attorney representing Derek Wulf’s parents, said the legal petition was filed just weeks before the election because of an Oct. 20 filing deadline.
“The judge in Derek’s foreclosure case required anyone who claimed ownership or a lien on Derek’s farm assets to speak now or forever hold their peace if they claim any ownership or interest in those seized assets,” the attorney said in a statement.
Craft added that the family has been working to privately resolve this issue for a long time.
“They are very private individuals and are embarrassed at the mess this has caused many good people in a very public way,” the attorney’s statement continued.
The Zach Lahn for governor campaign was said to not have immediately responded to requests for comment regarding his running mate’s situation.

title: Prosecutor says he will seek death penalty for mom charged with murder in twins’ deaths
text:
BOISE, Idaho (AP) — An Idaho prosecutor is seeking the death penalty against a woman charged with murder in the 2025 deaths of her twin toddlers.
Andrea Shaw, 23, has pleaded not guilty and has said the 18-month-old twins became sick and died after receiving flu shots and routine childhood vaccinations. But Payette County Prosecutor Mike Duke wrote in court documents that an autopsy revealed symptoms consistent with smothering and wrote that suffocation “is the only conceivable explanation” for their deaths.
Deputy prosecuting attorney Ryon Sirucek notified the court of his intent to seek the death penalty last week.
In the court document, Sirucek said the state would try to show that four aggravating factors make capital punishment appropriate in the case: That more than one murder was committed at the time; that the killings were especially heinous, atrocious or cruel; that the defendant showed “utter disregard” for human life; and that she would likely pose a continuing threat to society.
“That’s outrageous,” said Shaw’s attorney, Joseph Filicetti. “They’re not going to be able to prove the underlying case beyond a reasonable doubt, so there’s not a chance the death penalty is going to come into play.”
Filicetti said the defense team will be filing a motion to dismiss the case. The county coroner found the cause of death to be undetermined but consistent with hyperthermia or overheating, Filicetti said, but the coroner was not on the witness list for the grand jury. It is not clear whether jurors were informed of his findings. The pathologists who examined the twins also said their causes of death were undetermined, Filicetti said.
The prosecutor’s office wrote in court documents that the temperature in the twins’ room would often reach 100 degrees, but that the children had survived high temperatures before and that their time of death didn’t correlate to the peak temperature of the day.
“They don’t have any motive, they don’t have any backstory, they don’t have any confession ... She didn’t do any of that, and they can’t prove she did any of it,” Filicetti said.
The twins were found dead in their shared bed May 1, 2025, according to court records. They had been vaccinated eight days earlier, and the day after their vaccinations Shaw took them to the emergency room, reporting that they were lethargic and felt feverish. The doctor felt the symptoms were a reaction from the vaccinations, and the twins were given Tylenol and a popsicle and sent home, according to the court records.
A few days after the twins’ deaths, Shaw went on an internet show produced by Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine group founded by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He has not been affiliated with the group since December 2024, when he formally resigned as chairman to join President Donald Trump’s administration.
Medical experts point out that the childhood vaccines at issue — hepatitis A, influenza and DTaP — are safe and effective for kids and recommended by various medical groups.
Shaw is also a plaintiff in a federal lawsuit brought by Children’s Health Defense and others against the American Academy of Pediatrics, accusing the organization of racketeering and lying about the safety of vaccinations. The American Academy of Pediatrics has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, calling it the “latest missive in a campaign targeting” the academy and its “use of science-backed evidence in vaccine policy.”
A grand jury indicted Shaw on the murder charges in July, and she is being held without bond. A trial has been set for January.
___
This story was first published on Oct. 21, 2026. It was updated on Oct. 22, 2026, to clarify that the grand jury did not hear testimony from the coroner, but it is not clear whether jurors were informed of his findings.”
___
Associated Press writer Josh Kelety contributed.

title: Campbell routs UMaine 35-6, ending Black Bears’ 9-game homecoming win streak
text:
One streak was extended and another came to a resounding end at the University of Maine football team’s homecoming game against Campbell University of North Carolina at Morse Field in Alfond Stadium in Orono on Saturday afternoon.
The Fighting Camels pummeled the Black Bears 35-6, expanding the home team’s losing streak to seven games and snapping a string of nine consecutive homecoming game victories.
The seven consecutive losses in one season are the most since the 1967 UMaine team went 0-8. Campbell is now 7-1 overall and 4-0 in the Coastal Athletic Association, while UMaine fell to 1-7 and 1-4.
The Fighting Camels racked up 562 total yards compared with UMaine’s 275, and senior quarterback Kamden Sixkiller completed 29 of 44 passes for 450 yards and three touchdowns. He was intercepted once.
Campbell scored 28 unanswered points after UMaine pulled to within 7-6 early in the second quarter on Caden Drezek’s 8-yard touchdown pass to Rashawn Marshall.
Sam Tremblay, who had missed his first field goal attempt in 11 tries this season earlier in the game, missed the extra point.
Trailing 7-6 late in the first half, the Black Bears had the ball on their own 29-yard line facing a second-and-1 situation.
But an incomplete pass and a Marshall run for no yards forced the Black Bears to punt, and it proved costly as the Camels marched 61 yards on four plays to take a 14-6 lead into the intermission.
Ethan Lawrence’s 10-yard touchdown run with 1:43 left in the half capped the drive after Sixkiller hooked up with an open Jyron Waiters for a 53-yard completion on third-and-12.
The Camels expanded the lead to 21-6 early in the third quarter, stringing together a 10-play, 89-yard drive finished off by a 28-yard pass from Sixkiller to tight end Brady Ambrose.
Ambrose broke a couple of tackles en route to the end zone with 9:01 left in the third period.
Sixkiller had extended the drive with a 20-yard pass to running back J.J. Cowan on third-and-6 at the Campbell 43-yard line.
The Camels all but sewed up the win on their next drive by covering 74 yards in 10 plays, with Jon Gullette’s 1-yard run making it 28-6.
Sixkiller used his legs to keep that drive alive by dashing 22 yards on third-and-10 from the Campbell 36-yard line.
The visitors completed the scoring 1:05 into the fourth quarter when Sixkiller found an open Waiters for a 59-yard TD pass.
The Camels opened the scoring on Sixkiller’s 53-yard TD pass to Gullette, but UMaine responded with a four-play, 27-yard drive after an Erv Wiggins Jr. interception and 30-yard return.
Drezek tossed a pass in the flats to a wide-open Marshall, who sprinted into the end zone untouched.
Waiters finished with seven receptions for 155 yards, and Christian Campbell had four for 49 yards. Thirteen different Camels caught passes, and seven had two or more receptions. Cowan was the leading rusher with nine carries for 33 yards.
Linebackers Charles Battaglia and A.J. Benton and free safety Ravel Cato led the Campbell defense with 10, nine and eight tackles, respectively.
For UMaine, Drezek completed 21 of 40 passes for 212 yards and a TD. He was intercepted twice. Evan Wallace had six catches for 67 yards, Nick Laughlin had four for 30 and Corey Rideout had four for 24 yards. Marshall was the leading rusher with 12 carries for 32 yards as the woeful Black Bear offense could only muster 63 yards on the ground.
Strong safety Jeremiah Gill’s 11 tackles paced the Black Bears. Linebackers Noah Carpenter and Sam Oppenheimer had 10 and nine tackles, respectively.

title: Undelivered mail ballots found in dumpster as Election Day nears
text:
RENTON, Wash. (KING) — An election-related problem was discovered and addressed by officials Friday in Washington state.
Eleven days before Election Day, Renton voter Jose Laraque is already turning in his ballot.
“If anyone has a question if voting is important or not, all you have to do is look in history,” Laraque said.
Laraque used one of roughly 100 ballot drop boxes across King County. Election officials said ballots deposited in the drop boxes go directly to their Renton facility, where hundreds of workers help process them.
“If you put it in a ballot drop box it’s going right into our hands,” said Kendall Hodson, with King County Elections.
Ballots found in dumpster
That direct route is getting new attention after 92 undelivered ballots were discovered in a dumpster near Seattle’s Golden Gardens Park earlier this week.
“Understandably alarming and the system is designed to make sure no one can take advantage of that,” Hodson said.
Election officials reported the discovery to Seattle police and the U.S. Postal Service.
The ballots had never reached their intended voters. All 92 have since been invalidated and replacements have been issued.
“This is generally mail theft is what is actually going on, and what we know from our law enforcement partners is that the target is almost never the actual ballots, and that’s why we see them left behind in these cases,” Hodson said.
Security measures in place
King County Elections said it sees a handful of similar cases during major elections.
Officials said possession of a blank ballot isn’t enough to cast a fraudulent vote. Each returned ballot is checked against voter registration records, screened for duplicate voting and has its signature verified.
“Those ballots out in the world isn’t a security threat, it’s not an opportunity for voter fraud,” Hodson said.
For Laraque, the discovery is a reminder of why he believes every vote matters.
“When you see that, if nothing else, don’t get discouraged. Instead, say, ‘I need to get out there and vote and tell everyone where you can safely vote, so that your voice can be heard and your voice can be cast,’” Laraque said.
Officials said voters who have not received their ballots can call King County Elections to request assistance.

title: Brewers’ Misiorowski breaks World Series pitching record: ‘So much adrenaline’
text:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Jacob Misiorowski stepped on the mound for a World Series debut like no other.
“I had so much adrenaline built up,” he said.
He threw a pitch the likes of which had never been seen in the Fall Classic.
The Miz broke the World Series velocity record with his very first delivery, a 103.5 mph fastball to the Tampa Bay Rays’ Yandy Díaz that was taken high out of the strike zone for a ball. He allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter, helping the Milwaukee Brewers to a 3-2 victory in Friday night’s opener.
“I don’t even know how to tell you how I felt,” the 24-year-old right-hander said a half-hour after the end of a crazy ninth inning, prolonged by a game-extending video review. “I still don’t know how I felt. I feel like I’m still trying to take everything in and understand what happened.”
Misiorowski gave up four hits and one walk, striking out a season-low three.
Aroldis Chapman of the Chicago Cubs had the previous mark for fastest Series pitch at 103.2 mph in the ninth inning of Game 2 in 2016, an offering that resulted in a groundout to second by Cleveland’s Coco Crisp. The previous high by a Series starting pitcher since tracking began in 2008 was 101.1 mph by the New York Mets’ Noah Syndergaard to Kansas City’s Ben Zobrist that was taken for a ball in the first inning of Game 3 in 2015.
Miz reached 100 mph with 38 pitches, topping the previous Series high of 24 by Chapman in Game 5 of 2016. The most by a starting pitcher in the Series had been six by Tampa Bay’s Tyler Glasnow in the 2020 opener against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Tampa Bay scored in the fourth when Jonathan Aranda walked, took third on Junior Caminero’s double over center fielder Garrett Mitchell and came around on Liam Hicks’ grounder to first baseman Jake Bauers.
Nearing the end of his first full major league season, Misiorowski has reached 100 mph with 134 of 260 postseason pitches. But his spin rate was down, a sign of a season in which he has pitched 188 innings — up from 141 1/3 innings last year. And he got just seven swings and misses, five on his fastball.
Tampa Bay batters fouled off 20 of his 78 pitches and tipped another.
During the regular season, Misiorowski reached 100 mph with 1,115 pitches, including a high of 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27.
“What we’re used to seeing in the regular season was Miz just mow through people and have two strikeouts an inning. That’s unrealistic,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. “This is the best team in the American League.”
Miz’s first pitch was so fast the scoreboard at American Family Field couldn’t keep up, flashing 103.4 mph — one-tenth of a mile less than it registered on MLB’s Statcast system.
“He’s such a special pitcher,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I felt like for him to be out of the game at five innings, there’s a small win in that.”
Misiorowski threw fastballs on 10 of his first 12 pitches, then mixed in more offspeed stuff. In all he tossed 48 fastballs, 17 cutters, seven sliders and six curveballs.
Miz finished with 30 pitches at 101 mph or higher, 11 of 102 mph or more and three at 103-plus mph.
Warming up in the bullpen, he couldn’t take in the introductions before Milwaukee’s first World Series game in 44 years. He thought about how far he had come, how he was at Double-A Biloxi two years ago.
“It was crazy,” he said. “It’s everything I dreamed of.”

title: Mom arrested after 12-year-old daughter found weighing 47 pounds, authorities say
text:
ORANGEBURG COUNTY, S.C. (WCSC/News) - A mother in South Carolina was arrested after her 12-year-old daughter was allegedly found severely underweight, according to authorities.
Chiquitta Dawkins, 43, was charged with unlawful conduct toward a child, deputies say.
Orangeburg County Sheriff Leroy Ravenell said deputies were called to a location in Bowman, where they found the child suffering from severe malnutrition, according to the arrest warrant.
The investigation found that the girl limped because of her condition, had frail bones and weighed 47 pounds.
Deputies also determined that there were no education records for the child after kindergarten, according to an incident report.
“There are no reasonable people on this planet who could possibly think this is fine,” Ravenell said. “Leaving a child to become this sick, this malnourished is the utmost in despicable.”

title: Officer fired, under investigation after allegedly helping son charged in double murder
text:
MANNING, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - A police officer in South Carolina has been fired after allegedly helping his son, who is charged in a double murder investigation.
Alexander Dukes Sr.’s son, Antwone Dukes, 22, was arrested on Oct. 6 and charged in the deaths of two men stemming from a shooting in a Dollar General parking lot.
Antwone Dukes was also shot, which Sumter County deputies believe was the result of a planned armed robbery.
Sumter County authorities said during the robbery investigation it was discovered that Antwone Dukes drove himself and another gunshot victim, 19-year-old Derek Parson, to his father’s home.
Alexander Dukes, a former Sumter County sheriff’s deputy who had since taken a position with the Manning Police Department, reportedly put a tourniquet on his son’s leg and told him to go to the hospital.
However, authorities said Alexander Dukes did not call 911, report the shooting, or request an ambulance.
Parson ended up dying at the hospital.
Keywaun Clark, 20, was also shot in the suspected robbery and died after crashing his vehicle into a tree near the parking lot, police said.
Filings submitted to the academy stated an investigation by the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division additionally revealed incriminating text messages on Alexander Dukes phone regarding communication with his children.
“From that phone search, texts were found where officer Alexander Dukes Sr. was informing his children that he could no longer notify them of police activity such as roadblocks and traffic stops due to Sumter County encrypting their radio channel,” part of the documents read.
Alexander Dukes failed a polygraph exam as part of the investigation, officials said, and was suspended on Oct. 8.
Authorities said Alexander Dukes has since been terminated from the Manning Police Department, stating that his actions may have hindered a criminal investigation and possibly delayed care that would have saved Parson’s life.
In the termination filing, Manning police said Alexander Dukes “failed his duty and acted in a manner unbecoming of a police officer.”
As of Friday evening, Alexander Dukes was not criminally charged in the case, but the investigation remains ongoing.
Meanwhile, Antwone Dukes remained jailed at the Sumter County Sheriff’s Office Detention Center. He was denied bond after his arrest.
