title: What do we owe our dogs when we put them in someone else’s care?
text:
Meredith Perdue and Michael Cain live in South Portland.
When we hand our dogs over to a dog walker, groomer, trainer or pet sitter, we are entrusting someone with a member of our family. We ask ourselves whether that person is kind, experienced and trustworthy. But how often do we ask the harder questions about exactly how they operate?
In June, our 6-year-old dog, Thatcher, was lost while in the care of a professional pack-style dog walker. After nearly 24 hours of searching, we found his body on I-95.
Since then, we have thought often about the questions we wish we had asked before handing over his leash. We hope other Maine dog owners will ask these questions in order to prevent a similar tragedy. Likewise, we would urge professional pet-care providers to use these questions and develop a plan for when the unexpected happens.
We were aware of some of the trails our dog would be visiting, but we did not know that he would be taken to a specific location surrounded by busy roads and so close to I-95. Had we known, we would not have agreed to it. We believe owners should know which trails and locations their dogs will visit, particularly when dogs are allowed off leash.
The day our dog went missing, the walker had eight dogs in their care at a land trust where posted signs indicated that only two off-leash dogs were permitted at a time. Dog owners should know not only how many dogs a walker is handling, but whether the size of that group is appropriate for the location and permitted by the property.
When our dog disappeared, we were told that his absence was not noticed until a head count was conducted. That leaves questions about supervision we wish we had thought to ask beforehand: When dogs are off leash, where is the person responsible for them? Are they positioned to see the dogs? What happens when a dog falls behind or runs ahead?
We were not notified that our dog was missing for multiple hours after he disappeared. We cannot know what might have happened if we had been called immediately. A missing dog is an emergency and hours matter. A lost dog has a much better chance of being found when the people who know him best are searching immediately and calling their name.
These are not unreasonable questions. They are basic questions about safety.
We tend to evaluate pet-care providers by how much our dogs like them, how happy they appear in photographs and whether other people recommend them. Those things matter. But they are not enough. A beautiful photograph of a pack of dogs running through the woods tells us very little about how those dogs are supervised, what happens when one disappears, or whether the environment itself is appropriate for off-leash dogs.
As dog owners, we have a responsibility. We need to ask questions before we hand over the leash. What are your credentials? Where will my dog go? How many dogs will be there? How are they supervised? What happens if one gets lost? How quickly will you call me? What happens if there is an injury or an accident?
Thatcher was a beloved member of our family. Like so many Maine dogs, he trusted the people around him completely.
We cannot change what happened to Thatcher. But perhaps we can use what happened to encourage other dog owners to ask more questions, and to encourage the people who care for our dogs to welcome those questions and have a plan.

title: Thornton Academy football dominates showdown with Bonny Eagle
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SACO — Behind the big-play ability of Logan LeBlanc, quarterback Noah Fullerton and an increasingly stingy defense, Thornton Academy rolled to a 49-14 win against rival Bonny Eagle in a Class A South football showdown Saturday.
Both teams entered with 7-0 records. Thornton is the unanimous No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine poll, and Bonny Eagle was the consensus No. 2 team.
It was Thornton’s seventh straight win against Bonny Eagle in the annual mark-your-calendar game. Bonny Eagle struck first and led 14-6 in the first quarter, but it was all Thornton from there, with LeBlanc catching three touchdown passes after getting the Golden Trojans on the board with a 90-yard kickoff return.
“That first touchdown definitely got my excitement way up, and from there I knew what I could do and kept my foot on the gas pedal and kept going,” LeBlanc said.
LeBlanc added TD catches of 26 and 44 yards as Thornton built a 28-14 halftime lead, then scored on a 28-yarder in the third quarter. That play initially looks like a designed quarterback run by Fullerton, who pulled up and lofted a pass to his open target.
“He’s a really good athlete and I like to go get it,” Fullerton said of LeBlanc.
Fullerton had touchdown runs of 1 and 5 yards and a tough 2-point conversion run that tied the game 14-14.
PIVOTAL PLAYS
Thornton led 21-14 when Bonny Eagle faced a fourth-and-3 on its own 42. Punter Ben Havu tucked the ball and ran but was tackled a yard short. Havu scored on a similar play against Oxford Hills this season. On the next play, LeBlanc popped wide open on a post pattern against 1-on-1 coverage with no safety help. Fullerton’s play-action pass hit the speedster in stride for a 28-14 lead.
Of the fake punt, Bonny Eagle coach Kevin Cooper said, “we let our kids make plays like that. We had three blockers for two TA defenders and we didn’t get them blocked.”
UNSUNG HERO
The fake punt was derailed by senior Brody Hadiaris, who accelerated toward Havu and stopped him a yard short.
THORNTON DEFENSE
The Scots’ first two drives went 60 and 76 yards, with Ben Noe finding creases up the middle for 31 yards on the first drive and 40 yards on the second. Both were capped by sweeps to the left, with quarterback Lucas Klehn scoring from the 12 and receiver Drew Gervais finding paydirt from the 22 on a jet sweep.
While Thornton’s overall yardage advantage was small — 288 to 258 — it was 288-122 after Bonny Eagle’s first two drives and the score difference was 43-0. What changed? “We’re not necessarily doing anything bettter,” said Thornton outside linebacker Chase Paquette, who had a sack and then an interception to set up the next-to-last TD. “We know we have more depth than any other team, and we’ll wear them down over time, and that’s all we had to do.”
Klehn, who had averaged well over 100 yards rushing per game, was held to 36 yards on 10 carries. Noe was a bright spot with 112 yards on 14 carries. A potential 48-yard score that would have cut the lead to 35-21 was wiped out by a holding penalty. Paquette intercepted Klehn three plays later.
STATISTICS
Bonny Eagle: Lucas Klehn (10 carries, 36 yards, 1 TD; 3 of 8 passing, 28 yards, 1 INT), Ben Noe (13 carries, 112 yards), Drew Gervais (3 carries, 48 yards, 1 TD)
Thornton: Noah Fullerton (12 carries, 47 yards, 2 TDs; 7 of 8 passing, 134 yards, 3 TDs), Logan LeBlanc (6 catches, 129 yards, 3 TDs; kickoff return TD, Brennan Tabor (16 carries, 78 yards)
THEY SAID IT
“Once we can’t get stops, that puts pressure on our offense, and they can’t quite perform as well as they did on the first two drives. They didn’t punt it. You’re not going to win any games if you don’t make the other team punt.” — Bonny Eagle coach Kevin Cooper
“I give our coaches credit. They had a great plan and (Fullerton) executed it. He’s playing great football for us. He really hasn’t gotten the press some others have, but we think he’s dynamite.” — Thornton coach Kevin Kezal

title: Will we succeed in saving the right whale?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Cindy Lowry is a Maine-based environmental advocate with more than two decades of experience protecting marine wildlife, including work on high-profile whale rescue efforts and national conservation campaigns.
To celebrate the United States’ first 250 years, a time capsule was buried in Philadelphia on July 4, to be opened in another 250 years. Maine contributed seven items, a vertebra from a North Atlantic right whale among them.
The bone was from a whale who was found dead near Boothbay in 2016. Researchers named her EgNo 3654. It was believed fishing gear was the cause of her death; she was found with fishing gear wrapped around her head, mouth, flippers and tail.
In addition to her vertebra being included in the capsule, her jaw and flipper bones will be on display when the Maine State Museum reopens on Oct. 24. Museum Director Bernard
Fishman proposed including her vertebra in the capsule. 
Fishman told the Portland Press Herald he wanted the capsule to ask the future a question: “Did we — did you — save the right whales?”
Only about 380 right whales are left, and only 70 of those are reproductive females, according to NOAA. Fishing gear and ship strikes are the leading causes of death.
Entanglement is rarely quick. Whales can drag gear for months, unable to feed or swim freely, before dying of infection, exhaustion or starvation. It’s up to us if we want to fight for a future where North Atlantic right whales continue to migrate off the Gulf of Maine every year, or if they’ll be gone by the time the capsule is opened.
In this time and place, we collectively have the moral obligation to protect our fellow sentient beings. Fortunately, options such as ropeless gear and other technologies exist that the fishing industry could use to ensure right whales have a future. Ropeless, or on-demand, gear keeps traps on the seafloor without a vertical line to the surface until fishermen send a signal to bring them up. Solutions like these should be worked out with lobstermen, not postponed for seven more years.
A bill pending in the Senate could have irreversible impacts on North Atlantic right whales. H.R. 9436, the Northeast Lobstermen Protection Act, co-sponsored by Reps. Jared Golden and Mike Lawler, would extend the pause on new federal right whale protections from the end of 2028 to 2035.
Since 2022, that pause has blocked new rules to reduce entanglements, such as added
gear requirements and fishery closures. No new protections could be added until 2035. The Senate is expected to vote on it in November. A pause on new protections risks more right whales dying in the way that EgNo 3654 did back in 2016.
If you want to be among the people who can make a difference both now and into the future, please call or write to the offices of Sen. Susan Collins and Sen. Angus King before the Senate votes in November, and urge them to oppose Golden’s bill.
EgNo 3654’s bones will be on display at the Maine State Museum in Augusta this fall and my hope is that her story inspires action. We are truly lucky to share our waters with North Atlantic right whales in 2026. Someday, someone will open the capsule and reflect on the vertebra and Fishman’s question. We still have time to decide how they react. Was this a species that we saved?
Let’s hope so.

title: White House holds little-known American art collection
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The White House, known as the home of the president of the United States, also houses an art collection that author Leslie Greene Bowman says rivals museums anywhere in the world.
Bowman, an American art historian, served under four presidents on the Committee for the Preservation of the White House. She has written a new book, “Art for the White House,” detailing the art collection inside the executive mansion.
“Most Washingtonians, most Americans, don’t really know very much about it. And yet here it’s just right on par with any of the great museums in this city and their American art collections,” Bowman said.
Bowman said the collection started with one image.
“The finest in the collection is the great, iconic, full-length portrait of George Washington as our first president. And it moved into the White House before any other furniture did,” Bowman said.
The White House art collection remained largely unchanged until First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy grew the gallery, using landscapes and portraits to represent the people, history and culture of the nation. Since then, every presidential administration has added to the collection.
Bowman said although beautiful, the collection serves a broader purpose.
“It’s a wonderful ambassador for our civilization and our culture through the lens of great art,” Bowman said.
People can view the White House art collection by booking an in-person tour, taking a virtual walk-through on the White House Historical Association’s website, visiting The People’s House, or reading “Art for the White House.”

title: Voskian Seeks to Continue Civil Service with County Commissioner Term
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The District 2 seat on the Lincoln County Board of Commissioners will be an uncontested election this year with Walter Voskian, D-Bremen, on the ballot.
The district includes the towns of Bremen, Bristol, Monhegan Plantation, Nobleboro, South Bristol, and Waldoboro. The seat is currently held by William Blodgett, who is ending his time on the board after over 30 years.
Voskian is a Bremen resident who spent 32 years working for the Central Intelligence Agency, where he was responsible for managing analysis in third world countries and using the information to inform the president of the United States.
Voskian said he has been involved with town and county government for 40 years, both in Bremen and when he lived in Virginia. He spent time on the Bremen Planning Board, the Bremen Budget Committee, the Bremen Ordinance Review Committee, and the Lincoln County Regional Planning Commission.
His time on these boards is what pushed him run for the Lincoln County Board of Commissioners District 2 seat.
Since deciding to run, Voskian has spent the past seven months sitting at almost every commissioners meeting. He said he would not have run for the seat if Blodgett was not retiring. Recently, other than serving on a program committee for the Camden Conference, an annual event to bring foreign affairs conversations to Maine, he said he has felt that public service has been missing from his life for the past year.
“It was sort of a combination of executive and legislative experience, and it seemed to fit together pretty well,” Voskian said. “It sounds to me, based on my experience, to be a good fit for someone who has done what I have done.”
Looking back at his time as a senior intelligence officer for the CIA, Voskian said he is able to “think on his feet” and come up with solutions quickly.
If elected, Voskian said he will bring good decision making skills he has learned from both his previous government and civilian experience, and the ability to sense what’s important to an issue, such as transparency, accessibility, and diligence, to the table. He said he “gets along with everybody.”
From sitting in the board’s meetings for over six months, he said he has a good sense of what needs to be done and what is currently going on. If elected, he said he would like to see the board continue to be run on a “solid foundational, economic basis.”
As a former member, Voskian called himself a “big fan” of the Lincoln County Regional Planning Commission, and would like to be an advocate for the organization’s funding if he were elected.
With this, he said he would also like to see more formalized training for elected officials, particularly planning board members. He suggested a mandatory training from the Maine Municipal Association because most planning board members are volunteers handling “sensitive” issues with property.
“They know they really want to do their job, but it takes them six months to a year to get up to speed, and by then they’re like a third of the way through their assignment,” Voskian said.
Throughout his time campaigning, Voskian has also noticed how little the general public knows about the role of the county commissioners. If elected, he said he would like to further efforts to bring more community members into the picture by either hosting informational meetings or bringing the commissioners to residents at their town’s meetings.
Overall, Voskian would like to see more contact between the commissioners, local municipalities, and representatives in Augusta.
“I know they’re all very busy, but I think there could be some way of making those three different arms of government, for the benefit of the people, work a little more closely,” Voskian said.
The public safety building search is something else Voskian said he would like to help with if elected, wanting to ensure that the process continues to go forward. In 2024, a comprehensive site and structural assessment of the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office in Wiscasset revealed nearly $8 million in repairs and renovations are needed, including replacements or repairs to the building’s exterior masonry, roof, doors, windows, plumbing, electrical and heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems, and sidewalks. Since the assessment was completed, the county has been searching for a new building.
There are two issues Voskian thinks the county is currently facing: rising property taxes and decreasing access to rural healthcare.
He said the long term issue is the “upward spiral of real estate taxes,” especially for those who are in a shoreland zone.
“It just goes up and up and up, and there has to be a more imaginative way of dealing with this because it is not sustainable and I recognize that has to be balanced against the need to provide for public safety, public security, and education and all of that,” Voskian said. “It’s a difficult balance.”
Voskian said rising taxes are not necessarily a responsibility of the board of commissioners, but would still like to “lend its weight to things like that.”
The other issue, which he said was more short-term, is the impending closure of the labor and delivery unit at MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta.
“You’re going to discourage young people from moving here, which would cut down on the birth rate, which was kind of a self-fulfilling prophecy,” Voskian said.
When working with other people, Voskian said he is good at communicating. Over the years, he has dealt with people he disagrees with on different issues but still found a solution through communication.
Voskian said he tries to educate himself on what he is struggling with so he can find a way through it. He gave an example of how he used to be bad at public speaking and made sure he got better at it. Now, he has written a book on the matter.
He said by practicing and confronting things “head on,” challenges are easier to navigate.
“Don’t assume people know what your position is,” Voskian said. “Get out and talk about it. Talk to people. Be accessible. Be transparent and be effective.”
If elected, Voskian said he looks forward to working with current board members, David Levesque and Evan Goodkowsky, and praised them for the work they have done. He admires people who can provide their expertise and professional background to support the community.
“The county is blessed with having a real good administrator and a good staff,” Voskian said.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: National Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial opens Saturday
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A new monument on the National Mall honors those who served in the first Gulf War.
The National Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial officially opened after more than four years of construction.
The memorial honors those who served while educating visitors about the conflict and the 34-country coalition that participated in the war defending Kuwait.
U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum spoke at the opening.
“We left our homes and our families and traveled thousands of miles and fought in strange places because it became our duty,” Burgum said. “We reflect on that powerful and effective coalition. And today, as a country and a world, we pray for a similar rallying together for freedom.”
The monument was constructed using materials reflecting the environment and battle conditions in the Gulf.
It is located just north of the Lincoln Memorial.

title: Hearts of Pine end 2026 with a fond farewell
text:
PORTLAND — Before their season-ending match Saturday, the Portland Hearts of Pine and their fervent fans thanked retiring captain Mikey Lopez for his contributions to the second-year franchise.
Then, on balky knees and in the final game of a 14-year professional career, the 33-year-old Lopez thanked them back in storybook fashion.
In the 53rd minute, Lopez banged in the rebound of his own penalty kick to give Portland the lead. It proved to be the winner in Portland’s 4-1 victory against the USL League One regular-season champions, the Charlotte Independence, at Fitzpatrick Stadium.
Lopez started the play that led to the PK. He intercepted a pass near midfield and fed the ball ahead. Walter Verala won the ball and worked hard to get past a defender, then was taken down in the penalty box by Charlotte keeper George Tasouris.
“I don’t think anyone could have written this,” Lopez said. “It was the best night possible. Getting the 4-1 victory. Getting on the scoresheet. Having my family here and being able to play my final game with (Hearts head coach) Bobby (Murphy). It truly is a storybook ending.”
Lopez was subbed out after his goal to another round of appreciative applause.
Unlike 12 previous times in the 2026 season, Portland did not give up the lead.
Instead, the Hearts tacked on. Diogo Barbosa scored in the 82nd minute. Aboubacar Camara’s second of the game in the 90th minute was his 10th in league play in his rookie season (11th overall).
It was a sweet ending to a tough 8-14-10 season and a reward for the 6,400-strong crowd who savored the Hearts’ sixth league win against seven losses and three ties at Fitzpatrick.
When the match was over, Murphy and Lopez thanked the fans over the public address system.
“From the bottom of my heart, I’m so thankful for you guys, for the love and appreciation that you have shown not only to me but to the rest of the guys all year,” Lopez said. “We certainly at times did not deserve it, but we are extremely appreciative and thankful.”
Lopez first played for Murphy when he was 12. That’s when the kid from Mission, Texas, left home for soccer for the first time, attending St. Stephens Academy, a soccer academy in Austin, Texas, run by Murphy. Lopez stayed there for the next five years before going to the University of North Carolina, where he helped the Tar Heels win the 2011 NCAA championship.
From there, Lopez was a first-round MLS draft pick and played in the top U.S. league for five seasons (2013-17). When Murphy asked him to join Portland in 2025, Lopez was coming off double Achilles surgery and had not played since 2023.
“Mikey’s family to me,” Murphy said. “I’m really grateful that he got to end his career in a place like this, and not so many other clubs that wouldn’t have been able to accurately congratulate him on a career.”
As a defensive midfielder, Lopez has never been a goal scorer. His Saturday night strike was just his 13th professional goal, and second with the Hearts.
Lopez said “he was down with it,” to take the penalty kick but admitted he got nervous standing on the spot. His low shot was not particularly well struck. Tasouris made a modest dive to his right and blocked it. But the keeper did not control it, and by rule, the ball is live. Lopez got to it first and banged it home, setting off a joyous team-wide celebration.
“We were joking, Who had Mikey Lopez for the winner on Kalshi?” Murphy said. “He didn’t want the penalty, he doesn’t like them, got bullied into it, but if he was ever going to score a penalty, it was going to be that way. It sort of sums Mikey up in a nutshell.”
Before the game, as fans chanted, “Thank you, Mik-EE!” Lopez was presented with a framed Hearts of Pine game jersey while surrounded by nearly two dozen family members, including his wife, Elena, his parents, brother, grandmother and various aunts and uncles. After a pause for photos, Lopez acknowledged the fans in each section, eliciting more chants of appreciation.
Lopez started the match and was very active. His quick accurate passes, crunching tackles and wise positioning demonstrated the talents that, while slowed, made him good enough to play in MLS for five years and were vital to the Hearts when they advanced to the USL1 semifinals in 2025.
Lopez has never shied from trying to dislodge the ball. He did that multiple times, including in the 24th minute when he drew his 18th yellow card in 54 games with Portland and 88th in his 286-match pro career.
“Like my brother said, it’s not a Mikey Lopez game if I don’t get a yellow card,” Lopez said with a grin.
But his final season has been tough. He’s had two knee surgeries and missed 15 of Portland’s 32 league games.
At Thursday’s training session, Lopez was clearly limping as he walked from physical training to the team locker room, unable to fully straighten his right knee.
Lopez admitted he had pregame doubts about how long and well he’d be able to play.
“My knee felt a little swollen and it felt like I couldn’t move it as smoothly and fluidly,” Lopez said. “But I guess just adrenaline took over and I said, ‘I’m not going to come off early and I going to try to come off in the 55th, and it was pretty close.
“I can’t explain it. Everything was pretty much just written. Some really good writer upstairs wrote something amazing and this is the perfect way to end it.”

title: Joey Brunelle will bring fresh vision to Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I love Portland for its scenic beauty, architecture, music scene, leafy neighborhoods, international diversity and opportunities for flânerie. With such an array, can one be blamed for not wanting to change a thing?
But then one day we all woke up to find coastal flooding, a housing shortage, a concomitant homeless crisis and a stagnant population in a growing world.
How did this happen? A major cause is decades of resistance to change and a gradual, incremental regression. Which is why I’m supporting Joey Brunelle for Portland City Council. Joey knows that what people value is each other and has the vision to say: “Let’s do this a little differently.”
Joey is uniquely prepared to serve our city, not just because he is a policy wonk, or because he has attended hundreds of City Council meetings, but that he has the guts and compassion to work for all of us.
Zack Barowitz
Portland

title: UMaine blanks Colgate 3-0 again to complete weekend hockey sweep
text:
ORONO, Maine — Senior goalie Albin Boija made 17 saves, and the Black Bears received goals from junior right wing Lee Parks, sophomore defenseman Loic Usereau and sophomore right wing Sam Alfano to complete a weekend sweep of Colgate with a 3-0 victory at Alfond Arena on Saturday night.
UMaine is now 4-2 overall and winner of three straight, while Colgate fell to 0-6 after the Black Bears also won 3-0 on Friday night.
Parks scored a power-play goal in the second period, extending his goal-scoring streak to five games. Usereau and Alfano sewed up the win with late third-period goals.
Usereau skated onto a pass from behind the net from Judah Makway and fired a one-timer past Colgate goalie Reid Dyck for his third of the season and second in as many games. Alfano scored his second of the season with a wrist shot from the inner half of the right circle.
Dyck finished with 29 saves as UMaine outshot Colgate 32-17, including a 27-7 edge over the last two periods.
UMaine took a 1-0 lead on Parks’ power-play goal at the 9:04 mark of the second period.
Max Scott had the puck behind the net and Parks skated to the bottom of the right faceoff circle, where he received a pass from Scott and beat Dyck with a short one-timer.
Lukas Peterson also earned an assist as his shot from the point wound up behind the net where Scott collected the puck and shoveled it out to Parks.
Dyck kept the Raiders within one with 13 saves in the period while Boija only had to make one stop.
UMaine outshot Colgate 14-1 in the period.
Dyck made a terrific save off Thomas Pichette, who skated onto a loose puck that took a crazy bounce off the boards behind the net and rolled into the low slot.
Colgate was clearly the better of the two teams in the scoreless first period, but Boija was outstanding and the Black Bears received some good fortune when Max Nagel’s wrister from the right faceoff circle glanced off the crossbar.
Boija made 10 saves in the period, including a pad save off Luke Pakaluk’s redirection from the edge of the crease off a Tobias Ohman feed and a glove save on Jack Brandt’s wrister off his break-in off the right wing.
Dyck was only forced to make five saves, but he did have a couple of quality stops, squeezing his pads on Will Gerrior’s wrister from the left circle and holding his ground to stuff Scott’s wraparound attempt.

title: L.L.Bean’s Freeport makeover is getting mixed reviews. Of course it is.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FREEPORT — Anyone who made a point of visiting the renovated L.L.Bean flagship store on its opening day last month was probably going to have nice things to say about it and, in local news coverage, did.
Just as surely, if you waited a minute, you were bound to find people on the internet criticizing the new premises.
Since its reopening, some of the 400,000 visitors have taken to Reddit, Instagram and Facebook comment sections to voice complaints about the store and, to varying degrees of relevance, about Maine’s signature brand as a whole, from the price of its clothes to the politics of the late Linda Bean.
While others have applauded the new look and layout, the most commonly shared critique of the physical space is that it lacks charm.
Now, I didn’t think the previous iteration was particularly quaint. And it does seem some of the naysayers are still lamenting a much earlier version of the store, complete with creaky floors and narrow stairs.
Still, the commentary made me curious enough to go see for myself. Here’s what I noticed.
There are a lot of places to sit
L.L.Bean is smart to take into consideration that not everyone who comes through its doors is interested in shopping. Many people might merely be accompanying someone who is. The more comfortable those people are, the more the actual customers can be left to spend.
That starts with giving them somewhere to sit, which now includes more benches throughout the store, Adirondack chairs around the grounds, camp-inspired nooks by the fitting rooms and living room-like setups with brown leather couches in front of fireplaces, at least one of which had a chessboard.
Anyone can find entertainment
While most of these people are probably content to play on their phones, anyone in search of amusement has options, starting with the trout pond and stream tank, where there’s information on different species, as there is by taxidermy displays throughout the store. (“The Final Charge,” a popular exhibit of two bull moose who got their antlers locked in combat and eventually died, is still in storage, waiting to be assessed for repair.)
History buffs can read about the evolution of the Boat and Tote bag and of the flagship store itself on shadow boxes containing products from throughout the years, which, these days, could easily fetch four figures on eBay. Kids can draw on giant chalkboards or get inside a rowboat surrounded by nature scenes, while the 21-plus crowd can play cornhole outside with a beer in hand from walk-up drink and snack shack The Outpost.
The cafe is corporate and pricey
An array of caffeinated beverages served at the new 1912 Cafe offers another way keep someone occupied — or energized for more shopping. If you’re considering it for lunch, though, know that this is where any lack of character was most apparent to me.
The single pastries on display, hardboiled eggs and hummus cups seemed plucked from Starbucks’ playbook. The corporate vibe continued into the seating area, where a few plaid accents couldn’t save it from feeling like a food court. With most sandwiches priced at $14.25 and (albeit large and Maine-made) bags of chips at $4.50, I’d rather spend my money on a sit-down meal elsewhere in town. However, I must say, “The Freeport,” its turkey, bacon and Swiss sandwich, was tasty and sizeable enough for most to share, especially if you decide to splurge on those chips.
Water bottles and pullovers rule
Another common complaint lodged online about the new store is how actual outdoor gear seems to have taken even more of a backseat to clothes that, as one person on Reddit described, are “for people who want to cosplay as outdoorsy.” Case in point were the shackets in the hunting section that caught my eye, despite a complete disinterest in killing my own food.
In the camping area, it seemed the most space was dedicated to water bottles — a whole “hydration” wall, in fact, with Nalgenes, canteens and store-branded versions of those ubiquitous giant cups with the built-in straws. Perhaps the only category of product that could compete in terms of variety is women’s pullovers, which I saw in ribbed, knit and quilted styles; sweater, sweatshirt and temperature-regulating material; wool and multiple weights of fleece.
Shoppers flaunt their brand loyalty
If I wanted to fit in, I would have worn my own L.L.Bean half-snap sweater fleece from several seasons ago, but I’ve always assumed the rule about not wearing the band T-shirt to the concert would apply here, too.
A surprising number of shoppers when I visited, however, weren’t afraid to be loud and proud about their loyalty, making it difficult to distinguish them from the flannel-clad staff. Judging by the number of pullovers I saw, the company seems to understand its customers.
It’s hard to fault a business for focusing on what sells. I get that L.L.Bean is more than a store to many Mainers but also a symbol of tradition, a holder of memories and a source of pride. Carrying all that meaning makes change hard, but if the company knows what it’s doing, we’ll be missing this version of the flagship one day.

title: High school football coach dies after medical emergency at game
text:
High school football coach dies after medical emergency at game
Ed Dawson, a high school football coach in western Pennsylvania, died at the hospital after medics responded to the sideline during Friday night's game
High school football coach dies after medical emergency at game
Ed Dawson, a high school football coach in western Pennsylvania, died at the hospital after medics responded to the sideline during Friday night's game
Ed Dawson, the football coach at Cornell High School in western Pennsylvania, died after a medical emergency during the team's game Friday night, the district superintendent said.
"I am extremely saddened and shocked to report that Coach Dawson has passed away," Superintendent Aaron Thomas said in a statement.
The Cornell Raiders were playing Rochester. Beaver County emergency dispatchers confirmed that medics responded to the sideline at the Rochester football field.
No additional details regarding the nature of the medical emergency were immediately released.
Statement from Cornell School District Superintendent Aaron Thomas
We want to update everyone on a situation that happened at the away football game this evening at Rochester High School. During the game Head Football Coach Ed Dawson experienced a medical emergency and was transported to a local hospital. I am extremely saddened and shocked to report that Coach Dawson has passed away.
This is an extremely difficult situation. To say Coach Dawson was an integral part of Cornell School District would be an understatement. It is hard to put into words what Coach Dawson means to Cornell and we are all heart broken, crushed, and in shock. We will work to ensure our students and staff have the resources they need and right now our thoughts and prayers are with Coach Dawson and his family. We have difficult days ahead and we will lean on each other to get through them the best we can. We love you Coach Dawson.
Statement from Coraopolis Mayor Michael Dixon
Tonight our community lost one of its giants. Coach Ed Dawson passed away this evening, and the Borough of Coraopolis joins Cornell School District, his players, and his family in heartbreak.
When Cornell stepped away from football in 2012, a lot of people assumed Friday nights here were over. Coach Dawson didn't accept that. When the Raiders returned in 2016, he started with a few dozen kids and a lot of faith.
They lost their first 18 games and kept showing up anyway, even at youth league games, making sure every young person in this town knew there was a place for them on his team.
By 2019, he had led the Raiders to their first section title in 36 years, the first WPIAL playoff win in school history, and the WPIAL semifinals. He took them back to the semifinals in 2021.
The wins mattered. The young men he shaped mattered more. Coach Dawson looked for the positive in every game and in every kid, and he taught them to sweat the details and never quit. Generations of Cornell and Nazareth Prep players grew into better men because he believed in them before they believed in themselves.
To Coach Dawson's family: Coraopolis grieves with you, and we will stand beside you in the days ahead. To his players and coaching staff: lean on each other and on this community. You were his team, and you are ours.
Thank you, Coach. We love you, and we will not forget what you built here.

title: Singing Maine’s praises, one county at a time
text:
Elizabeth Lardie Thompson couldn’t quite believe what she was hearing.
She was playing pub trivia in Sydney, Australia, more than 20 years ago. The quiz master began the bonus round by saying, “There’s this silly song Americans sing if they grow up in Maine and it’s got all the counties in it.” Could anyone in the pub sing it?
“We sang that song at least once a week in fourth grade, and then it just carried into something we did incessantly, even into to high school,” said Thompson, 43, a theater performer and writer who lives in Bath. “So when they asked if anyone could sing it, I was like, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me.'”
The “Maine County Song” has been taught in Maine schools for decades, at least since the 1950s. It began as an easy way for kids to learn some strange-sounding Maine county names, like Androscoggin, Piscataquis or Sagadahoc. Today it’s a grassroots Maine tradition, a source of pride for adults who can still sing it at a moment’s notice.
The fact that a quiz master in Australia had heard about it — from another Aussie who had spent a college semester in Maine — is testament to how unique and long-lasting the 30-second song is.
In Maine, people talk about the divide between rural and urban areas, locals and tourists, the 1st District and the 2nd District. But for several generations, the “Maine County Song” is a unifier to the tune of “Yankee Doodle.”
“I just think it’s a point of pride, that we all know the 16 counties because of that song,” said Denise Michaud, 61, administrative assistant for South Portland Public Works. “It’s like ‘Oh, you don’t know the counties in your state? I know the counties in my state, because I can sing them.'”
A SINGING SUCCESS
As an educational tool, the song’s success is undeniable. It’s so well-known that it’s become part of the state’s popular culture.
The Downeasters Chorus, a Maine-based barbershop harmony group, added it to their repertoire this year and sang it at the Yarmouth Clam Festival in July. Marpheen Chann, of Portland, who is running for Cumberland County commissioner in November, posted a video of himself singing the song on social media after reading a ton about Maine county government in preparation for his campaign. He said he first sang it at Acton Elementary School.
The Law Offices of Joe Bornstein produced a series of TV ads a couple of years ago to celebrate the firm’s 50th anniversary, featuring “American Idol” finalist Julia Haven (formerly Julia Gagnon) of Cumberland, singing the song. The firm wanted to create a “unifying message” for its anniversary and thought the “Maine County Song” was the perfect way to do that, said Nate Bergeron, the marketing director.
Emily Little, a nurse who grew up on Mount Desert Island but now lives in Virginia, has taught the song to her three kids. She laments that they’ll never know the joys of singing about all of the counties in their state —Virginia has 95 counties, way too many to remember or fit into a song.
On a summer visit to Maine last year, her kids, husband and parents joined her in making a video of the whole family singing the song, one voice at a time.
When Little went to Vassar College in Poughkeepsie, New York, she organized Maine-themed parties with other students from the Pine Tree State and singing the county song was always part of the program.
“No one else had a state party. It was like no other state had its own identity. And singing the county song was part of that,” said Little, 41.
Three classes of fourth graders at the Congin School in Westbrook were learning the song this month as part of a Maine studies unit. Kids could be heard at recess or in bus lines singing it.
In class on a recent Tuesday morning, they sang it repeatedly without any missteps — though some students admitted having trouble pronouncing some of the counties at first, including Androscoggin and Sagadahoc.
Most had heard of Cumberland County, which includes Westbrook, and nearby York County. They were also learning about the structure of U.S. government, and how it’s broken down by state, county and towns so that all people, in every place, can have a voice.
Part of the lesson is that “one person cannot do it all, so having local help makes it easier for everyone,” said Wendy Nugent, a fourth grade teacher.
WORD OF MOUTH
The song’s origins seem to be organic. Some people remember learning it in their public school classrooms as early as the 1950s, and it’s easy to find many who learned it from the 1970s on. Several teachers interviewed for this story said it had been taught in their schools since at least the ’80s or ’90s.
The song is not a mandated part of any curriculum and there’s no single official version, so a few of the words and the order of the counties are sometimes different. Some people call it “The 16 Counties Song.”
But hundreds of teachers have used it during the fourth grade year as part of the required Maine studies unit.
Michaud said she was “shocked” when her son, Ben Michaud, came home from school and sang a version of the “Maine County Song” that was different than the one she learned at Dora Small School in South Portland in the 1970s.
Ben Michaud, now 30, had learned a version that ended with “Oxford and Penobscot” instead of “Aroostook and Penobscot.” While being interviewed for this story, Michaud sang her version of the song, to prove she still could.
The Maine Secretary of State Kids’ Page lists lyrics to two versions of the song, along with audio clips. But a spokesperson for the office says no one there knows when the information was added to the website, or when the song was first taught.
The first version on the website is: “The 16 counties in our state are/Cumberland and Franklin/Piscataquis and Somerset/Aroostook, Androscoggin/Sagadahoc and Kennebec/Lincoln, Knox and Hancock/Waldo, Washington and York/Oxford and Penobscot.”
The second version reads: “There are 16 counties in our state/There’s Cumberland and Franklin/Piscataquis and Kennebec/Oxford, Androscoggin/Waldo, Washington and York/Lincoln, Knox and Hancock/Sagadahoc and Somerset/Aroostook and Penobscot.”
Both are sung to the tune of “Yankee Doodle” and both sound pretty much the same to those of us who didn’t learn the song in school. But dozens of people responding to a Facebook query were adamant that the version they learned was the correct one.
SCARES BEARS, PAYS FOR COLLEGE
Emma and Nora Conrad have found myriad uses for the “Maine County Song” since learning it in Winthrop as grade schoolers. The sisters sang it to pass the time on long car trips, sometimes shouting it out the window at passing traffic. They sang it at a Christmas parade in their father’s Pennsylvania hometown. They sing spontaneously when walking, kayaking or hiking.
Once, while hiking in Colorado, they sang it to scare any nearby bears. It was a song they knew well enough to sing at the top of their lungs, a sort of default safety song.
Emma Conrad, who works for the Natural Resources Council of Maine, said the song is a comfortable way to break the ice when she meets other people who grew up here.
“Maine is a big small town and, with just 16 counties, you’re never far removed from people all around the state,” said Conrad, 28, of Portland.
The song has helped put Maine students through college. Massachusetts-based dairy company H.P. Hood promoted its Milk Money Scholarship program in Maine in the late 1990s by offering a $4,000 scholarship to one student in each of the 16 counties.
To apply for the scholarship, students had to show up in person and successfully sing the county song. Grades and recommendations, interviews and other non-musical criteria were considered, too.
Lauren Rioux, 45, grew up in East Machias in Washington County and applied for the scholarship in 1999. She sang the county song at the University of Maine at Machias and later found out she had gotten the $,4,000 award, which she used while studying music at the University of Southern Maine.
Rioux, who lives in Scarborough, is a fiddler who teaches at her home studio and at Waynflete School in Portland. Sometimes when people ask her to sing the “Maine County Song,” she jokes that she once got paid a lot of money to play it. But she’s happy to play it for free, and to teach it to others.
During the pandemic, when she couldn’t teach in-person, Rioux made videos. She made one singing the “Maine County Song.” Her baby daughter, Caroline, is seen sleeping in a carrier as she sings. Rioux said she can’t remember exactly why she decided to record the song. But she’s glad she did.
“It’s part of our state’s lore, it’s fun and it’s happy.”

title: Undelivered mail ballots found in dumpster as Election Day nears
text:
RENTON, Wash. (KING) — An election-related problem was discovered and addressed by officials Friday in Washington state.
Eleven days before Election Day, Renton voter Jose Laraque is already turning in his ballot.
“If anyone has a question if voting is important or not, all you have to do is look in history,” Laraque said.
Laraque used one of roughly 100 ballot drop boxes across King County. Election officials said ballots deposited in the drop boxes go directly to their Renton facility, where hundreds of workers help process them.
“If you put it in a ballot drop box it’s going right into our hands,” said Kendall Hodson, with King County Elections.
Ballots found in dumpster
That direct route is getting new attention after 92 undelivered ballots were discovered in a dumpster near Seattle’s Golden Gardens Park earlier this week.
“Understandably alarming and the system is designed to make sure no one can take advantage of that,” Hodson said.
Election officials reported the discovery to Seattle police and the U.S. Postal Service.
The ballots had never reached their intended voters. All 92 have since been invalidated and replacements have been issued.
“This is generally mail theft is what is actually going on, and what we know from our law enforcement partners is that the target is almost never the actual ballots, and that’s why we see them left behind in these cases,” Hodson said.
Security measures in place
King County Elections said it sees a handful of similar cases during major elections.
Officials said possession of a blank ballot isn’t enough to cast a fraudulent vote. Each returned ballot is checked against voter registration records, screened for duplicate voting and has its signature verified.
“Those ballots out in the world isn’t a security threat, it’s not an opportunity for voter fraud,” Hodson said.
For Laraque, the discovery is a reminder of why he believes every vote matters.
“When you see that, if nothing else, don’t get discouraged. Instead, say, ‘I need to get out there and vote and tell everyone where you can safely vote, so that your voice can be heard and your voice can be cast,’” Laraque said.
Officials said voters who have not received their ballots can call King County Elections to request assistance.

UCF hosted previously undefeated No. 2 BYU on Saturday at the Acrisure Bounce House, the highest-ranked opponent to visit the Knights in program history, taking the victory 39 to 31 in a double-overtime thriller.

UCF made several key plays to challenge the Cougars. title: Retired custodian gets new elementary school named in her honor
text:
AUBREY, Texas (WFAA) — A new elementary school in Texas will be named after Marilyn Hampton, a retired custodian who worked for the district for 39 years.
The Aubrey Independent School District surprised Hampton with the announcement during a red carpet presentation at Wednesday’s board meeting.
Surprise announcement
Hampton was asked to roll out a red carpet, a task similar to those she performed during her career as a custodian. It took her several seconds to realize what the carpet was for.
“Oh my goodness,” Hampton said. “Oh, God. You all are the best.”
The school, previously known only as Elementary School Number Five, will be named Marilyn Hampton Elementary.
“I still can’t believe it. I haven’t stopped crying,” Hampton said.
A 39-year career
Hampton spent 39 years as an Aubrey Independent School District custodian.
Superintendent Shannon Saylor said Hampton did more than custodial work during that time, including buying and delivering school supplies and helping students study for tests.
“She is truly Aubrey ISD,” Saylor said.
Saylor said Hampton left behind “her teaching legacy” about being kind, working hard and persevering.
Hampton is one of eight siblings and the only one to graduate high school. She said she used to think of herself as a failure for not going to college.
“I just thought, ‘You know, Marilyn? God put you where you are supposed to be.’ And I’m very happy with the way things turned out,” Hampton said.
Second career
Hampton now spends time in a rocking chair at the Aubrey Independent School District Early Bird Learning Center, feeding a young girl named Claire.
“She’s a sweetheart. She’s got pretty eyes,” Hampton said of Claire.
The district gave Hampton a Marilyn Hampton Elementary shirt to mark the announcement ahead of the school’s opening.
“Can you believe it? I can’t. I cannot. All I can say is God is good,” Hampton said.
Marilyn Hampton Elementary opens next August.

title: How reliant is Ukraine on US support — and could Kyiv carry on without it?
text:
How reliant is Ukraine on US support — and could Kyiv carry on without it?
It has been a bewildering period in U.S.-Ukraine relations, after U.S. President Donald Trump slammed his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky for failing to negotiate an end to the war and Kyiv accused Washington of withholding key military support.
Related video above: Russia and Ukraine agree to resume peace talks as American freed after four years
Trump then sent his envoy to Norway and Russia to try to advance the peace process, but Washington walked away with only a plan to resume trilateral talks.
Meanwhile, deadly Russian attacks continue, as Ukraine raises concerns about cracks in support from the U.S.
The latest tensions are far from the first bout between Kyiv and Trump, who began his second term by halting aid for Ukraine’s war effort. Since then, Europe has picked up the tab, and Kyiv has built up its own defense industry at a rapid pace.
So how much does Ukraine still rely on U.S. support? And can it carry on fighting without it?
Experts say there are three broad levers of pressure the United States can apply to Kyiv — economic, military and political — as it seeks some sort of Ukrainian capitulation to end the war started by Russia.
Economic: Ukraine aid already cut
The Trump administration halted new aid packages for Ukraine at the beginning of 2025.
Before then, the U.S. had sent at least $131.5 billion in total aid to Ukraine, which still makes it the largest single donor since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, according to data from the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, a German think tank that tracks wartime aid to Ukraine. Some of the weapons from American manufacturers purchased during the Biden administration are still flowing to Ukraine, but many of those contracts have been fulfilled.
European Union countries and institutions as a bloc now outpace the U.S. in their total donations, sending at least $228.5 billion since 2022, Kiel Institute data shows.
Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands and Sweden have given the largest amount of military aid among the EU states. The United Kingdom and Norway have also contributed a significant chunk of military aid from outside the bloc.
Many of the donations come in the form of NATO allies purchasing U.S.-made weapons that they then transfer to Ukraine.
But those European weapons transfers still require Pentagon authorization, giving the Trump administration another source of leverage.
Zelensky addressed Ukraine’s critical shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors Friday, saying, “The delivery of interceptors to protect us against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed. We are waiting for interceptors that were already agreed on, but they are still not coming.”
Last week, Ukraine ran out of Patriot interceptors — one of the few defensive weapons capable of knocking down a ballistic missile — leaving it far more vulnerable to Russian attacks.
None of the ballistic missiles that slammed Kyiv overnight into Thursday were intercepted — an indicator that Patriot stocks are still empty or critically low. Zelensky told CNN hours after that attack that Ukraine primarily needs two things from its allies at this critical moment: “Not to lift sanctions from Putin … (and) to give us better missiles.”
Given that those weapons orders are a boon for American defense companies, analysts say it’s unlikely that any slowdown or blocking of purchases would continue for a long time.
Military: Intel sharing and satellite internet
Although American financial support has collapsed, Ukraine still relies heavily on U.S. intelligence and technology.
It has no replacement for unique American systems like the Patriot interceptors, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet called Starshield and advanced missile-warning technology.
“That is something Europeans don’t have, and they don’t have it because we (the U.S.) have told them for the last 30 years not to develop it … because they can rely on us,” said Max Bergmann, the Russia program director at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank.
“We’re in a situation where America is proving to everyone in Europe that it simply can’t be relied upon,” Bergmann told CNN.
“This could be really devastating for Ukraine in the sense that it could cause tremendous economic damage, tremendous loss of civilian life, civilians leaving,” he said. “But I doubt it’s going to actually break Ukraine’s will to fight.”
Zelensky said earlier this week that on multiple occasions Ukraine had received no U.S. intelligence warnings of ballistic strikes. That resulted in Russian missile attacks hitting without the usual air raid sirens warning residents to head to bunkers, and Ukrainian officials have said more civilians died as a result.
The U.S. State Department and Trump himself have denied limiting intelligence sharing.
By Tuesday night, Zelensky said that the intelligence sharing with the United States “now works” again.
The country’s defense ministry said Saturday full access to Starshield has been restored, though it was not immediately clear whether the restoration of Starshield speeds could be felt across the country. One source on the ground in Ukraine’s Donetsk region told CNN Saturday morning that the speed in their area continued to be limited to 160 kilometers per hour.
The restrictions, which disrupt any military ordnance moving at high speeds, have hindered Ukrainian interceptor drones in defending against Russian attacks and upended Ukrainian military operations in many areas of the front line, Ukrainian officials said.
Trump and some of his top officials have denied making the call to throttle Ukraine’s use of the Starshield service, without offering any clear explanation for what had actually happened. Earlier this week, Trump said he was not involved.
Musk has denied taking unilateral action, though, saying in a social media post that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”
In the short term, any further disruptions or restrictions to U.S.-backed systems are likely to hit Ukraine incredibly hard, experts said. In the long term, it’s likely that European allies will pump more money into developing their own systems to help Ukraine.
“I think the Ukrainians probably didn’t think that the United States would stoop this low, would betray it this much, because this isn’t really an act of charity that the United States is doing. … This is a service that Ukraine is spending money on,” Bergmann said of Kyiv’s Starshield contract and Patriot interceptor purchases.
“What the administration is doing actually has far larger ramifications for the basic reliability of the U.S. as a technology and defense supplier,” Bergmann added.
Political: Giving hope to Putin
The falling-out between the U.S. and Ukraine also has wider geopolitical ramifications, analysts said, and could end up being a gift to the Kremlin’s war effort.
It comes after a number of controversial moves by the Trump administration this month, including waiving new sanctions on Russia before they could kick in and striking a deal to allow Russia to export diesel. Meanwhile, the Kremlin has so far not budged on its maximalist demands to end the war.
Washington’s willingness to place unprecedented pressure on Kyiv “gives Russia a certain hope that if they continue fighting this war, eventually the European resolve will also fade away,” said Natia Seskuria, a senior research fellow on Russia and Eurasia at the Royal United Services Institute, a U.K.-based defense think tank.
John Lough, head of international partnerships at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, had a similar view.
“I think the Russians must feel quite pleased with themselves at the moment with the strain all this recent activity is putting on Europe, by getting Trump to pressurize Ukraine, break the sanctions regime and not follow through with the Lindsey Graham bill,” he told CNN. “It’s just accentuating the fact that Europe and the United States are not aligned.”
Trump has directly tied the waiving of sanctions to the release of detained American Stephen Hubbard, despite stating earlier that the U.S. gave Moscow “nothing in exchange” for his freedom.
Experts said some of the tension — particularly on issues related to diesel, with Trump blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring prices rather than the war in Iran — may dissipate after the U.S. midterms. But the problem of high gas prices and the unpopularity of the war in Iran are here to stay for the remainder of Trump’s presidency, Lough argued.
Lough said that Ukraine’s efforts to continue attacks on Russian oil refineries have been like “a red rag to a bull” for Trump. “It makes Ukraine the easy target if you’re trying to deflect responsibility for what’s happened with Iran.”
CNN’s Becky Pinnington contributed to this report.

title: Maine men make a big difference for the community over beer and wings

Maine men make a big difference for the community over beer and wings
"100 Men Who Care" is a group that truly lives up to its name, oftentimes over some good beer and wings.
Maine men make a big difference for the community over beer and wings
"100 Men Who Care" is a group that truly lives up to its name, oftentimes over some good beer and wings.
Every four months, a group of men at the Stockhouse in Westbrook make a big difference for charities in southern Maine.
"100 Men Who Care" is an organization that does just that, and they even add in some cold beer and wings.
"It's crazy the amount of fun and business that gets conducted here," said Bo Balcavage, one of the leaders of the group.
"100 Men Who Care" is open to men from all sorts of careers and backgrounds.
"If you were to survey what businesses they are from, there is really no pattern in there. We have got bankers, urologists, farmers, fishermen," Balcavage said.
Here is how this all works: every four months, these men get together and each pitch in $100 that will go toward a southern Maine nonprofit. Each man also nominates a charity near and dear to them and puts it in a basket. Three charities are then chosen and the man who nominated the charity must stand up and share a story about it.
"We are suckers for small nonprofits and very personal stories," Balcavage said.
It is a democratic system at Stockhouse, because the charity that wins the popular vote gets the money.
"Any time that you can give back to the community that you live in, it's a good thing," one member said.
At the last meeting, more than $9,000 was awarded to Caring Resources for Living, an organization that helps provide essential materials and comforts to children dealing with life-threatening conditions. This time, that same amount was given to The Dream Factory, which helps send children dealing with medical issues on the trip of a lifetime.
If you would like to learn more about "100 Men Who Care" or join yourself, you can learn more on their website.

Sen. Collins announces funding for improvements at Rockport Harbor

Sen. Collins announces funding for improvements at Rockport Harbor
The almost $700,000 will support components of the town's East Side Working Waterfront Resilience Project.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, announced almost $700,000 towards Rockport Harbor's East Side Working Waterfront Resilience Project.
The $698,750 will come from the U.S. Department of Transportation Maritime Administration’s Port Infrastructure Development Program. It will support improvements to the town's working waterfront infrastructure to strengthen its long-term sustainability, safety and resilience against coastal storms. The project includes installing 12 timber piles, a heavy timber pier deck, marine-grade connectors, a vessel fendering system, and basic electrical and water utilities.
“Improving Maine’s infrastructure and strengthening our coastal communities are essential to our state’s long-term economic success,” said Collins. “This investment will help protect Rockport Harbor’s working waterfront from coastal storms and ensure that it remains a safe and reliable resource for the fishermen, businesses, and families who depend on it."

title: Falmouth’s Georgia Moon outkicks her rivals in A South cross country regional
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
CUMBERLAND —Georgia Moon’s game plan Saturday was to stay with the pack until she felt ready to kick, and then just go for it.
Moon timed her move perfectly as was able to hold off Portland’s Nora Schmidt by just over a second to win the Class A girls race in the Southern Maine regionals at Twin Brook Recreation Area.
Moon, a senior at Falmouth, finished in 18 minutes, 11.51 seconds, while Schmidt’s time was 18:12.63.
“(My strategy) just ended up being challenging,” Moon said. “But it works out in the end. Down the stretch, I just kept thinking ‘I know I have (strength) in my legs.’ I’ve done the workouts, I’ve done the physical work. I know it’s there. I just had to trust that I know it’s there.”
Allie Schmitt of Cheverus (19:00.38) finished third. The results were a swap from last year’s regional final, when Schmidt held off Moon, with Schmitt rounding out the top three.
Moon also won the girls race at the Festival of Champions in Belfast last month.
Portland once again swept the Class A South boys and girls titles. In the girls race, the Bulldogs scored 63 points, followed by Thornton Academy (70) and Falmouth (71). Portland (47 points) cruised to the boys title, beating out Thornton (64) and Bonny Eagle (117). The Bulldogs had four boys in the top 10, led by Ambrose Clarke (17:12.41), who was sixth.
Scarborough senior Atticus Merriam, the winner at the Festival of Champions, had a strong finishing kick to hold off Falmouth’s Mateo Diaz (16:32.94) and win the Class A boys crown with a time of 16:21.36.
“I was trying to be a little conservative today, try to save myself for states a little bit,” Merriam said. “I ended up fighting pretty hard. Mateo and Ryan both gave me pretty good races. But I felt strong enough that I could make a move, and it worked out … I’m feeling good (for states). I’ve gotten some quality training in. My coaches have helped me out a lot. I’m just doing my workouts and feeling great.”
Ryan Bolduc (16:48.49) of Thornton was third.
Lincoln Academy’s Karen Higgins had the most dominant race of the day, winning the Class B title in 19:14.29. She was more than a minute faster than Freeport teammates Ella Oshteski (20:17.99) and Stella Kryzak (20:18.04).
“This race has been one I’ve wanted to win for a while,” Higgins said. “It was good to do it, and it was fun. (The trail) wasn’t muddy. The only issue I had (with the course) was the pebbles weren’t pebbles. They were pretty big rocks. That was a little difficult to navigate, but I just stayed on the trail.”
Freeport (50 points) repeated as B South girls champion, followed by Yarmouth (63) and Cape Elizabeth (67).
Yarmouth junior Bowen Mitchell (16:38.98) held off teammate Jackie Chalmers (16:47.06) for the individual boys title.
“There’s no better feeling than a win,” Mitchell said.
The duo led a dominant day for the Clippers, who placed four runners in the top five. Eli Chalmers (16:52.01) finished third.
“From day one of summer training, Jackie and I have been saying we’re going to go 1-2 at states,” Mitchell said. “Our team was so great (today), and I definitely think it’s a possibility.”
Yarmouth scored 23 points, finishing well in front of Freeport (78). The Falcons were led by fourth-place finisher Mungu Tussing (16:54.70). Cape Elizabeth (92) was third.
Dirigo senior William Morris, who won the Mountain Valley Conference championship last weekend, continued a strong postseason by winning the Class C boys race with a time of 16:19.81. James Vaillancourt (16:42.79) of North Yarmouth Academy was the runner-up and Winthrop freshman Sawyer Wess (16:43.66) was third.
Winthrop (44 points) repeated as team champion, with Maranacook (106) the runner-up. Carrabec (124) was third.
Reagan Mattson of Maranacook (19:52.98) won the Class C girls race and celebrated the victory with a cartwheel as she crossed the finish line. McKenzie Boyle (20:36.89) of Dirigo finished second and Kylie Van Tassel (20:46.30) of Winthrop placed third.
Maine Coast Waldorf (60 points) won the C girls crown, followed by Boothbay/Wiscasset (91) and Maranacook (101).
Temperatures were ideal for running, in the high 50s with blue skies and little cloud coverage.

title: Dozens of students forced to relocate after they say mold found in university dorm
text:
TUCSON, Ariz. (KOLD/Gray News) - A mold outbreak has recently forced dozens of students to move out of a University of Arizona dorm.
Lily Kingsbury and Ryleigh Beitler, both freshmen at the university, said they felt something was wrong shortly after moving into the Coronado Dorm.
“Everybody was like continuously sick on our floor, and when we saw these spots in the bathroom we were like, well it definitely looks like mold,” Kingsbury said.
The students ran a mold culture test and called maintenance after getting alarming results.
“Maintenance came in there and looked at everything, and then after they checked their rooms, they were checking our rooms, our neighbor’s room, like kind of just the whole hall, and it turned out there was a mold infestation,” Beitler said.
Two hours later, students said they received an email telling them to move out immediately because of repairs needing to take place in their room.
It was unclear how many students received that message, but KOLD said they spoke with at least a dozen students who were told to relocate.
Other students affected
Cate Schneider, a freshman who lives on a different floor, also moved out Friday.
“I’m just kind of like upset because I feel like the dorm and the school are like focused more on like other things than like actual health issues,” Schneider said.
Schneider added that she had been sick for months. She also said that she didn’t receive any communication from the university about her relocation and instead learned about it through word of mouth.
Schneider’s mother, Suzanne English, called the situation disappointing.
“I’m upset because when you drop your kids off at college or take them to college, the last thing you expect is to have them in an unsafe environment in the dorm where they should feel safe,” English said.
On Friday, Coronado Dorm residents said they received an additional email from the university confirming that localized areas of microbial growth were identified near a window.
The email stated there was “no indication of a systemic mold issue or other indoor environmental quality concerns.”
However, Beitler said she still has questions.
“I haven’t been able to get my hands on the documents and the reports, and I want to know who’s actually looking at it. What are you actually doing about it? Are you making sure it’s actually safe?” Beitler said.
The University of Arizona said environmental health professionals would review findings and remediation efforts to ensure rooms are safe before students move back in.
When asked if she would feel comfortable moving back in if the university said it was safe, Beitler said she was not sure.
“They’re not telling us any of what’s actually happening or what they’re doing to get rid of it, so how do I know that it’s actually going to be safe?” Beitler said.
The university said it takes these concerns seriously and was offering alternative housing for affected students.
The number of students who had to be moved due to mold growth was not immediately shared.
University of Arizona’s full statement regarding the situation is below:
On October 21, 2026, University of Arizona (UA) Housing and Residential Life (HRL) received a request from a student resident on the 7th floor of Coronado residence hall to inspect their room for mold.
UA Environmental Health & Safety (EHS) responded the same day to assess the room and identified localized areas of suspected microbial growth associated with moisture intrusion at an exterior window. During the assessment, other students reported similar instances of water intrusion and concerns of suspected mold within individual HVAC surface components. EHS personnel conducted a comprehensive assessment at each location where a concern was identified.
EHS assessments focused on identifying suspected mold, evaluating potential moisture sources, and determining appropriate corrective actions consistent with relevant guidance from the American Industrial Hygiene Association (AIHA), Institute of Inspection, Cleaning and Restoration Certification (IICRC), and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
Suspected mold observed on non-porous surfaces, such as HVAC grates, was treated immediately by UA custodial staff. EHS has engaged an outside firm specializing in mold remediation to assess and treat affected porous materials, such as drywall. It is important to note that each resident room in Coronado residence hall is equipped with an independent HVAC unit, with no shared ductwork or direct air distribution between rooms.
At this time, there is no indication of a systemic mold issue or other indoor environmental quality concern. Qualified environmental health professionals will review findings and remediation efforts to ensure corrective actions are completed appropriately and affected spaces are suitable for occupancy.
What should students do?
Students who notice water intrusion, observe suspected mold growth, or identify other indoor environmental quality concerns should submit a maintenance request to notify HRL. Maintenance requests can be submitted online at housing.arizona.edu/maintenance-request. Requests will be reviewed and appropriate follow-up will be coordinated with EHS.
If remediation requires students to temporarily relocate, alternative accommodations will be provided.
The University of Arizona takes these concerns seriously and is committed to addressing reported conditions and providing a safe environment for all students.

title: Woman sentenced after faking pregnancies, including with ‘The Bachelor’ contestant
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) — A woman convicted of tricking men into thinking she was pregnant, including “The Bachelor” contestant Clayton Echard, will spend 30 days behind bars after a plea agreement.
After a plea agreement, prosecutors laid out how they said Laura Owens manipulated the men as she was sentenced.
Echard targeted, prosecutors say
Prosecutors said Laura Owens faked pregnancies to force men into relationships and filed a lawsuit that included several allegations, including abortion coercion and domestic violence. Prosecutors also said Laura Owens stole a woman’s ultrasound and passed it off as her own.
Prosecutors said Laura Owens contacted Echard, a former contestant on “The Bachelor” and Scottsdale realtor, on May 17, 2023, about a real estate deal. The two had oral sex on May 20, prosecutors said, but no intercourse, and Laura Owens claimed she was pregnant on June 1 after obtaining HCG injections from a spa, which she claimed helped improve her skin. She filed for paternity in August 2023, prosecutors said.
“The method that she chose was HCG,” a prosecutor said, describing how she created false positive pregnancy tests.
Stolen ultrasound
Prosecutors said Laura Owens stole a twin ultrasound from Stormy Mitchell, who said she lost one to vanishing twin syndrome.
“It is the only photo I will ever have of my twins together,” Mitchell said in a statement read in court.
Prosecutors also said Laura Owens edited photos to look pregnant.
“Parts of the body are obscured and taken away so you can make yourself look pregnant,” a prosecutor said.
Victims speak
Echard told the judge, “I’ve been fighting for the last three and a half years.”
In a statement read in court, victim Greg Gillespie said Laura Owens caused him to spend years defending his reputation, livelihood and name. He is seeking nearly $300,000 in restitution, according to the statement.
Parents ask for mercy
Laura Owens’ mother, Jan Owens, said Laura lives in a casita on their property and is a vital caregiver. She said Ronn Owens, Laura Owens’ father, has several medical issues and relies on his daughter for daily care.
Jan Owens said over the past 10 years, it has been gut-wrenching to watch her daughter as the target of unspeakable emotional and physical abuse and cyber harassment.
“She has been pregnant. She has had verified medical proof of pregnancy. She has been abused. She has been suffocated and strangled by men she has been with,” Jan Owens said.
She asked for probation only for Laura Owens.
Ronn Owens, 81, a longtime Bay Area radio broadcaster, told the court, “I love my daughter more than I can put into words.”
He asked the court not to take Laura Owens away for whatever time he has left.
Laura Owens emotional over threats
Laura Owens became emotional talking about threats she said she and her family received. She said supporters of victims sent death threats, posted her family’s address online and told her to take her own life.
“We didn’t know what was gonna happen if this person was going to actually come to my family’s house and shoot my mom, and I felt so guilty about it,” Laura Owens said.
She also told the court, “I want the rest of my life, and not just my words today, to show how completely, terribly sorry I am for everybody I’ve harmed.”
The judge said in deciding the sentence he weighed “whether or not she’s this sophisticated con person or a very sad individual making some poor choices.”
“Obviously, I think it’s the latter,” the judge said.
The judge imposed 30 days of flat time plus 12 months of deferred jail starting Oct. 22, 2027. Laura Owens faces up to 12.5 years in prison if she violates probation.

title: Voters must not let Elon Musk’s money win
text:
Elon Musk’s spending of $366 million in support of 2026 Republican candidates is, for me, the straw that broke the camel’s back.
As a Maine independent voter and former business owner, I strenuously object to the richest folks in our society funding the “war chests” of those politicians who support the tax policies that encourage the growing divide between the wealthiest and the poorest.
My votes, and my political contributions, will be for those who will: vote to repeal Citizens United; promote tax policies that reduce the chasm between rich and poor; offer more opportunities for workers to share in their employer’s success; and commit to working together in a bipartisan fashion.
Jim Van Fleet
Yarmouth

UMaine celebrates opening of new GEM building

text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Ahead of homecoming weekend, the University of Maine celebrated the opening of its new GEM building.
An open house was held this afternoon as part of Learner-Center R1 Showcase Month.
The 50,000-square-foot GEM facility advances manufacturing research and education through AI-enabled 3D printing, materials science and digital manufacturing. The building houses UMaine’s Factory of the Future and supports hands-on student learning with entrepreneurs and industry partners.
Although it’s attached to the Advanced Structures and Composites Center, school officials say the building is meant for everybody.
“It’s easy to think about this space as an engineering space or a computing space, but we really want to challenge that notion because we look at manufacturing as a solution. It’s a part of a toolkit and it’s really the first of its kind on our campus and there’s not many around that intersection between industry and learning, research, all in one,” said Taylor Ward, director of outreach and engagement at the Maine College of Engineering.
The building has been in the works for years. The concept originally came about as school officials were scaling up manufacturing at the university.
Ward said the new building will also be used as a catalyst for economic development in the state.
