Maine’s outdoor heritage is one of our greatest treasures. As a sportsman, I want our elected officials to preserve the outdoors and advocate for hunters and fishermen. That’s why I support Matt Dunlap for Congress.
Matt Dunlap served as the executive director of the Sportsmen’s Alliance of Maine (SAM) and expanded membership. He also received an A+ rating from SAM. As a state representative, Matt served as House chair on the Committee on Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, where he wrote the bill for lifetime hunting licenses and fought for an expanded season for bow hunting.
On the other hand, Paul LePage has held back crucial conservation bonds and refused to protect our lands from being bought up by developers. LePage also pulled out of SAM’s questionnaire process in 2022 and refused to release his answers to the public.
I believe Matt will be an independent voice in Congress that will not be beholden to any party and will stand for Maine.
On Nov. 3, I think sportsmen should vote for Matt Dunlap.
Roger Corrow
Bangor

title: Portland’s city government must work for all of us
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kate Snyder is a former mayor of Portland and a candidate for City Council at-large.
We know today’s issues: housing, affordability, safe streets. What we don’t know is what’s around the corner. The question isn’t just where candidates stand today. It’s whether they have the qualifications, experience and temperament to make sound decisions under pressure when something unforeseen lands on the council’s agenda.
I served on the Portland School Board from 2007 to 2013. After the 2008 financial crisis, the state curtailed school funding midway through a school year, and we met the moment, reopening contracts and delivering flat and reduced budgets, always focused on students and teachers. That took our board, staff and unions working together.
I was three months into my four-year term as Portland’s mayor when COVID arrived. Together with city staff, we did something no one at City Hall could remember doing: we declared a state of emergency to keep us all safe. Then, four months later, voters created a Charter Commission to rethink how city government works. So we steered Portland through a global pandemic while the rules were under review. None of us had run for office with a plan for any of that.
We rebuilt the city’s leadership. All three positions the council hires and oversees came open during my term as mayor. I led every search, and every vote to hire was unanimous. We restored city functions that had been allowed to lapse: annual city manager reviews and regular tax revaluations to keep taxes fair.
When more than 1,200 people a night, many of them asylum seekers, filled our shelters, the city manager and I traveled often to Augusta to brief our delegation. The council added beds to the city shelter and rejected a proposal to suspend Portland’s camping ban, keeping the city focused on providing emergency shelter and other services to those in need.
There’s much we can do about housing, affordability and safe streets. Since our 25% inclusionary zoning requirement took effect, fewer than 1 in 10 approved housing units has been built, as interest rates and construction costs climbed. We should revisit that requirement so approved homes get built. We should also invest in sidewalks, crosswalks and bike lanes, so getting around is safe for everyone. We need city leaders who work to address resident concerns and priorities in the annual budget.
Respect for differences is how durable policy gets made. But when factions dominate issues by claiming the only answer, we lose a cornerstone of our democracy. Debate and disagreement about ideas ought to be productive, not combative and riddled with gotchas. Renters and homeowners aren’t opponents, and builders aren’t villains. We can only get better together. A city of allies and enemies isn’t a community.
This is city government, and ahead of serving any ideology, party agenda or national group, a councilor’s allegiance should be to Portland and its residents. I’ll hear every side, weigh the facts and keep an open mind before I decide, and treat everyone who reaches out with respect.
For me, this isn’t politics. It’s 32 years of life here: renting, then owning a home, raising our kids, working, volunteering and being a neighbor. Since leaving office, I’ve served as a trustee of the University of New England, joined the working committee for First Light Commons, our new waterfront park, and helped raise funds for the Rising Eddy Community Pool.
My years in office made me stronger, steadier and more experienced in collaborative, responsive leadership. I’m ready to do this job now and over the next three years, and I am optimistic about Portland’s future.
I am loyal to Portland and its people. Above all, I believe in doing the work to make our city a safe, affordable, great place to live. I ask for your first-place vote for City Council at-large on Nov. 3.

Support group helps Lewiston community process trauma of mass shooting, three years later
"Can We Talk?" started its first Maine chapter to help the Lewiston-Auburn community process the weight of the state's deadliest mass shooting.
Support group helps Lewiston community process trauma of mass shooting, three years later
"Can We Talk?" started its first Maine chapter to help the Lewiston-Auburn community process the weight of the state's deadliest mass shooting.
It has been nearly three years since the deadliest mass shooting in Maine's history, which left 18 people dead across the city of Lewiston.
"It still feels surreal. How could anyone decide that other people need to be just slaughtered?" said Karen Choate, a Lewiston resident of 40 years.
As the community continues to heal, support groups have been a helpful part in allowing people to talk through trauma and what is on their minds. "Can We Talk" is a national group that planted its first roots in Maine at High Street Congregational Church in Auburn this past March.
"Though I am a pastor, we are not churching people; we are welcoming people of all faith, no faith, little faith and big faith," said the Rev. Debbie Duval, who leads the church.
Duval said the group does not focus exclusively on the mass shooting, and people can show up to share whatever they are dealing with in a safe space.
Each session, which typically happens on the first Tuesday of each month, starts with a home-cooked meal and then transitions to the sanctuary where there is music, discussion and reflection. Duval said it is all about support and being present with one another.

title: Cliff diver Molly Carson makes history, becomes first woman to dive off iceberg
text:
Cliff diver Molly Carson makes history, becomes first woman to dive off iceberg
'Definitely the scariest thing I’ve ever done,' Carlson said
Cliff diver Molly Carson makes history, becomes first woman to dive off iceberg
'Definitely the scariest thing I’ve ever done,' Carlson said
Red Bull just broke another record.
Cliff diver Molly Carlson became the first woman to dive off a free-standing iceberg.
Related video above: Most enduring and biggest iceberg breaks apart, with more splintering to come in its death spiral
Carlson completed a backwards dive off of a massive, moving chunk of ice off the coast of Twillingate, Newfoundland, Canada, nearly 50 feet above the water. The record event was sponsored by Red Bull and made into a short documentary.
"This is definitely the scariest thing I’ve ever done," Carlson said.
Carlson is an experienced high diver, making the podium at several Red Bull diving events in recent years. The iceberg dive at Twillingate was Carlson's highest backwards dive to date.
One big difference between a regular high dive and Carlson's iceberg dive is that the ice was free-standing, meaning it was not rooted to a landmass.
"Icebergs are incredibly dangerous," Carlson said. "They can split, collapse or roll without warning."
Before she could make the dive, Carlson had to make the climb — meaning she had to learn how to ice climb before even considering diving. She trained, and climbed, with Will Gad, another Red Bull athlete and veteran ice climber.
She also reached out to the first person to jump off an iceberg, fellow Red Bull athlete and cliff diver Orlando Duque. Duque took a dive off an iceberg in Antarctica in 2018.
"I remember messaging him back in 2023, like, 'Was this fun? Should I try to bring this to Canada and be the first woman to dive off an iceberg?'" Carlson recalled. "And he was like, 'Molly, if there's one project that changed my life, it was diving off an iceberg.'"
In addition to having the bravery to jump off an iceberg in the freezing cold, Carlson has also struggled with her mental health and eating disorders. She told CNN in 2023 that she refers to the lowest point in her career as her "mental injury."
"Bravery, though, is not about getting rid of fear, but about not letting it decide what you're capable of," Carlson said.

title: At Maine Maritime, the football program’s rebuild continues
text:
CASTINE — Maine Maritime Academy has already given Matt Gagin so much.
“I’ve always really wanted to sail. I’ve crossed the Atlantic five or six times now. I’ve been all over the world,” said Gagin, a junior from Upton, Massachusetts. “I’ve gotten to see things I never would’ve seen without this school.”
There’s one thing Gagin would love to give back to MMA before he graduates: a win in a football game. The Mariners came so close to that goal Saturday at Ritchie Field, falling 17-14 to New England College. It was MMA’s closest game since the school announced the program was coming out of mothballs in 2023.
Close isn’t a win, though, and now the Mariners’ losing streak stands at 43 games.
MMA’s last win came on Oct. 14, 2017, just over nine years ago, when the Mariners prevailed 34-16 against Coast Guard. On its face, the victory drought is misleading. The Mariners did not play from 2020 through 2022, then played one game in 2023 and three in 2024 before resuming a full varsity schedule last season.
Maine Maritime paused the football program in 2020, citing the budget concerns that came with the COVID-19 pandemic. A few years later, alumni spearheaded a fundraising effort that brought in more than $560,000, and football was reinstated.
The Mariners are past the point of moral victories. New England College is like them, a new program just starting out. The Mariners saw the contest Saturday as a winnable game, and left the field with the frustration of a team that let one slip away. Heads down. Shoulders slumped.
An interception inside the Pilgrims 5-yard line squashed one scoring opportunity. A blocked field goal at the end of the first half evaporated another.
The Mariners know they’re improving, and sooner or later that improvement won’t be measured in a good play, or a good drive. It will be quantified with a win.
“They see (the improvement), and know,” said MMA coach Nick Sheehan. “You can see from our reaction, it’s a tough one.”
Sheehan’s sales pitch to recruits is simple. Come build something at one of the finest engineering schools around. Come to a school where graduates routinely step into six-figure jobs right after earning their diploma, and help rebuild a once-proud and thriving football program. Play right away.
That all sounded great to Gagin. Newcastle native Lucas Houghton thought it sounded good, too. He went to Lincoln Academy, a school without a football team, but he remembered the joy he had playing peewee football, and thought rebuilding something sounded fun.
“It was the best sport, because as long as you gave your best effort, you could feel like you accomplished something,” said Houghton, a junior defensive back who led the Mariners with 12 tackles Saturday. “I’ve played all kinds of sports. Soccer, baseball, basketball, whatever. There’s nothing that compares to football.”
Bill Mottola knows what MMA football can be, because he knows what it was.
MMA’s athletic director, Mottola grew up around the team. His father, also Bill Mottola, was MMA’s head coach from 1968 to 1978 and was AD for 25 years after that. Bill the younger grew up on the sidelines of Mariners games, going to team dinners, working as a ball boy, and seeing the way his father built relationships with his players.
It led Mottola into the football coaching, and he spent time at Division I schools Kent State, Miami (Ohio) and Army. The athletic director at MMA since 2024, Mottola views the football program’s pursuit of a victory as a personal quest.
“It will be sooner rather than later. We’re making progress,” Mottola said. “I’ve seen football players. I know what they’re supposed to look like, and I know what the game is supposed to look like.”
What he sees on the field now is a team making strides, Mottola said. Anonymous trolls on social media who see the lopsided scores of many games and mock the team, who look at the losing streak without context, don’t see below the surface. They don’t see what’s being built, he said.
The players see that a bond has formed, and it’s tight.
“No team in the country has been through what we’ve been through the last three years. I just want to keep fighting for these guys,” said Gagin, a linebacker who made 10 tackles on Saturday.
One play at time, one game at a time, Sheehan said. You create the bigger picture by focusing on the little ones.
“In 10 years, when I look back and the program is winning games and being successful, hopefully I’ll be proud of everything we accomplished,” Houghton said.
The Mariners’ next chance for a win comes next Saturday, at home against Endicott.

title: Referred to new Maine surgeons, she was shocked when they wouldn’t accept her traditional Medicare
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Martha Buisman of Gorham considers herself lucky to have had quality health insurance during her adult life. She had a “gold standard” health insurance plan when she worked for the United States Postal Service for 29 years.
Now retired, the 71-year-old has traditional Medicare with a supplemental federal plan from Blue Cross Blue Shield — coverage she considers top notch.
So she was shocked when she learned surgeons at InterMed, which has practices in Portland, South Portland and Yarmouth, would not take her traditional Medicare plan when her doctor referred her to the medical group for a gynecological surgery in April.
InterMed, which employs more than 200 physicians and other providers in primary care and specialties, told her it accepts Medicare Advantage plans as well as traditional Medicare plans from existing patients, but it does not accept traditional Medicare from new patients or those being referred for care.
After paying into Medicare for decades, Buisman said she was flabbergasted as to why any medical provider wouldn’t accept the federal insurance for Americans 65 and older — or be allowed to not accept it.
“It’s inexplicable to me because everybody in the country is forced to pay into Medicare their whole lives,” Buisman said. “You’ve got thousands and thousands and thousands of dollars in this nationwide system. Now any old provider can just say, ‘Screw you, we’re not taking Medicare.’ I mean, if everybody did that, then we’d have no health care system at all.”
Medicare covers about 20% of the United States population but 27% of Maine’s population — and more people are signing on each year as they age. Many choose traditional Medicare. But a growing number in Maine are picking a Medicare Advantage plan, which must be approved by Medicare but is offered by private insurance companies. Medicare Advantage plans often bundle all the coverage into one plan rather than break it up into Medicare Part A for hospital coverage, Part B for medical coverage and Part D for prescription coverage.
The vast majority of medical providers across the country — an estimated 99% of non-pediatric physicians — still accept Medicare, according to KFF, a health policy research institute. But some doctors and policymakers have raised concerns in recent years that providers will opt out of Medicare due to reductions in Medicare payments for many Part B services, potentially creating a shortage of doctors willing to treat people with Medicare, according to KFF.
It’s not clear which providers in Maine have opted out of Medicare, but, as of 2024, 1.5% of Maine physicians had done so, according to KFF.
InterMed confirmed that it currently accepts new patients enrolled in certain Medicare Advantage plans but does not accept new patients with traditional Medicare, including outside referrals. Patients who are already established with InterMed can continue receiving care when they transition to traditional Medicare, however, allowing them to continue receiving care from doctors they already know. Its policy has been in place for at least five years.
“We recognize how important it is for patients to have access to the care they need. Like many medical practices, InterMed must balance growing demand for services with the resources available to provide high-quality, reliable care to our patients. We regularly evaluate our policies as patient needs and healthcare conditions evolve,” Roger Poitras, CEO of InterMed, said in a statement.
It is rare for general physicians and surgeons, such as those with InterMed, to opt out of Medicare. Nationwide, psychiatrists opt out at the highest rate, 8.1%, according to KFF. Next highest are plastic and reconstructive surgeons, with 4.5% opting out, and neurologists, with 3.2% opting out.
Casey Schwarz, senior counsel for education and federal policy at the Medicare Rights Center, said there’s no mechanism in the United States to compel providers to accept all Medicare patients that come to them. In this case, InterMed is still accepting some Medicare patients.
“If we had a situation where a provider was required to accept any Medicare patient who wanted to be seen by them, they couldn’t manage their patient population,” Schwarz said.
For Buisman, the idea that providers won’t accept certain Medicare patients reflects a two-tiered system. She and her husband each pay $203 a month out of their Social Security checks for Medicare, plus an additional $304 a month for their supplemental plan. That’s $6,084 a year each.
“If it gets to a point where so many providers are allowed, apparently, to just withdraw from the Medicare system, and then all the rich people can just pay for their concierge doctors, and then screw the rest of us. The whole trend is very disturbing,” she said.
In the end, Buisman went back to her doctor and got a referral for a different surgeon. She had hoped to have a female surgeon because it was a gynecological surgery, which is how she ended up at InterMed. But now she is working with a male surgeon who takes her insurance, and she is happy with him, she said.
“It all worked out, but it just sticks in my craw that the whole thing happened at all,” she said.
Open enrollment for Medicare plans began Oct. 15 and runs through Dec. 7.
Have you encountered a Maine doctor who doesn’t take Medicare? Please write to reporter Rose Lundy at rose@themainemonitor.org. We will not use your information without your permission.
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: Ex-soldier sentenced to 59 years in prison for killing wife, stuffing body in storm drain
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - An Alaskan man was sentenced this week, three years after authorities say he murdered his wife and attempted to conceal it.
On Friday, former U.S. Army Spec. Zarrius Hildabrand, 24, was given a 59-year prison sentence for fatally shooting his wife, 21-year-old Alaska National Guard Spec. Saria Hildabrand, on Aug. 6, 2023.
Both were actively serving at the time of the murder.
Hildabrand was convicted on second-degree murder and tampering with physical evidence charges in June, although he was also acquitted of a first-degree murder charge.
The prosecution said during the nearly two-week trial that after a night out celebrating his 21st birthday, Hildabrand shot his wife after she discovered him cheating.
The defense pushed back against the state’s argument and claimed that Saria Hildabrand died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Following Saria Hildabrand’s death, authorities said Zarrius Hildabrand reported her missing and moved her body to a storm drain near the couple’s apartment.
The former soldier then assisted in search efforts until her body was later discovered.

title: Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday, saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally.
Trump and first lady Melania Trump arrived at their West Palm Beach polling location at the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections office together after the president spent the morning at his nearby golf course. Trump has been criticized in the past for voting by mail despite his long history of railing against that method of submitting ballots.
Asked if he voted the party line, Trump, who was wearing an “I Voted” sticker, said, “Very much so.”
Speaking to reporters at the poll site, Trump again defended an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. The ad has faced intense blowback for featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton, who lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.
Trump also defended his decision to instruct his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
As for the war in Iran, he said, “I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they’ll make a deal, but I’m not sure. Either way, we win.”
Melania Trump, who this week brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid could be delivered and civilians evacuated, was asked whether she might travel to Ukraine.
“We will see,” she told reporters.
In Florida, Trump has endorsed Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who is running against David Jolly, a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat, to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.
He has also campaigned for Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, who is running to fill the last two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s former Senate term against progressive state lawmaker Angie Nixon.
___
Colvin reported from New York.

title: Obama assails 'cruelty' and indecency from Republicans in midterm campaign
text:
Obama assails 'cruelty' and indecency from Trump and his allies in the midterm campaign
Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation's ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in battleground Ohio.
Video above: Former President Barack Obama endorses Josh Shapiro for Pa. governor
Obama took specific aim at Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.
"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she's experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness."
"There's a decency we should expect out of our public officials," Obama continued. "And I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior are so low that somebody could run an ad like that."
Obama, 65, who remains the Democratic Party's best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House, was set to campaign in Michigan later Saturday night. The midwestern battlegrounds will help determine the balance of power in American politics on Nov. 3, when the final votes are cast in the 2026 midterm elections.
Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted.
Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it's been a hotly contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy's ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.
Video below: Barack Obama at presidential center: 'Democracy is precious'
Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game. Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.
"My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it's not going to work," she said. " Decency still matters." She added: "Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won't stoop."
After wrapping up in Ohio, Obama was heading to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who is working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.
Obama's appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster support for El-Sayed among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.
El-Sayed criticized Obama after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama "was not the right choice — he just wasn't the wrong one."
El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month he appreciated the former president, calling him "foundational" to his ability to run for office, but there were still elements of Obama's presidency he disagreed with.
Video below: Presidential museum showcases political and personal sides of Obama
Michigan also has open races for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, is slated to appear along with others down the ballot. Benson is running against Republican Rep. John James.
Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.
In Ohio, Obama also called out Trump's inability to lower costs, a key campaign promise, noting that the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.
"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," he quipped. "He should be on HGTV." He went on: "There's gold everywhere. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."
The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump's allies, he said.
"We're not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said. "After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence … you get a chance to say enough is enough."
Peoples reported from New York. GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Pine Tree Camp hosts fifth annual “Flutie 5K for Autism”
text:
ROME, Maine (WABI) - It may have been a chilly start to the day — but that didn’t stop runners from getting out to support a good cause.
Participants of all ages and abilities gathered this morning at Pine Tree Camp to run the fifth annual Flutie 5K for Autism.
The Doug Flutie Jr. Foundation for Autism hosts several programs alongside its nationwide 5Ks, all in support of helping those with autism live their lives to the fullest.
All proceeds from the race go to the camp and support them in their mission to help Maine children and adults with disabilities, including autism, experience barrier-free recreation and belonging.
The race was extra special for some local runners.
Three generations of grandfather, mother and son all ran the 5K together — and they say being able to run together is what keeps them close to their family and to their community at large.
“It brings the community together and it’s nice to be running with your neighbors and your family and it’s just fun. It’s a beautiful day too,” said Paige Brown, who ran the 5k alongside her son Adrian and Father Eric.
82-year-old Eric Brown’s secret for other older runners? “Don’t stop.”
To learn more about the Pine Tree Camp and their work with the Doug Flutie Jr. Foundation for Autism, visit this link .

title: Cornhole tournament held at Just-In-Time Recreation in honor of Lewiston mass shooting victims
text:
Cornhole tournament held at Just-In-Time Recreation in honor of Lewiston mass shooting victims
Sunday marks three years since 18 people were killed and 13 others were injured in a mass shooting in Lewiston.
An annual cornhole tournament was held on Saturday in honor of the victims at Just-In-Time Recreation, one of the sites where the shooting occurred.
"You want to move forward, right? But you also don't want to forget either," said Tyler Babb.
Babb owns and operates TB Events, which put on Saturday's tournament along with the first two that were held in the wake of the shooting.
Babb mentioned that the first year focused on the resiliency of the area and the second year was centered around "Lewiston Strong." This year, Babb stated, was all about "Lewiston StrongER."
"Everyone's here to just play," Babb said. "Remember, the people that can't play today."
Two of the players were Keith Tremblay and Ryan Dalessandro, both survivors of the shooting.
"Just the day after it happened, like I told myself I wasn't going to let him, he already took so much for us," Dalessandro said. "Like, he wasn't going to take this from us too, right?"
While the day carried heavy emotion, many of the survivors, family of victims and more present wanted the event to be centered around the community smiling together.
"Grief isn't just one thing and the way you deal with grief, it's not one specific way every time," Tremblay said. "Just to deal with grief doesn't mean you have to have a somber day. You can deal with grief and still have a good time remembering those that you lost, those that you love, those that are still with us."
The Maine Resiliency Center was a beneficiary of the tournament.
It's an organization that was created just weeks after Oct. 25, 2023, with a vast amount of support and services for those who were impacted by the shooting.
"Just watching them care about each other," said Maine Resiliency Center Associate Director Meredith Stack. "Not just this week or today, but in every day of their lives. And leaning on each other for support is, I don't know, there just aren't words for something like that."
On Saturday morning, Gov. Janet Mills directed flags around the state to be lowered on Sunday in respect for the anniversary of the shooting and to honor the survivors and the victims from Oct. 25.

title: Here’s why shoppers may be buying less candy for Halloween this year
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start this year as U.S. consumers grapple with high living costs and eye-popping chocolate prices.
Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm. Nielsen also noted an 11.7% decline in candy sales in mid-September, erasing the preseason gains that Halloween candy enjoyed the previous two years.
Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said high gas prices have worsened Americans’ concerns about affordability, and that’s dampening demand for Halloween treats. As of Friday, the average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. was $4.29, up nearly 40% from the prior year.
“I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food,” Costagli said. “Some of the decisions they’re making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, ‘I notice it’s more expensive than last year,’ it’s, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I’ve paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’”
Small bags of candy were the only sizes seeing sales growth through mid-October, Costagli noted. Large and extra-large bags were seeing the biggest declines.
U.S. candy prices have been climbing faster than the rate of inflation for several years. As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44% over a five-year period, according to government data. Prices for all food eaten at home rose 22.5% in the same period.
This week, discount grocer Aldi was advertising a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolate bars – including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers – for $19.87. That’s almost the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece variety pack five years ago.
Cocoa prices are the main culprit. Global cocoa prices reached a record high of $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 because of poor weather in West Africa – which supplies 70% of the world’s chocolate -- and speculative trading in the cocoa futures market, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Cocoa prices had been falling steadily since then, and hit $3,241 per metric ton in March. But they began climbing again in the spring as the Iran war disrupted Africa’s fertilizer supplies. The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to hurt production, with hot, dry conditions expected through February.
But Costagli noted that even in cases where prices are lower than last year, consumer demand is muted. The average price of non-chocolate Halloween candies, like gummies and lollipops, was $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, which was about 3% lower than last year, according to Nielsen data. But that didn’t lead to a bump in sales.
Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser for the market research company Circana, said one way U.S. consumers have been handling higher grocery prices is by making smaller and more frequent trips to the supermarket and buying products right before they intend to use them. That makes her wonder if shoppers are waiting until closer to Halloween to buy candy this year.
“People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general,” she said. “I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed.”
The National Confectioners Association, a trade group that represents candy makers like Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic about Halloween sales.
“We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong,” the group said Friday in a statement.

title: Jacob Misiorowski makes history in 2026 World Series
text:
Jacob Misiorowski makes history on the first pitch of the 2026 World Series
Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Jacob Misiorowski made history during the first pitch of the 2026 World Series.
He pitched at a speed of 103.5 mph, according to MLB.
Video above: The crowd before Game 1 of the World Series in Milwaukee
That's the fastest recorded World Series pitch in the pitch-tracking era, which started in 2008.
Misiorowski became just the second pitcher in Brewers history to start Game 1 of a World Series, joining Mike Caldwell in 1982.
"It's just another game," Misiorowski said Thursday. "It's honestly an honor to be in that situation and be able to go out and try and propel the team to a win."
Video below: Little League slugger meets Jacob Misiorowski
Misiorowski threw 78 pitches over five innings in Game 1 of the World Series. He gave up one run on three hits, struck out three and did not surrender a walk in the opening game against the Tampa Bay Rays.
A sold-out Milwaukee crowd created a festive atmosphere at American Family Field for the Brewers' first World Series game in 44 years.

title: Voters must not let Elon Musk’s money win
text:
Elon Musk’s spending of $366 million in support of 2026 Republican candidates is, for me, the straw that broke the camel’s back.
As a Maine independent voter and former business owner, I strenuously object to the richest folks in our society funding the “war chests” of those politicians who support the tax policies that encourage the growing divide between the wealthiest and the poorest.
My votes, and my political contributions, will be for those who will: vote to repeal Citizens United; promote tax policies that reduce the chasm between rich and poor; offer more opportunities for workers to share in their employer’s success; and commit to working together in a bipartisan fashion.
Jim Van Fleet
Yarmouth

title: Police say 110,000 people march in Paris as protest ends with tear gas and water cannon
text:
PARIS (AP) — Clashes erupted in Paris as a mass march drew to a close Saturday, with more than 400,000 people rallying across France over school funding and soaring living costs in a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron. Police made nearly 1,000 arrests, the government said.
The Paris march began peacefully, a week after widespread rioting and looting during protests across the country. But near the demonstration’s endpoint in eastern Paris, masked protesters hurled objects and fireworks at police, who answered with clouds of tear gas, deafening sound grenades and jets of water cannons.
Officers with megaphones urged protesters to disperse. Some demonstrators panicked as tear-gas canisters landed in their midst, scattering with screams. Veteran protesters shouted after them: “Don’t run!”
The Interior Ministry put nationwide turnout at 410,000 — fewer than the 550,000 it said protested last weekend — while the CGT union that helped organize some of Saturday’s protests estimated nearly 800,000. The ministry’s estimate included 110,000 in Paris, where authorities confined the march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the center. The CGT put the number of protesters in Paris at 250,000.
Unrest is challenging Macron’s final months in power
More than a month of unrest that started with protests in high schools for more funding and teachers is testing Macron’s authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May.
The stakes are high: The far-right National Rally party has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for its candidate Marine Le Pen. On the far left, presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has backed demonstrators and criticized policing that has left some teenage protesters with life-changing injuries.
As dusk fell Saturday, violence erupted at the end of some of the 289 protests counted by the Interior Ministry nationwide. Street fires burned in the cities of Marseille and Lyon. Police used tear gas in Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Strasbourg and Bordeaux and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Nice, far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown and 11 people were arrested, regional authorities said.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police made nearly 1,000 arrests but added that the number is expected to increase significantly as more are counted.
Nuñez said beefed-up policing, with 70,000 officers backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and other support, helped prevent a repeat of widespread looting and damage to shops the previous weekend.
A small protest became a national movement
What began last month as a protest over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris spread nationwide, drawing students demanding more funding for education and workers seeking help with soaring costs for fuel and other necessities.
In Paris, Bénédicte Pittion, a 46-year-old teacher, marched with her 16-year-old daughter, Garance, a high school student — in their first protest together.
“The young people who have been demonstrating have not been heard, and as a parent and as a teacher, I stand with them,” Pittion said.
Garance said she’d been “really scared” after seeing the previous weekend’s violence, but felt that staying away would hand the government a victory.
Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.
Some protests were banned
Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, complained that authorities in Paris wanted to stifle protesters by making them march on the capital’s outskirts, keeping them away from the center where the Louvre and other major museums closed exceptionally.
“But it won’t stop the movement. It won’t stop students from demanding better conditions in schools,” she said.
Other protesters expressed anger about record poverty and wealth inequality under Macron. Camille Chesnier, 27, said she hasn’t found work despite having an engineering degree and a master’s degree.
“There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren’t privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it’s very tough,” she said.."
In Marseille, police put attendance at 17,000, while the CGT union estimated 100,000. In the southwestern city of Toulouse, 26,500 people joined the protests, according to authorities. Authorities had banned rallies in cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier.
Trade unions criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
Thousands also marched Saturday in Orléans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Le Pen’s National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.
Shops board up and museums close
Gendarmes stood guard Saturday beneath the Arc de Triomphe and shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician’s shop.
“I got the call last night,” he said. “The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life.”
Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
Students and workers are angry
Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system.
Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros ($224) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.
Energy prices in France were 21.3% higher in September than a year earlier, helping drive overall inflation to 3.1%, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE.
Paris protester Louis Ledoux--Xatard voiced frustration over inequality.
“Looking at countries like the United States, we don’t want to end up like them, where part of the population has everything and the others have nothing,” he said.
“I never imagined that I’d be taking to the streets so much before my thirties.”
___
Associated Press writers Samuel Petrequin and Sylvie Corbet in Paris contributed.

title: Survivors of Lewiston mass shooting mark anniversary, honor victims with cornhole tournament
text:
LEWISTON — Jason Barnett tossed a beanbag in the air. It hit the cornhole board opposite him with a thud. He threw another that flew into the hole, earning the familiar nod of his teammate, John Petrocelli.
Barnett and Petrocelli were cornhole partners Saturday, like they were nearly three years ago at Schemengees Bar & Grille in Lewiston when they survived the mass shooting that killed 18 people and injured 13. They played this weekend at Just-in-Time Recreation, the bowling alley the shooter attacked on Oct. 25, 2023, before he headed to Schmengees.
Just-in-Time closed after the tragedy but reopened six months later, while Schmengees permanently shuttered. This was the third year TB Events held a cornhole tournament around the anniversary of the attack to raise funds for Maine Resiliency Center — an organization dedicated to helping people navigate the impacts of the shooting — and to unite survivors, families of victims and others who were affected.
“It gets us all back together, it keeps that alive, and it heals us at the same time,” Barnett said.
In April, Just-In-Time owners Justin and Samantha Juray began ripping out six bowling lanes to create a carpeted space for cornhole. The change combines the two activities many of the survivors of the shooting love, but found too painful to participate in, in the months and years after the attack. Survivors of the shooting wore shirts that said “Survivor” on the back and “Lewiston Strong” on the front.
“To see people get over that fear and walk through those doors for the first time again is pretty awesome,” said Justin Juray, who survived the attack while running the bowling alley.
Danielle Jasper said she and a group of other survivors who endured watching other cornhole players die in the shooting regularly get together to play weekly, not just on the anniversary.
“People that I didn’t know before that night are like family now,” Jasper said.
Tyler Babb, owner of TB Events, said turnout at the event exceeded his expectations — he had laid out eight games, but added two more to accommodate the nearly 170 people who signed up across the afternoon and evening tournaments. Entry was $20 per team, which the Maine Resiliency Fund uses to help connect people affected by the shooting with counseling and other resources.
It was not only survivors and the immediate family members of victims who came to play — some drove multiple hours because they enjoy cornhole and wanted to support the fund.
Kathy Bartley, of Houlton, organizes a weekly cornhole league at home and tries to travel to other Maine towns to play, too — she has a friend who was injured in the shooting at Just-in-Time. And Trina Cayford, a professional cornhole player from Bangor who competes nationally with her husband, Phil Cayford, said she came just to connect with people and support the cause.
“Everyone grieves in their own kind of way,” Babb said. “For a lot of people, they’re die-hard cornhole players and community members. And I think that means more to them than anything else ever would.”
The Maine Resiliency Center will hold a candlelight vigil at Simard-Payne Memorial Park,46 Beech St., from 6-8 p.m. It will begin at the entrance of the park, with attendees walking together to the Longley Bridge for the vigil.

title: 8 places to hike in Maine where there's no hunting
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
This story was originally published in October 2017.
As deer hunting season gets into full swing in Maine, many people — hunters and non-hunters alike — are looking for places to hike and bike that are off limits to hunting, simply to avoid even the possibility of a mistake or conflict.
Hunters and non-hunters generally are successful at safely sharing the use of properties around the state. The vast majority of hunters in Maine are responsible people who take great care to hunt away from public trails, roadways and dwellings. However, as a hiker, sometimes it’s more comfortable to hike in areas reserved just for this passive recreation activity.
Don’t get me wrong, as a woman who has grown up eating deer meat that my father harvests each fall, I respect the state’s hunting traditions and have directly benefited from these traditions in the kitchen. But I do understand why some folks might prefer to hike in a hunting-free zone.
So I did some digging and realized that there are many public trail networks that are off limits to hunting. Below I’ve listed a few for you, but it’s far from a complete list. There are many additional Maine trails where hunting is prohibited, and that information can often be found online or by calling the organization — such as a land trust — that manages the trail.
That being said, even though the following list of places is off limits to hunting, it’s still important to wear plenty of blaze orange this time of year when spending time outdoors. A small percentage of the population don’t follow the rules, or they don’t make it their business to know them in the first place. Why not be as safe as possible?
Wear orange. Be visible.
While most of the trails owned and maintained by the Coastal Mountains Land Trust are open to hunting, the land trust’s 328-acre Fernald’s Neck Preserve is not. Occupying much of a peninsula that juts out into Megunticook Lake, the preserve is home to an old evergreen forest, nearly 4 miles of shoreline, The Great Bog and about 3.5 miles of intersecting walking trails. Dogs are not permitted.
Donated to the State of Maine in 1971 by a local resident named Anita Harris, the park covers 1,230 acres and features about 7.5 miles of marked hiking trails that visit a variety of habitats, including old fields, a pond, an estuary and saltwater marsh, the mossy evergreen forest covering Backwoods Mountain, a beaver flowage, and rocky beaches on the Penobscot Bay. The park also features a number of old family cemeteries, old foundations and impressive stone walls that remain from people who used to live and farm on the land. Dog are permitted on leash.
Holbrook Island Sanctuary State Park is one of Maine’s 48 State Parks and Historic Sites. Some of these sites are open to hunting, some are not. According to the state website, hunting is not permitted at any time at State Historic Sites of Memorials, or at any of the following state-owned properties: Andrews Beach State Park; the portion of Bradbury Mountain State Park west of State Route 9; Cobscook Bay State Park; Crescent Beach and Kettle Cove State Parks; Damariscotta Lake State Park; Ferry Beach State Park; Holbrook Island Sanctuary State Park; Mackworth Island; Nickerson Lake State Park; Owls Head Light State Park; the portion of Quoddy Head State Park within 1,000 feet of the lighthouse; Reid State Park; Sebago Lake State Park; Shackford Head State Park; Two Lights State Park; and Wolfe’s Neck Woods State Park.
A narrow strip of forestland on Hancock Point, the preserve was conserved by the Frenchman Bay Conservancy for public recreation. A 0.5-mile walking path, marked with blue painted blazes, winds through the 18-acre property, spanning from a cobble beach to Hancock Point Road. The preserve is named after a salt pond that is located at one end of the trail, separated from the ocean by a cobble beach littered with rocks, seashells, driftwood and seaweed.
While most of Frenchman Bay Conservancy properties are open to hunting, this small preserve is not. Hunting is also prohibited at FBC’s Simon Trail in Lamoine. Dogs are permitted at both preserves if on leash.
Also known as the Bangor City Forest, this 680-acre forest is owned by the city of Bangor and features more than four miles of access roads and more than nine miles of trails for running, hiking, biking, snowshoeing and cross country skiing.
Hunting is prohibited throughout the entire forest, and it’s also prohibited in the adjacent Walden-Parke Preserve, owned by the Bangor Land Trust. Walden-Parke Preserve is about 300 acres in size and features more than 3 miles of trails. Dogs are permitted on leash.
Fields Pond Audubon Center is a 212-acre wildlife sanctuary with about 5 miles of intersecting trails that wind through fields, wetlands and forestland, and along the shore of the 85-acre Fields Pond. The property also features the L. Robert Rolde Nature Center, which is a small museum and gift shop open 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Thursday through Saturday. Hunting is not permitted, and dogs are not permitted.
Hunting is not permitted anywhere within Maine’s sole national park on Mount Desert Island, opening up a lot of great hiking options for people who prefer to hike outside of hunting territory.
Easy hikes in Acadia include (but aren’t limited to) Jordan Pond Path, Wonderland Trail, Ship Harbor Trail and the park’s many carriage roads. And challenging trails include the many trails up Cadillac Mountain, Dorr Mountain, Pemetic Mountain, Penobscot Mountain, including Jordan Cliffs Trail, and Champlain Mountain, including the famous Precipice Trail. Moderately challenging hikes include trails exploring The Bubbles, Beech Mountain, Flying Mountain, Beehive, Great Head and Acadia Mountain.
Dogs are permitted on most trails in Acadia if kept on leash no longer than 6 feet at all times. There are a few trails that include steep slopes, rungs and ladders in the park that are off limits to dogs.
Currently in the national monument, hunting is not permitted on lands west of the East Branch of the Penobscot River, and this is where some hiking and biking opportunities are located, including the hike up Barnard Mountain (to a stunning view of Katahdin), the hike or bike ride into the scenic Orin Falls, and the hike or bike ride into Haskell Pitch and Grand Pitch.
Hunting is prohibited in most of Baxter State Park. However, certain types of hunting are permitted a northern section of the park — specifically north of Trout Brook and Wadleigh Brook in T6 R9; in T6 R10; and in T2 R9 and in T2 R10 north of the West Branch of the Penobscot River, east to the thread of Abol Stream and west to the thread of the West Branch of the Penobscot River.
Most trails in the park are on the property that is off limits to hunting, including the trails the climb Katahdin, The Brothers, South Turner Mountain, The Travelers, Trout Brook Mountain, Horse Mountain, The Owl, Mount Coe, Mount OJI and the trails that circle the park’s many pristine ponds, including Daicey Pond and Kidney Pond. Dogs are not permitted anywhere in the park.

title: Brewers win Game 1 of World Series
text:
Brewers withstand Rays' comeback attempt to win Game 1 of World Series
Trevor Megill struck out Jonny DeLuca with runners on second and third to wiggle out of a ninth-inning jam as the Milwaukee Brewers escaped with a 3-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.
Video above: Brewers fans without tickets watch through windows of American Family Field
DeLuca's strikeout came after Tampa Bay's Liam Hicks had hit into an apparent game-ending double play that was overturned after a replay review. The review determined that Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt's right foot was slightly off the bag when he caught a throw from second baseman Brice Turang.
Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run over five innings to earn the win.
Christian Yelich hit an RBI triple to spark a two-run rally in the first inning that put the Brewers ahead for good and delighted a sellout crowd reveling in Milwaukee's first World Series game since 1982. Jackson Chourio and William Contreras provided two hits each, and Contreras also threw out two potential base stealers.
Video below: Brewers superfan names his son after baseball legend, dad and son head to World Series
This marks the first World Series featuring two potential first-time champions since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league teams without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.
The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.

title: Charting Trump’s bloodlust
text:
President Trump’s bloodlust dates back at least to when he asked if the military could shoot demonstrators “in the legs” (June 2020).
Trump’s bloodlust canceled all funding and withdrew from the World Health Organization. Trump has canceled programs that were designed to help Americans. He considers these programs to be nonessential. The programs are not military-related; Trump diverts the money back into the military budget. Trump and Defense Secretary Hegseth’s military budget wants people to die in the name of national security.
Trump’s bloodlust has been demonstrated over and over again by his bombing of Iran. Trump desires the Iran war (not regime change) to continue after the midterm elections. Trump wants to demonstrate he has power to take lives without any remorse, or guilt.
“I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose any voters,” Trump said in 2016.
Trump and Hegseth explored a Dec. 3 public execution by a military firing squad. They have amply demonstrated how to inflict fear on the American public. ICE is now a working example of their “shoot to kill” motto.
“He who fights with monsters should look to it that he himself does not become a monster.” — Friedrich Nietzsche.
Paul Baresel

title: Hoping for an afternoon at the Oval Office

title: Cooper Flagg diagnosed with mild shoulder sprain
text:
DALLAS — Mavericks star Cooper Flagg will miss Saturday night’s home game against the San Antonio Spurs after an MRI revealed a mild sprain of his left shoulder suffered just before halftime of Dallas’ win at Indiana a night earlier.
Last season’s Rookie of the Year will be reevaluated next week.
Flagg, of Newport, was driving to the basket after making a steal near midcourt Friday night in the final minute of the first half. As he went up for a dunk, he was fouled from behind by Aaron Nesmith, a play that was ruled a Flagrant 1 foul. Flagg landed behind the baseline on his left shoulder and didn’t reenter the game.
Flagg was leading all scorers with 14 points in 17 minutes, along with five rebounds, six assists, three steals and a block. Dallas led 77-43 at halftime and went on to beat the Pacers 121-105.
Flagg scored 32 points in the Mavericks’ opener on Wednesday night, a 128-110 loss at Houston. Last season, he averaged 21 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists.
Saturday’s game will be the home debut of Mavericks coach Dusty May, who led Michigan to the NCAA championship last season.

title: Three Years On, Maine MILL Preserves, Curates Oct. 25 Artifacts From Bates, Lewiston
text:
In the wake of the Lewiston shooting on Oct. 25, 2023, Bates students lined campus with cards, posters, and other displays of support for the community. Three years later, some of these artifacts can be found at the Maine Museum of Innovation, Learning, and Labor (MILL).
Objects from Bates in the MILL’s Oct. 25 collection include cards made for Campus Safety employees, “Lewiston Strong” socks and a t-shirt worn by Bates athletics teams after the shooting, a banner hung on Chase Hall and maple leaves decorated with drawings of the “Hopeful” sign made by Bates students at the one-year memorial event, according to MILL Executive Director Rachel Ferrante.
“Bates is obviously an important part of Lewiston/Auburn, and so we wanted to make sure that student experience is also reflected in the collection,” Ferrante said.
As soon as the night of the shooting, Ferrante said, it became clear that the MILL could become a home for artifacts from the event. Located in Lewiston’s historic mill district, the MILL already hosted thousands of items of interest to local history.
“We care for objects every day, and so we could also care for these objects,” Ferrante said. “So that work pretty much began immediately.”
The Campus Safety cards and Chase Hall banner were donated by Harward Center Associate Director of Community-Engaged Research and Learning Morgan Kinney, Ferrante said, while the Hopeful leaves were given directly by the students who made them.
Eighteen people were killed and three were injured in the Oct. 25 mass shooting between two locations, Just-In-Time Recreation and Schemengees Bar and Grille. The deadliest shooting in Maine history, Oct. 25 saw the most people murdered in a single mass shooting in the U.S. in 2023.
“Unfortunately, Oct. 25 was a really important part of Lewiston’s history, and so collecting these objects is a reminder of not only what happened that night, but also how the community comes together and remembers and tries to heal and move forward,” Ferrante said.
An extensive manhunt following the shooting on the evening of Oct. 25 had residents in Lewiston and surrounding towns, including Bates students and other community members, sheltering in place while law enforcement searched for the shooter, who was later found dead.
After lockdowns lifted, community members quickly came together to build makeshift memorials at the sites of the shooting and in downtown Lewiston. People left flowers, photos, trinkets, and carved pumpkins, because the shooting was just days before Halloween. Because of the sheer volume of artifacts collected and curated by the MILL, Ferrante said she does not have a favorite.
“The collective of having all of them, it just really shows how the community was coming together and all trying to support each other in myriad ways,” she said. “Whether that was writing letters or as part of the sports that you’re already a part of, or something artistic, or a sign that you see on your everyday walk. For me, it’s the taken as a whole that’s really powerful about them.”
This year for the third anniversary, the MILL has created and displayed replicas of pumpkins left by mourners outside Just-In-Time. Previous annual exhibits have included art made from the 261 flower bouquet sleeves left at the memorials and from bowling balls and pool balls from the sites.
The pumpkins, on display until next September, are a temporary piece within a permanent exhibition at the MILL. The museum has a memorial room, the October 25th Memorial Archive which features the doors from Just-In-Time and a light fixture from Schemengees with bullet holes. The collection continues to grow, as Ferrante said staff from Lewiston High School recently donated more items.
“With a little time and distance from the event, I think it’s become even clearer why we need to save these objects,” Ferrante said. “I appreciate working with the various artists we’ve worked with over the last three years who help figure out ways to interpret, use, and interpret the memorial collection in important and impactful ways.”
The shooting is a sobering piece of Lewiston history, but Ferrante said that the MILL’s exhibit has been valuable for the community.
“People are really grateful that the museum has done this work in preserving the objects and in having a physical space that is about this horrible but important part of Lewiston’s history,” Ferrante said. She says while each visitor is moved in a different way, “I, at a minimum, hope it can be a space for remembrance and quiet reflection.”

title: The sunshine parade continues through most of next week
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The stunning stretch of fall weather we have been in will continue through almost all of next week. High pressure will continue to control the pattern over the state and the pattern of comfortable days and cooler nights will continue for the foreseeable future. Lows will be chilly overnight, with most nights into the 20s but highs will get close to 60 at least through the weekend and early next week. A weak cold front will pass through the state Monday brining down temps but likely won’t bring any rain with it.
Today: Sunny and comfortable
Highs will reach into the 50s for most and few if any clouds will be visible. Overall another top notch fall day. Winds will be light.
Tonight: Usual chilliness and clear
Temps will be seasonably chilly with lows dropping close to or into the 20s for most inland with 30s along the coast. Winds will be light.
Sunday: A few degrees warmer, still clear skies.
Another flawless late October day. We may reach up into the 60s for some with everyone else still in the 50s. Winds will again be quite light.
Sunday night: A few clouds and a couple degrees warmer
Fewer areas may see the 20s on Sunday night with more areas likely staying in the 30s. A few clouds may also drift by, though nothing of major note.
Monday and beyond: The beat goes on with clear days and chilly nights
There is little if any precip on the horizon here in Maine which does not help our drought conditions but my goodness is this a stellar stretch of sun filled fall weather. If you have the chance to be outside this week take advantage because weeks like this aren’t exactly typical once we get into the true winter season on its way.
Saturday: Sunny with highs in the 50s. Winds light.
Saturday night: Clear with lows in the 20s and 30s. Winds light.
Sunday: Sunny with highs in the 50s and 60s. Winds light.
Sunday night: Mainly clear with lows in the 20s and 30s. Winds light.
Monday: Mainly sunny after a few early clouds with highs in the 50s. Winds light.

title: Justice Department to send monitors to polls in Portland, Lewiston
Husband receives prison sentence, culminating family’s years-long fight after wife’s AIDS death
text:
CONYERS, Ga. (ANF/Gray News) - A Conyers man accused of spreading HIV to multiple women — one of whom later died — will avoid trial on murder charges after pleading guilty to three counts of reckless conduct.
Cleveland Broadie was sentenced Oct. 7, 2026, to 15 years in prison, with possible release after eight years. If released, he must stay out of Rockdale County; have no contact with victims’ families; share medical records with probation; and stay on HIV medication.
One of Cleveland Broadie’s victims was his wife Denise Broadie, who died April 2, 2022, from pneumonia and respiratory failure “due to Human Immunodeficiency Virus-Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome,” according to her death certificate. They’d been been married since 2014.
Denise Broadie didn’t learn she had HIV - which progressed to AIDS - until shortly before her death. Doctors said it went undiagnosed and untreated for years. Denise had been in and out of the hospital fighting cancer so her family never thought her struggles could be coming from an additional illness. They didn’t discover until it was too late.
Denise Broadie’s daughters, Karen Young and Tammy Hammonds, alleged their mother had not been active sexually with anyone else. (NOTE: Cleveland Broadie is not related to Denise Broadie’s daughters.)
“Our main goal was to hold him accountable and we’ve done that,” Tammy Hammonds said after the plea deal.
“We’re satisfied that we have some justice,” Young said.
Atlanta News First Investigates first reported on the case in 2023, and Hammonds and Young believe the media attention led to a police investigation.
“Had it not been for [Atlanta News First Investigates], we would not be in this position,” Young said. “We fought tooth and nail trying to get attention and get police to investigate.”
The Rockdale County Sheriff’s Office eventually arrested Cleveland Broadie for reckless conduct-HIV infected person. The warrant said he knew his HIV status since 2006 but did not tell his wife, Denise Broadie.
The case grew at two other women came forward saying Cleveland Broadie did not disclose his status prior to unprotected sex.
Cleveland Broadie was eventually indicted on five charges: malice murder, felony murder, and three counts of reckless conduct.
In a May 2025 hearing, Rockdale County prosecutors argued Cleveland Broadie intentionally hid his diagnosis; was not regularly taking medication; and had unprotected sex with his wife as well as other women.
His defense attorney argued he had disclosed his status to his wife in writing before they married, a claim Denise Broadie’s family disputed.
The plea deal brought Hammonds and Young peace.
“It’s better for our mental health [and] our wellbeing to accept an outcome, because no amount of time was going to be sufficient enough for our mother’s loss of life,” Hammonds said.
“We’ve been through a lot and we’re ready to move on in life and mourn our mother, which we haven’t had a chance to do and enjoy life like she would’ve wanted us to.” Young said. “I think she’s proud we saw it through and got justice for her and the other victims.”

title: Trump says he called Google to rename the Atlantic Ocean. Here’s how they responded
text:
(Gray News) - President Donald Trump said he called Google CEO Sundar Pichai and asked to rename the Atlantic Ocean.
Trump, who made the remarks at a South Carolina rally for U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, said he told Pichai that Google was “really great with the lake,” referencing when Google Maps relabeled the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
“I only like two oceans: The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. I’m not going to put either Trump or America on any other ocean but these two,” he said. “I said: ‘Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean.’”
Trump said Pichai told him, “No, no, no. This time I’m not doing it. Oceans are different, sir. They cover a lot of countries. Please don’t ask us to do that.”
Trump told the crowd, “I’ll probably pass.”
“I think let’s keep it the Atlantic Ocean,” he said.
Trump also talked about how he signed executive orders to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America and the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
He told the crowd that he has been looking for a river to rename, possibly the Hudson River or Mississippi River.

title: Six Flags says it will install seat belts on Georgia roller coaster after rider’s death
text:
(AP) - The chief executive of Six Flags says the company will install seat belts on the Georgia roller coaster from which a rider fell to his death earlier this month. The company’s rides with similar restraints will also get the safety upgrade.
The theme park operator announced the extra safeguard less than two weeks after 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta died after being ejected from his seat on the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia.
“We are reinforcing safety precautions at our parks and taking additional measures, including adding seat belts on Goliath and other coasters with a similar restraint,” John Reilly, president and CEO of Six Flags Entertainment Corporation, said in a statement Friday.
Goliath remains shut down while state and local officials investigate the Oct. 12 death.
Reilly didn’t specify which other Six Flags coasters will get seat belts. But it has temporarily closed eight additional roller coasters at five other parks in the U.S. and Canada. Those rides all share the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system.
Six Flags hasn’t said when those coasters are expected to reopen. Reilly’s statement said Six Flags has enlisted independent engineers and inspectors to review safety procedures for all rides at its theme parks.
Investigators haven’t said what went wrong on the Georgia coaster. Witnesses said they saw Kariem rise up out of his seat and fall headfirst back into the cart before being ejected. Some people who rode Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints.
All nine of the Six Flags coasters taken offline were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard. They also feature similar clamshell restraints that sit at the top of a vertical bar between each rider’s knees. The bar locks a padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.
The U.S. patent granted to Bolliger & Mabillard for the restraint system in 2001 says it’s designed to make each rider feel “that he is seated on a flying carpet or that he is at the controls of a kind of flying scooter, while still guaranteeing optimum security.”
Following the death in Georgia, non-Six Flags theme parks SeaWorld Orlando in Florida and La Ronde in Montreal, Canada, also temporarily closed one roller coaster apiece that use clamshell restraints.
SeaWorld reopened its Mako coaster Tuesday after it had been offline for a week. The Associated Press emailed the company Saturday asking if seat belts or other safety upgrades were planned for the coaster.
The AP also emailed a spokesperson for La Ronde seeking an update on its shuttered coaster.
In addition to Goliath in Georgia, eight coasters remain closed at Six Flags parks in Gurnee, Illinois; Jackson Township, New Jersey; Charlotte, North Carolina; Mason, Ohio; and Vaughan, Ontario.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia.
