title: Catherine Breed completes 900-mile swim as first to swim California’s entire coast
text:
Catherine Breed completes 900-mile swim as first to swim California’s entire coast
Catherine Breed, Mill Valley, Calif., resident, has finished her roughly 900-mile swim of California’s entire coast. To achieve this unprecedented feat, the 33-year-old swam through open water for about five to eight hours per day — and faced an unexpected foe.
Related video: Shows Catherine when she reached the Monterey Bay and spoke with KSBW 8
Since starting at the Oregon border in July, Breed experienced this year’s historic El Niño changing the Pacific Ocean in real time. She shared what she witnessed and how El Niño complicated her team’s journey with SFGATE on Saturday afternoon, two days before her ceremonial finish.
In this conversation, Breed voiced concern about a surprising current, which seemingly flowed north as she attempted to travel south. Josh Willis, a senior research scientist for NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, told SFGATE that El Niño has not changed the far offshore California Current, which flows north to south, but he had another theory. “Near shore, there is a small coastal jet that also goes from north to south most summers, driven really by the upwelling and the winds near shore,” Willis wrote via email. “But during an El Niño year, those upwelling winds tend to reverse and the coastal jet can stop or reverse as well. This is probably what Catherine was experiencing.”
This interview was edited for length and clarity.
SFGATE: What happened on your swim today?
Catherine Breed: I swam from Point Loma to Mission Bay, which was about 8 miles. When we were coming back into the San Diego harbor, there was so much trash — like more than I’ve seen the entire trip. There were a lot of plastic bags.
Breed: The Tijuana River is a global, national and California crisis. Essentially, raw sewage comes out of the river and spills into the ocean. The pollution zone is about 1.5 miles offshore, so I’ll be finishing around 3 miles offshore, crossing the border at sea. That’s why no one’s gonna see me finish. The strategy for avoiding the pollution crisis is to 1) avoid, and 2) I’ve started taking prophylactic antibiotics at the guidance of my medical team. Thank goodness it’s at the end.
SFGATE: How are you feeling so close to the end?
Breed: Physically and emotionally, I feel great. We had a really fun day in the ocean today. My body’s holding up great. I think, mentally, I am ready to be done. I’m ready to be home. I’m a little overwhelmed at some of the attention that’s going to come from the finish.
SFGATE: What should Californians know about your observations underwater?
Breed: I want to underscore how challenging this was during the super El Niño. I picked this year out in 2023, and I had no crystal ball saying it would be a super El Niño. It really forced us to work with Mother Nature every single day. It proved extremely challenging for the swim … My message to people would be to get involved in local ocean conservation to understand what’s happening in your backyard. I do believe that this year is an alarm for us.
SFGATE: What signs of El Niño did you notice?
Breed: We’ve definitely been feeling the warmer water. We started noticing that all the way up in San Francisco, where it was warmer than it typically has been in other years. The fact that there was so much activity, in the form of hurricanes and tropical storms in the Pacific, was also very noticeable. We were in Hurricane Rachel, and we definitely got swell from the other storms. Having a lot of big swell from the west or the south made it difficult to anchor at times.
The other thing we’ve noticed is the shifting current. It seems to be going in the opposite direction than it typically does, but I need to do some research on that … The current plus the hurricanes and tropical storms meant that I had to reverse direction sometimes. Instead of all my [segments] swimming north to south, I did some segments where I swam south to north. That doubles our time in the ocean. It doubles transit time. It forces us to really think about our day in a very strategic way.
SFGATE: What kinds of marine life did you see?
Breed: We saw a lot of manta rays, which I thought was pretty unique. We saw them as far north as Malibu. They are a tropical species, so having them this far up north was interesting. We definitely saw tuna and marlin. We also saw many sea lions affected by domoic acid in Monterey.
And there were lots and lots and lots of whales — in the hundreds. I had a whale swim underneath me in Humboldt County, and then I had dolphins swim right near me in Mendocino. Bottlenose dolphins in Santa Barbara played with me for like 10 minutes, which was so amazing. Up around Morro Bay on the Central Coast, a baby humpback and a mother humpback swam within like 15 to 20 feet of me, and that was probably the coolest experience of my life.
We were seeing like 10 to 20 whales per day. And then, all of a sudden in the Santa Barbara area, we didn’t see any whales anymore. That could also be because it was warm.
SFGATE: And the shark sightings?!
Breed: They’re pretty uneventful. The crew is always looking out, and I’m swimming very close to the boat. If the crew sees a fin, they just tell me, “Cat, shark!” I hop out within about 5 seconds. If we see it again, we evaluated whether we should get back in the water or just be done for the day. One day, we did make the call to be done. But most of the time, I resume my swim, and that’s it.
SFGATE: After this incredible accomplishment, what’s next for you?
Breed: I’m going to a wedding in Central America, so I’m gonna go enjoy a little vacation. And then I will really just focus on my next step in life professionally. I want to see how I can use this swim to share a story that inspires not only ocean conservation but also more people to go after big goals and push themselves.

title: George Stevens runner pulls off big upset at North cross country regionals
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
BELFAST — Shock, pain and disbelief. There was an outpouring of multiple emotions as George Stevens Academy’s Ripley King-Ofsiany crossed the finish line Saturday at Troy Howard Middle School.
The junior had never in her life won a cross country race. What better time then Saturday, as King-Ofsiany crossed the finish line in 20 minutes, 43.77 seconds to win the Class C girls race at the Northern Maine championships.
“I’m so happy,” said King-Ofsiany, who was still crying tears of joy 10 minutes after her win. “It’s just something I’ve really been working for. I can’t believe the first race I’ve won was Northerns. I’m just so proud of myself.”
Caribou’s Emma Graves (Class B, 18:44.40) and Hampden Academy’s Addison Elliott (19:21.39) won the other girls races at Troy Howard. Pierce Gorneault of Caribou (Class B, 16:01.03), Brady Cox of Orono (Class C, 16:48.44) and Sam Bergmark of Bangor (Class A, 15:51.07) won the boys races.
The Caribou boys (61 points) and Mount Desert Island girls (40 points) were Class B team champions, and the Houlton/Greater Houlton Christian Academy boys (26) and GSA girls (46) won in Class C. The Hampden Academy boys (63) and girls (27) swept Class A.
Gorneault, a sophomore, easily defended his Class B regional title. His time was the best in a B North boys race since Medomak Valley’s Connor Daigle (15:53.52) in 2021. Daigle’s younger brother, Colby, was runner-up to Gorneault in 16:53.72.
A third-place finish from Tewolde Stewart (16:59.73) and a fourth from Peyton Gorneault (17:12.04) helped power the Caribou boys to victory over John Bapst (83 points) and Presque Isle (83, lost tiebreaker). Paxton Darrell (17:15.20) of Presque Isle rounded out the top five.
“I wish I could have shaved off one second (to finish sub-16), but I feel good about it,” Pierce Gorneault said. “I’m really happy with how my teammates performed, and I hope to see them grow in the future even more.”
Caribou’s success continued in the girls race, with Graves beating out MDI’s Kulani Granholm (18:54.88). The Vikings (84 points) placed third behind MDI, which claimed its seventh consecutive B North championship by beating out Presque Isle (64 points).
“I had hoped (I could beat Granholm) because I had beaten her or gotten close to her at some of the other meets,” Graves said. “The weather was great, and the course was in good condition. … Our team did really good; one of my teammates (Isabella Albert) got a PR.”
Cox was followed in the Class C boys race by a quartet of Houlton/GHCA runners: Malachi Witmer (16:52.80), Brayden Drake (16:59.00), Wyatt Quint (17:01.89) and Logan Witmer (17:13.72). That helped the Shiretowners beat GSA (48 points) and Orono (71) for the team title.
Then came King-Ofsiany’s win in the C girls race. King-Ofsiany finished fourth to Orono’s Ellie Arsenault and Ruby Beane and teammate Paige Carter a week earlier at the Penobscot Valley Conference championships. This time, she finished ahead of Beane (20:52.01) and Carter (21:17.19), while Arsenault dropped out because of an injury.
“I think (finishing fourth at PVCs) kind of lit a fire in me to really push harder today,” King-Ofsiany said. “I knew I could do it; I just told myself, ‘This is my race,’ and I just followed through on me. … (That belief), I think, is what made me win.”
And she helped GSA claim the team title, too. Olesya Shafarina (21:20.27) finished third for Orono, giving the Eagles and Red Riots two runners each in the top four. With the two teams pretty much even the rest of the way, GSA edged Orono by two points to dethrone the Red Riots as champs.
Bergmark defended his Northern Maine title in Class A, ahead of the Mt. Blue duo of Lucas Demarco (16:09.98) and Wyatt Oliver (16:33.25). Noah Seigh (16:55.77) of Camden Hills took fourth, while Jack Scott (17:03.38) finished fifth for champion Hampden.
Elliott’s win for the Hampden girls was her second straight North title. Elsie Mann of Camden Hills took second in 19:38.71. Isabelle Clark (19:56.99) placed fourth for the Broncos, who defended their Northern Maine crown.

title: What to know about the Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky
text:
What to know about the Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky
Key details, including how the truce will be monitored and where evacuees will go, have not been released
What to know about the Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky
Key details, including how the truce will be monitored and where evacuees will go, have not been released
A small city in southern Ukraine, cut off for months by fighting, is set to get a brief pause in the 4 1/2-year-old war so that aid can get in and residents can get out.
U.S. first lady Melania Trump brokered the localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine around Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city she said is "on the brink of disaster."
Related video above: Trump temporarily waives Russia sanctions as part of negotiating tactic in Ukraine war
Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached the deal Friday. Officials on all sides have confirmed it, but many details have not been released.
Oleshky has been without power, heat or water
Oleshky is located in Ukraine's partially occupied Kherson region. It sits on the Dnipro River, which separates Ukrainian forces from the city's Russian occupiers. Moscow's forces captured it on the first day of the full-scale invasion in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned.
In June 2023, floodwaters swamped the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed in an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Once home to about 24,000 people, the city has had scarce food and medical supplies for months. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads out of town are mined and lined with burned-out cars, and drones buzz overhead. With another harsh winter approaching, those still there face death from hunger or disease.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. As the occupying power, Russia is obligated under international law to make sure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Ceasefire, aid, then evacuations
The deal sets out three stages: a ceasefire, then delivery of humanitarian aid, then evacuation of civilians who want to leave Oleshky, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman and its chief negotiator in the talks.
Before any aid moves, mines will be cleared on the routes into the city, Lubinets said.
Russia's human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, who took part in the negotiations, said firstly they plan to establish what residents need and then deliver food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials. She said anyone who wants to leave the combat zone will be guaranteed safe passage.
The pause begins Tuesday and will last several days
Lubinets told the AP that the ceasefire will begin Tuesday, two days before the humanitarian mission starts, and will last several days.
Russia's chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces "will cease fire on the Kherson axis" from 4 a.m. Tuesday Moscow time, which is late Monday in the United States. He said Russian forces would also carry out "engineering reconnaissance" and ensure the "humanitarian convoy" can move safely into the city.
Ukraine's General Staff said the ceasefire will begin at 3 a.m. Tuesday Kyiv time, since Ukraine moves its clocks back an hour on Sunday while Russia does not.
Lubinets said the pause would apply across the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation.
Key details have not been released
Lubinets gave no details on how the ceasefire or the aid mission would be monitored or carried out, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. He declined to say whether Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said people who want to leave Oleshky will be able to. He would not say whether they would be taken to Russian- or Ukrainian-held territory. Asked how long the evacuation would last, he said only that it would most likely take several days.
"The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement," Lubinets said.
The first lady took up the issue at the UN
The first lady began talks on Oleshky after she heard about the situation at one of her events during the U.N. General Assembly session in September, the White House said. She and a representative then worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to set the terms. She had already been working with officials from both countries on a separate matter.
"When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination," Lubinets said. He said the sides spent several weeks discussing ideas and developing "new approaches, mechanisms and tools" to help civilians there survive.
Helping children in conflict zones has become one of her signature issues during her husband's second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year. Last year she wrote to Russian President Vladimir Putin about efforts to reunite families with children she described as "displaced by the war." Her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, says she has helped reunite nearly three dozen children.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has lobbied various world leaders for help reuniting children he says were taken by Russia after the invasion began in 2022. The International Criminal Court in 2023 issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv are rising
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine's government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with President Donald Trump and other top U.S. officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel fuel and pushed Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the ceasefire in Oleshky during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank, on Friday. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold.
He also spoke of the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.

title: Hearts of Pine end 2026 with a fond farewell
text:
PORTLAND — Before their season-ending match Saturday, the Portland Hearts of Pine and their fervent fans thanked retiring captain Mikey Lopez for his contributions to the second-year franchise.
Then, on balky knees and in the final game of a 14-year professional career, the 33-year-old Lopez thanked them back in storybook fashion.
In the 53rd minute, Lopez banged in the rebound of his own penalty kick to give Portland the lead. It proved to be the winner in Portland’s 4-1 victory against the USL League One regular-season champions, the Charlotte Independence, at Fitzpatrick Stadium.
Lopez started the play that led to the PK. He intercepted a pass near midfield and fed the ball ahead. Walter Verala won the ball and worked hard to get past a defender, then was taken down in the penalty box by Charlotte keeper George Tasouris.
“I don’t think anyone could have written this,” Lopez said. “It was the best night possible. Getting the 4-1 victory. Getting on the scoresheet. Having my family here and being able to play my final game with (Hearts head coach) Bobby (Murphy). It truly is a storybook ending.”
Lopez was subbed out after his goal to another round of appreciative applause.
Unlike 12 previous times in the 2026 season, Portland did not give up the lead.
Instead, the Hearts tacked on. Diogo Barbosa scored in the 82nd minute. Aboubacar Camara’s second of the game in the 90th minute was his 10th in league play in his rookie season (11th overall).
It was a sweet ending to a tough 8-14-10 season and a reward for the 6,400-strong crowd who savored the Hearts’ sixth league win against seven losses and three ties at Fitzpatrick.
When the match was over, Murphy and Lopez thanked the fans over the public address system.
“From the bottom of my heart, I’m so thankful for you guys, for the love and appreciation that you have shown not only to me but to the rest of the guys all year,” Lopez said. “We certainly at times did not deserve it, but we are extremely appreciative and thankful.”
Lopez first played for Murphy when he was 12. That’s when the kid from Mission, Texas, left home for soccer for the first time, attending St. Stephens Academy, a soccer academy in Austin, Texas, run by Murphy. Lopez stayed there for the next five years before going to the University of North Carolina, where he helped the Tar Heels win the 2011 NCAA championship.
From there, Lopez was a first-round MLS draft pick and played in the top U.S. league for five seasons (2013-17). When Murphy asked him to join Portland in 2025, Lopez was coming off double Achilles surgery and had not played since 2023.
“Mikey’s family to me,” Murphy said. “I’m really grateful that he got to end his career in a place like this, and not so many other clubs that wouldn’t have been able to accurately congratulate him on a career.”
As a defensive midfielder, Lopez has never been a goal scorer. His Saturday night strike was just his 13th professional goal, and second with the Hearts.
Lopez said “he was down with it,” to take the penalty kick but admitted he got nervous standing on the spot. His low shot was not particularly well struck. Tasouris made a modest dive to his right and blocked it. But the keeper did not control it, and by rule, the ball is live. Lopez got to it first and banged it home, setting off a joyous team-wide celebration.
“We were joking, Who had Mikey Lopez for the winner on Kalshi?” Murphy said. “He didn’t want the penalty, he doesn’t like them, got bullied into it, but if he was ever going to score a penalty, it was going to be that way. It sort of sums Mikey up in a nutshell.”
Before the game, as fans chanted, “Thank you, Mik-EE!” Lopez was presented with a framed Hearts of Pine game jersey while surrounded by nearly two dozen family members, including his wife, Elena, his parents, brother, grandmother and various aunts and uncles. After a pause for photos, Lopez acknowledged the fans in each section, eliciting more chants of appreciation.
Lopez started the match and was very active. His quick accurate passes, crunching tackles and wise positioning demonstrated the talents that, while slowed, made him good enough to play in MLS for five years and were vital to the Hearts when they advanced to the USL1 semifinals in 2025.
Lopez has never shied from trying to dislodge the ball. He did that multiple times, including in the 24th minute when he drew his 18th yellow card in 54 games with Portland and 88th in his 286-match pro career.
“Like my brother said, it’s not a Mikey Lopez game if I don’t get a yellow card,” Lopez said with a grin.
But his final season has been tough. He’s had two knee surgeries and missed 15 of Portland’s 32 league games.
At Thursday’s training session, Lopez was clearly limping as he walked from physical training to the team locker room, unable to fully straighten his right knee.
Lopez admitted he had pregame doubts about how long and well he’d be able to play.
“My knee felt a little swollen and it felt like I couldn’t move it as smoothly and fluidly,” Lopez said. “But I guess just adrenaline took over and I said, ‘I’m not going to come off early and I going to try to come off in the 55th, and it was pretty close.
“I can’t explain it. Everything was pretty much just written. Some really good writer upstairs wrote something amazing and this is the perfect way to end it.”

title: Rare bird in Maine sparks frenzy, echoes past birding crazes
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Stop the presses. A grey heron has been identified in Cape Elizabeth. Hundreds of birders have already rushed to view it in its adopted farm field. If it lingers, more people will go.
The grey heron is strikingly similar to our great blue heron. They are common and widespread throughout Europe, Asia and Africa, but very rarely seen in North America.
That makes sense. The Atlantic Ocean is a nearly insurmountable barrier. Birds that swim might make the jump. Northern birds occasionally leapfrog from Europe to Iceland to Greenland to Newfoundland. It’s exceedingly rare for a wading bird to make the crossing. One exhausted grey heron found its way to Canada in 2018 by landing on a ship 200 miles east of Newfoundland. This new grey heron is the first recorded visitor to Maine.
Or should I say, “gray” heron. I looked it up on eBird, and apparently we spell it correctly over here. The Brits incorrectly spell it “grey.” But then, the Brits also say the bird’s “colour” is grey. And the Brits also misspell “common loon” as “great northern diver.” Spelling is hard.
Let me be frank. I probably would have misidentified this gray heron. I would have passed it off as a slightly odd great blue heron, and thought nothing further about it. According to Maine Audubon, here’s how to recognize one of the rarest birds ever seen in Maine.
“Gray Herons have clean white on the wrist and thigh, where these feathers are rufous on Great Blue Herons. In flight, the white wrists are often described as looking like bright headlights on the bird. The neck pattern is also fairly distinctive, with more contrast on young Grays than you see in Great Blues. Proportionately Gray Herons are also smaller, with shorter legs (in flight the feet barely stick out beyond the tail, while you see more of the legs [the tarsus] on a Great Blue Heron), and a smaller bill that is not as “heavy” or long as on a typical Great Blue Heron.”
We’ll see what happens next. In 2018, a great black hawk astonished birders by showing up in Portland’s Deering Oaks Park. This tropical hawk held on for several months before finally succumbing to Maine’s frigid winter. It became so famous, Portland erected a statue in the park, commemorating the visit. The dead bird’s carcass was mounted, and it’s on display in the Maine State Museum.
People still talk about the Steller’s sea-eagle that first appeared in Maine’s mid-coast on December 30, 2021. This wayward raptor left its Siberian home range and wandered across the Bering Sea to Alaska, then down to Texas, and finally here. That bird is still alive, and living permanently in Newfoundland. It’s made a lot of money for the professional bird guides in the area.
I’m racking my brain, trying to think of what might be the fourth rarest bird seen in Maine. Candidates could include the tufted puffin that has been showing up along the Maine coast for the last several summers. That’s a species native to the Pacific Northwest. Its appearance in Maine is further evidence that the planet is warming. Arctic sea ice is not quite the barrier it used to be.
Melting sea ice also likely facilitated the passage of a yellow-billed loon that showed up in Portland Harbor in 2010. That’s another bird with a range limited to the arctic regions of the northwest. The last yellow-billed loon I laid eyes on was in Seward, Alaska.
At least the puffin and loon live on this continent. A little egret that wandered into Maine in the spring of 2011 doesn’t. This Eurasian bird spent several summers around Scarborough Marsh. Ironically, it was on Maine Audubon property when I stopped by to see it.
Little egrets bear a close resemblance to the snowy egrets found on this continent. They can interbreed, and as I recall, this one did. Every summer since then, hybrid egrets have been reported in the marsh.
I am in awe of the people who first identified these very rare birds. Admittedly, nothing else looks like a Steller’s sea-eagle. It’s hard to misidentify a bird so big it could swallow a bald eagle whole. But the other rarities resemble species normally found in Maine. It takes a keen observer, likely someone with birding experience on the other side of the Atlantic, to recognize some of these interlopers. I’m not one of those people. I would have screwed it up.

title: Fraternity suspended until 2030 after hazing investigation
text:
TUSCALOOSA, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - A University of Alabama fraternity has been suspended for nearly four years.
According to a report on the university’s End Hazing website, Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc.’s Eta Chi chapter will not be recognized by the university through May 2030.
The report cites an investigation that found seven people hazed new members,
The report continued, stating that members were subjected to verbal and physical abuse, which included forcing or coercing the members into participating in acts of personal servitude, physical discomfort, illegal activities and degrading activities.
The report claimed these activities led to some members being hurt while alleging new members were denied privileges and provided alcohol and drugs.
The incident was said to have occurred off campus in September 2025 and was reported through an anti-hazing hotline nearly a month later.
The report noted an investigation was resolved in May. No arrests were made.
The University of Alabama and Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc.’s national headquarters did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the situation.

title: No Kings draws another significant crowd
Officer fired, under investigation after allegedly helping son charged in double murder
text:
MANNING, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - A police officer in South Carolina has been fired after allegedly helping his son, who is charged in a double murder investigation.
Alexander Dukes Sr.’s son, Antwone Dukes, 22, was arrested on Oct. 6 and charged in the deaths of two men stemming from a shooting in a Dollar General parking lot.
Antwone Dukes was also shot, which Sumter County deputies believe was the result of a planned armed robbery.
Sumter County authorities said during the robbery investigation it was discovered that Antwone Dukes drove himself and another gunshot victim, 19-year-old Derek Parson, to his father’s home.
Alexander Dukes, a former Sumter County sheriff’s deputy who had since taken a position with the Manning Police Department, reportedly put a tourniquet on his son’s leg and told him to go to the hospital.
However, authorities said Alexander Dukes did not call 911, report the shooting, or request an ambulance.
Parson ended up dying at the hospital.
Keywaun Clark, 20, was also shot in the suspected robbery and died after crashing his vehicle into a tree near the parking lot, police said.
Filings submitted to the academy stated an investigation by the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division additionally revealed incriminating text messages on Alexander Dukes phone regarding communication with his children.
“From that phone search, texts were found where officer Alexander Dukes Sr. was informing his children that he could no longer notify them of police activity such as roadblocks and traffic stops due to Sumter County encrypting their radio channel,” part of the documents read.
Alexander Dukes failed a polygraph exam as part of the investigation, officials said, and was suspended on Oct. 8.
Authorities said Alexander Dukes has since been terminated from the Manning Police Department, stating that his actions may have hindered a criminal investigation and possibly delayed care that would have saved Parson’s life.
In the termination filing, Manning police said Alexander Dukes “failed his duty and acted in a manner unbecoming of a police officer.”
As of Friday evening, Alexander Dukes was not criminally charged in the case, but the investigation remains ongoing.
Meanwhile, Antwone Dukes remained jailed at the Sumter County Sheriff’s Office Detention Center. He was denied bond after his arrest.

title: Obituary: Jeffrey Alan Brooks
text:
TOPSHAM – Ret. Navy Lt. Jeffrey Alan Brooks, 61, died Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.
He was born on Dec. 10, 1964, in Lancaster, N.H., a son of John and Gloria King Brooks. He attended Lancaster schools and was a graduate of University of Phoenix. He married Rebecca Dawson Aug. 13, 1994 in San Diego, Calif.
Jeff was a decorated U.S. Navy officer having served deployments to the Persian Gulf through Operation Desert Storm and Operation Desert Shield. He was a member of the American Legion, Post 202, Topsham. He was a member of St. John the Baptist Catholic Church, Brunswick.
Jeff was a volunteer with the Brunswick/Topsham Land Trust. He also coached at the Maine Special Olympics and for Highlander Adaptive Hockey Program.
He is predeceased by a sister, Amy Brooks; a daughter, Shiloh Brooks.
He is survived by his wife, Rebecca Brooks of Topsham; a son, Dawson Brooks of Topsham; a daughter Reyann Brooks of Topsham; a brother, John Brooks of Salley, S.C.; two sisters, Lynette Westcott of Lancaster, N.H., Angela Brooks-Kenison of Lancaster, N.H.
Friends and family are invited to visit from 5-8 p.m., Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, at the Brackett Funeral Home, 29 Federal Street, Brunswick. A Mass of Christian burial will be celebrated 3:30 p.m., Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, at St. John the Baptist Catholic Church, 39 Pleasant Street, Brunswick.
Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.
Memorial contributions are encouraged to the America’s Wounded Warrior Foundation (www.americaswoundedwarriors.org).

title: Woman settles with Maine State Police after lawsuit alleges excessive force
text:
The Bangor Daily News was the first to report this story. What you’re reading here would likely not be made public without the efforts of professional journalists asking questions, interviewing sources and obtaining documents.
A Maine woman who alleged she was the victim of excessive force during a March 2024 arrest reached a settlement with two Maine State Police troopers.
Marie Searles, of Chelsea, sued Maine State Police trooper Hunter Belanger, alleging she was unlawfully arrested by him, during which she was slammed onto the hood of a cruiser, causing bruised ribs.
The lawsuit, filed October 2025 in U.S. District Court of Maine in Bangor, also alleged there was a culture within Maine State Police that allows excessive force and unreasonable arrests. It also named Lt. Aaron Turcotte and said he failed to supervise and discipline Belanger.
Searles will receive $54,000 in the settlement for “alleged physical injuries and emotional distress,” according to the document obtained by the Bangor Daily News through a Freedom of Access Act request.
No one admitted liability in the settlement, according to the agreement signed Oct. 13. It was signed by Assistant Attorney General William Hagedorn on behalf of Belanger and Turcotte.
“Marie stood up to the Maine State Police and shined a much-needed light on its use of force practices,” her attorney Matthew Morgan said. “She is ready to move on from the suit and is happy to have reached this settlement.”
Turcotte, a spokesperson for Maine State Police, did not respond to a request for comment.
A dismissal of the lawsuit must be filed by Nov. 2.
Belanger had been previously accused of excessive force only two months before his interaction with Searles. The lawsuit alleged Maine State Police have a long-standing practice of not properly investigating cases of excessive force.
Another lawsuit alleging excessive force by state police is still pending. Justin Savage was arrested six days after Searles and his violent arrest was captured in dashcam footage.
It shows troopers tackling him to the ground and punching him in the face while he was handcuffed. That arrest and subsequent fall out was the subject of an award-winning series written by the BDN and the Maine Monitor.
Savage’s complaint was one of 33 excessive force complaints the agency received over the previous decade, none of which were sustained, an investigation by the media outlets found. Searles’ lawsuit cites that record as evidence that the agency has “created a culture of tacit approval of excessive force.”
Searles’ arrest came after Belanger responded to a vehicle stuck in the mud on Marie Lane in the Kennebec County town of Chelsea on March 10, 2024. A man wanted on multiple warrants lived at the address, and other homes used the same driveway, according to the lawsuit.
Searles was walking outside near Belanger’s cruiser when he asked her to speak with him and she walked away, the lawsuit said.
Belanger then “grabbed ahold of Searles, flipped her body up into the air, and slammed her body onto the ground,” the lawsuit said. He then pinned her neck to the ground with his knee, causing pain and bruising.
Searles was arrested for refusing to submit to arrest and Belanger then searched her body while she was at the front of the cruiser, according to the lawsuit. She tensed up and pulled away when Belanger was pat searching her.
“Belanger responded by grabbing Searles by her shoulders and slamming her body onto the hood of his cruiser,” the lawsuit said. “Searles’ ribs were slammed into the front of Trooper Belanger’s cruiser resulting in significant pain and bruising.”
Shortly after Searles’ arrest, Kennebec County District Attorney Maeghan Maloney wrote a two-page letter to Maine State Police Capt. Jeff Love that called Belanger’s conduct “completely inappropriate.”
Maloney told the BDN in October 2025 that she considers the matter resolved.

title: Where the candidates in Maine stand on affordability
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: Where the candidates for office in Maine stand on affordability
Maine's Total Coverage asked viewers what issues they are most interested in learning more about heading into the midterm election.
After hundreds of submissions, one of the top issues on voters' minds is affordability. Maine's Total Coverage asked all the candidates for governor and congressional office about their stance on the issue.
Gubernatorial candidates
The race for the Blaine House began with two crowded primaries. Republican Bobby Charles was the winner of a seven-way ranked-choice voting primary and Democrat Hannah Pingree won in a five-way race. Independent Rick Bennett, who left the Republican Party last year, was the only independent who got the required number of signatures to get on the November ballot.
All three candidates have made affordability a centerpiece of their campaigns, unveiling policies to make life more affordable for Mainers.
Bennett said affordability issues all come down to the state budget, which will be one of the first things the next governor has to tackle once inaugurated. He added that lowering taxes will lower costs.
"My budget will include measures to help property taxpayers," Bennett said. "The Property Tax Fairness Credit, which was expanded recently due to some legislation that I put in, needs to take effect when the person is paying their property taxes, not as a reimbursement months later. That's why it's undersubscribed."
Charles agreed with Bennett that lowering taxes will help. He added that energy costs are also part of the problem, as well as fraud.
"We're going to go after fraud and get those costs down by maybe $500 million if you believe public reporting," Charles said. "We had an IG from HHS that came and looked at our autism program. They found $45 million in overspending, lack of oversight in those programs. I believe we can get a lot out of the waste and duplication side."
Pingree said she hears most about people struggling to find affordable housing and healthcare. But on day one, the next governor will have another affordability problem to face.
"I think we're going to be faced with a heating crisis with $6 oil," Pingree said. "Our LIHEAP [Low Income Heating Assistance] Program that helps low-income people just heat their homes for the winter, it's going to have half as much impact as last year because of the price of oil. I think we're going to have to provide immediate relief. If this war in Iran does not end, then Congress doesn't provide relief."
Senate candidates
The highly anticipated Senate race has been closely watched for months. Senator Susan Collins is seeking a historic sixth term in Washington. Democrat Troy Jackson replaced Graham Platner as the party's nominee in late July after Platner dropped out following a sexual assault allegation he denies.
The two candidates heading into November weighed in on how they want to help curb costs.
Collins said she's been using her position in the Senate to help support Mainers struggling with costs. Most recently, the Department of Energy said it will release more than 300,000 barrels of home heating oil after Collins urged them to.
"I've also worked to expand and get early release of the Low Income Home Heating Assistance Program, which I increased funding for just last year by $20 million to $4 billion," Collins said. "That is a really important program to low-income families and seniors in the state of Maine."
Collins' opponent, Jackson, says there are several ways to help voters struggling with everyday costs. For him, that means ending the war in Iran and making childcare, healthcare and prescription drugs more accessible.
"People are working harder than ever just to keep their heads above water," Jackson said. "They're cutting back, they're saving up, they're trying to take care of their families and they're still falling behind."
Candidates for Congress in Maine's 1st District
The race for Maine's 1st Congressional District is a rematch. Army veteran Ron Russell is challenging Congresswoman Chellie Pingree for her seat in Washington.
Pingree has held the congressional seat for nearly two decades. Russell ran against her back in 2024, but lost.
Russell secured the Republican nomination back in June, defeating newcomer Joshua James Pietrowicz.
Russell says costs will drop once the war in Iran is resolved. He adds that once the cost of fuel goes down, other prices all around will decline.
For his campaign this election cycle, Russell says he's pushing for the U.S. to be energy independent.
"The cost of groceries is going to go up because it costs more money to power the grocery store and to transport the goods to the grocery store," Russell said. "All of those things, those costs increase, and naturally, the cost of the commodities that are sold in the store are going to increase."
Congresswoman Pingree says lowering costs is top of mind for her if she's re-elected. Like Russell, Pingree says the cost of heating oil, diesel fuel and gas will go down once the war in Iran is over. She also says she will look at pricing tools used at the grocery store.
"I think we're going to look across the map, whether it's breaking up monopolies or helping individual farmers and doing everything we can to support the cost of food," Pingree said. "Food is also really impacted by diesel prices. Food gets transported and all those things get added into the cost."
Candidates for Congress in Maine's 2nd District
Maine's 2nd Congressional District race began when Congressman Jared Golden still planned to run for his seat.
Former two-time Republican Governor Paul LePage got in the race to take on Golden. LePage was uncontested in the primary. Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap filed paperwork to primary Golden.
Golden eventually left the race, and three other candidates got in to primary Dunlap.
Dunlap won in a four-way ranked-choice voting primary in June to take on LePage.
Affordability is an issue many Americans are hoping Congress can do something about to bring down costs when lawmakers return in January.
On affordability, Dunlap said Congress needs to "tame inflation" while also looking at things that are driving up costs, like the war in Iran, because that impacts more than just gas prices, and people who are on fixed incomes can't afford it.
"A lot of people depend on Social Security and not much else," Dunlap said. "We need to take the cap off the contribution level. So right now, instead of about $184,000, if you make $25 million a year and there are people that do, they only pay Social Security up to the $184,000 level. If you took that cap off and had them contribute their full due, not only would you secure Social Security, but you would also expand the footprint of benefits."
LePage said affordability is even more critical in the second district because most people have to travel farther distances to get to work.
"That's why I say suspend all taxes on gas and fuels and get the tax off tips and overtime," LePage said. "Give them a little bit more money to people that they have in their pockets. Here in Maine, it's $400 million a year. So if you put $400 million in the hands of 1.4 million people, everybody's going to get a little bit."

title: Charting Trump’s bloodlust
text:
President Trump’s bloodlust dates back at least to when he asked if the military could shoot demonstrators “in the legs” (June 2020).
Trump’s bloodlust canceled all funding and withdrew from the World Health Organization. Trump has canceled programs that were designed to help Americans. He considers these programs to be nonessential. The programs are not military-related; Trump diverts the money back into the military budget. Trump and Defense Secretary Hegseth’s military budget wants people to die in the name of national security.
Trump’s bloodlust has been demonstrated over and over again by his bombing of Iran. Trump desires the Iran war (not regime change) to continue after the midterm elections. Trump wants to demonstrate he has power to take lives without any remorse, or guilt.
“I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose any voters,” Trump said in 2016.
Trump and Hegseth explored a Dec. 3 public execution by a military firing squad. They have amply demonstrated how to inflict fear on the American public. ICE is now a working example of their “shoot to kill” motto.
“He who fights with monsters should look to it that he himself does not become a monster.” — Friedrich Nietzsche.

title: Bruins rally in third, stretch unbeaten streak to eight
text:
BOSTON — David Pastrnak and James Hagens scored in a 40-second span in the third period, and the Boston Bruins extended their points streak to eight games with a 6-4 victory over the San Jose Sharks on Saturday night.
Casey Mittelstadt, Marat Khusnutdinov, Fraser Minten and Will Borgen also scored for the Bruins, who have won seven of their last eight. Jeremy Swayman made 21 saves for his seventh victory.
Michael Misa, Kiefer Sherwood, Dmitry Orlov and Will Smith scored for San Jose, and Alex Nedeljkovic made 29 saves. The Sharks had won two in a row.
The game was tied at 2-2 through two periods, with the Sharks responding each time the Bruins took a one-goal lead.
San Jose grabbed its first lead of the game when Orlov fired a one-timer on the power play at 4:03 of the third. It was the third special-teams goal of the game for the Sharks, and Orlov’s second goal of the season.
Pastrnak exited the penalty box and took a feed from J.J. Peterka before firing in a shot from the right circle for his seventh goal of the season at 8:27 of the third. The goal pushed Pastrnak into a tie for third place with Patrice Bergeron on Boston all-time goal-scoring list (427).
Just 40 seconds later, Hagens put in the rebound of an Elias Lindholm shot. Minten then scored a power-play goal with 8:00 remaining to make it 5-3.

title: Man who fatally hit deputy after his son was killed by police is convicted of murder
text:
CINCINNATI (WXIX/Gray News) - A jury has found an Ohio man guilty of killing a Hamilton County deputy last year.
Rodney Hinton Jr. was found guilty of murder, reckless homicide and felonious assault for deliberately hitting and killing Deputy Larry Henderson on May 2, 2025.
He will be sentenced on Nov. 16. Prosecutors said they want Hinton to serve 15 years to life in prison.
“His family will never truly be able to fill that void, but we hope that today’s verdict brings them some sense of justice and peace,” prosecutors said.
Hamilton County Sheriff Charmaine McGuffey said the verdict gives her office some sense of closure after reliving Henderson’s death throughout the trial.
“We do believe that is an appropriate finding,” McGuffey said. “Now we can come together and hug each other and tell each other, we’re here. We have some finality.”
Two sides of the case
The jury was tasked with determining if Hinton purposefully tried to kill Henderson as he directed traffic near Burnet Woods.
The crash occurred hours after Hinton watched body camera video of his son, Ryan Hinton, 19, who was fatally shot by a Cincinnati police officer.
Hamilton County Prosecutor Connie Pillich said Rodney Hinton’s son was running from police, dropped a gun and later picked it back up. That shooting was later deemed justified.
Defense attorney Clyde Bennett argued Rodney Hinton was not aiming for the deputy.
Bennett claimed his client was suffering from acute psychotic symptoms and severe mental illness, meaning he did not understand the wrongfulness of his actions at the time.
Prosecutors said the evidence left no doubt that Hinton intentionally drove his car into Henderson.
They argued Hinton saw Henderson’s uniform, reacted to losing his son, and decided to take the life of one of their own.
Appeal to come
Bennett talked with reporters after the verdict was announced Friday.
He said he was “disappointed” in the jury’s verdict, adding he thinks the video of the crash is what sealed the murder conviction.
Bennett plans to file an appeal within 30 days of Hinton’s sentencing.
State AG responds
Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson issued a statement on the verdict:
“The senseless murder of Deputy Larry Henderson Jr. shattered a family and left a community mourning the loss of a dedicated public servant. We are thankful to the jury for its verdict, which accurately reflects the evidence in this case.
Deputy Henderson spent 33 years honorably serving his community in law enforcement. He died fulfilling his duty. His death is a painful reminder of the risks that law enforcement officers face every day while working to keep us safe. They deserve our gratitude.’

title: This surf shop in Kennebunk runs free surf lessons for moms
text:
This surf shop in Kennebunk runs free surf lessons for moms
Aquaholics is holding free surfing lessons every Tuesday and Saturday morning
This surf shop in Kennebunk runs free surf lessons for moms
Aquaholics is holding free surfing lessons every Tuesday and Saturday morning
Even deep into October, moms are coming together in Kennebunk for free surf classes being offered by Aquaholics Surf Shop.
Tuesdays and Saturdays, the group meets up as the sun rises to get out on the water at Gooch's Beach. Joseph Bohenek works at the shop; he says that about a dozen, sometimes fewer, come out every week.
It started off being called "Mom's Morning," but a new name has been floating around: "Women of the Waves." Bohenek says that's because they are flexible about the definition of mom. They can be plant moms, animal moms, or just women who really want to get out on the water.
Despite the water being 50 degrees Fahrenheit and the air temperature being even colder, the moms that take part say the wetsuits keep them plenty warm.
Melissa LeClerc is in her 60s and started taking surfing lessons a few weeks ago. She has been back for a couple of sessions, and says she enjoys spending the time with other women out on the ocean.
"It's like being eight years old. It really is. And, and you try to stand up, and if you do, that's amazing. And if you don't, you tumble into the water. And in its own way, that is kind of amazing, too."
Aquaholics has surf lessons going late into fall. Anyone interested can sign up on the surf shop's website.

The Maine Celtics selected Josh Roberts sixth overall in the NBA G League Draft on Saturday, one of three picks they made to round out their roster for the upcoming season.
Maine also selected Kaleb Lowery with the 23rd pick and Desmond Cambridge with the 37th pick.
Roberts, a 6-foot-9 power forward, was named the MAAC Defensive Player of the Year while at Manhattan College in 2023. He has played for various teams overseas the last three seasons.
Lowery played one season for the University of Nevada, averaging 4.6 points and 3.1 rebounds. Cambridge played 35 G League games last season between Santa Cruz and San Diego, averaging 6.0 points and 3.1 rebounds.
